title: Exposure-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Increases Connectivity Between the Central Executive and Salience Networks in Pediatric Anxiety
journal: J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Exposure is considered the most active element of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for pediatric anxiety. Yet many youth do not respond to CBT, and exposure is the component patients most often find difficult to tolerate. Cognitive control and its supporting neural substrates may enhance exposure efficacy by helping youth remain engaged with feared stimuli despite urges to avoid. However, little work has identified how exposure-based CBT modulates intrinsic connectivity of tripartite networks that support cognitive control (e.g., central executive [CEN], salience [SN], and default mode networks [DMN]), limiting efforts to develop strategies to improve and personalize treatment. Progress may be limited by individual variability in network connectivity in anxiety, which may obscure treatment-related effects in group-averaged analyses. This randomized clinical trial (RCT) leverages person-specific network modeling to test how exposure versus relaxation components of CBT influence resting-state connectivity of cognitive control networks in pediatric anxiety.

METHOD: Youth aged 7-18 years with an anxiety disorder (N = 100) or low/no anxiety (L/NA; N = 35) completed resting-state fMRI scans at baseline. Patients were randomized to exposure-focused CBT (EF-CBT) or relaxation mentorship training (RMT). Resting-state connectivity was reassessed following treatment (or after a commensurate interval in L/NA youth) in 112 participants. Changes in within-CEN, CEN-SN, and CEN-DMN density were examined using Group Iterative Multiple Model Estimation, which yields sparse, person-specific networks capturing both shared and individual connectivity structure.

RESULTS: At baseline, anxious youth exhibited lower density within-CEN and between CEN-DMN than L/NA youth. Treatment effects differed by intervention: EF-CBT selectively increased CEN-SN density, whereas RMT increased within-CEN density.

CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate dissociable effects of exposure and relaxation on cognitive control network organization in pediatric anxiety. These results indicate that exposure-focused CBT is uniquely associated with increased connectivity between control and salience systems, consistent with a mechanism supporting top-down control of threat-related signals during exposure. Person-specific measures of tripartite network connectivity may inform future efforts to identify candidate neural targets for optimizing and personalizing treatment.

title: Menarche and ADHD: associations between puberty, ADHD traits and mental health in female adolescents
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may be more vulnerable to cooccurring mental health challenges during puberty, and some evidence suggests that puberty impacts ADHD traits. However, pubertal influences on psychological outcomes in female adolescents with ADHD are poorly understood. We investigated how menarche relates to ADHD traits and its potential moderation of associations between ADHD status or traits and mental health.

METHODS: Analyses used Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development SM  Study data from baseline to wave 3 (N = 5,318; 100% female; baseline age M = 9.9, SD = 0.6; 52.3% non-Hispanic White). ADHD traits, internalising difficulties and externalising difficulties were measured using the Child Behavior Checklist. Bayesian generalised linear mixed models examined cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between menarche status and ADHD traits. Interactions between menarche status and ADHD status or traits as predictors of mental health outcomes were also investigated. In comparative analyses, breast development replaced menarche status.

RESULTS: ADHD traits did not differ between pre- and post-menarche adolescents in cross-sectional analyses, but post-menarche adolescents had higher ADHD traits the following year. Complete breast development (vs. not started) also predicted higher ADHD traits the next year. Interactions between menarche and ADHD status were not associated with mental health outcomes cross-sectionally or longitudinally. Positive associations between ADHD traits and mental health difficulties were marginally stronger in post-menarche adolescents. The association between higher wave 2 ADHD traits and greater wave 3 externalising difficulties was substantially stronger with more advanced breast development at wave 2.

CONCLUSIONS: Longitudinal findings provide preliminary evidence that more advanced gonadarche in early adolescence is prospectively associated with elevated ADHD trait expression in females when controlling for individual differences in ADHD trait levels. More advanced breast development may reflect physiological and psychosocial changes that could contribute to a stronger relationship between higher ADHD traits and greater subsequent externalising difficulties.

title: Hormonal effects on ADHD symptoms in adolescents across the menstrual cycle
abstract: Female-specific risk factors for ADHD in adolescence have been vastly understudied despite increased impairment and comorbidity during this period. In adults, the premenstrual phase and rapid decreases in estradiol levels are associated with increased risk for ADHD symptoms. The current project aims to evaluate the effects of day-to-day changes in estradiol and progesterone on ADHD symptoms across the menstrual cycle in adolescents. Participants were 13 adolescents aged 12 to 17 years over-recruited for ADHD. Participants collected saliva samples and completed measures of ADHD symptoms daily. Generalized additive mixed models were used to explore symptom trajectories across the menstrual cycle and examine the relationships between hormones and ADHD symptoms. Inattention and hyperactivity severity exhibited significant menstrual cycle-related variation, but average symptom trajectories across the cycle were largely flat. Significant person-specific cycle effects and individual differences in estradiol-symptom associations suggest substantial heterogeneity in menstrual cycle influence on ADHD symptoms. These findings suggest that menstrual cycle-related changes in ADHD symptoms are not characterized by a uniform pattern across adolescents and instead may reflect individual differences in hormone sensitivity. Future research should prioritize identifying distinct hormone-symptom response profiles and determine their clinical relevance for personalized ADHD management.

title: Suicide risk in first- and second-generation young migrants: a 12-month cohort study
abstract:
PURPOSE: Evidence on the impact of migration on suicidal behavior among adolescents remains limited. Particularly, there is scarce knowledge concerning clinical populations and second generations of migrants. This cohort study examined differences in clinical, psychosocial and behavioral profiles associated with suicidal behavior among non-migrant, first-generation and second-generation migrant adolescents presenting to a Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Emergency Department (ED) in Madrid.

METHODS: Adolescents aged 8-17 years (N = 1,281) presenting with suicidal ideation or behavior were identified at an index ED visit, and their electronic medical records were retrospectively reviewed over a 12-month follow-up period. Sociodemographic, clinical and psychosocial risk factors-including socioeconomic adversity, family psychiatric history, maltreatment, family conflict, victim of bullying and eating problems-were systematically recorded. Reasons for consultation, methods and severity of suicidal behavior were compared across migration groups. Cox proportional hazards regression models, including age- and sex-adjusted and two multivariable models, examined whether migration status independently predicted time to repeat suicidal behavior during follow-up.

RESULTS: Migrant adolescents-both first- and second-generation-presented with a higher burden of psychosocial adversity and more severe self-harm methods at index ED visit compared to non-migrants. Migrant adolescents, particularly first-generation, were less likely to have had prior outpatient mental health follow-up. In fully adjusted multivariable models accounting for sociodemographic, psychosocial and clinical covariates, including previous suicidal behavior, second-generation migrant background remained an independent predictor of repeat suicidal behavior, whereas first-generation background did not show a statistically significant effect.

CONCLUSIONS: Second‑generation migrant background was associated with a more severe clinical presentation and repeat suicidal behavior, even after adjusting for psychosocial and clinical covariates. These findings suggest that generational migration status is a relevant factor to consider when assessing and following up on suicide risk for adolescents of migrant origin, particularly those from a second-generation background.

title: Longitudinal trajectories of cognitive reserve in youth offspring of patients with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder and the role of obstetric complications
abstract: Cognitive reserve (CR) is a construct reflecting the brain's capacity to flexibly use neural resources to cope with pathology. This study aimed to examine the longitudinal development of CR in offspring of patients with schizophrenia (SzO) or bipolar disorder (BpO) compared to community controls (CcO), and whether a history of obstetric complications (OCs) plays a role in CR trajectories during youth. The study involved 515 datapoints (99 SzO, 205 BpO, 211 CcO) from 50 SzO, 87 BpO, and 91 CcO with assessments at different time points over a 12-year period. CR was assessed using a composite score including intelligence quotient, sociability, academic performance, and parental socioeconomic status. History of OCs was assessed and grouped according to complications during pregnancy, and complications in delivery. Although CR increased over time in all groups, levels of CR remained consistently lowest in SzO, followed by BpO A significant age-by-complications during pregnancy interaction was found in the whole sample, and in SzO and BpO, indicating reduced CR accumulation over time in those with a history of OCs. Having three or more OCs was associated with lower age-related gains in CR in the entire sample. SzO and BpO showed lower CR levels from an early age, which persisted over time, and a history of complications during pregnancy was associated with less CR accumulation. These findings highlight the impact of early-life factors on CR during youth, suggesting that early interventions in high-risk groups could help mitigate long-term complications.

title: Supportive parenting moderates the association between neural synchrony and irritability: Evidence from mother-son dyads
abstract: While research on parent-child neural synchrony using fNIRS hyperscanning has expanded, its association with child psychopathology, especially transdiagnostic symptoms such as irritability, remains poorly understood. Moreover, no prior studies have explored the potential contextual factors that may moderate the link between parent-child neural synchrony and children's irritability. The present study therefore investigated whether and how neural synchrony would interact with maternal supportive parenting to shape irritability. Forty mother-son dyads participated, consisting of school-aged boys with varying levels of irritability (M age  = 7.53 years, SD = 1.25 years) and their mothers (M age  = 39.35 years, SD = 4.53 years). Neural activity was recorded via fNIRS during a frustration-eliciting task. Results indicated that neural synchrony was identified in the prefrontal cortex and the temporoparietal junction. Furthermore, moderation analysis revealed that in dyads with low maternal supportive parenting, higher neural synchrony was associated with higher child irritability, whereas in dyads with high maternal supportive parenting, neural synchrony was not significantly associated with child irritability. This study advances our understanding of irritability by dissecting neuro-parenting interactive mechanisms.

title: Resting state functional connectivity associated with maternal anxiety: preliminary evidence that infant rsFC moderates the association between behavioral inhibition and anxiety/depression
abstract: Postnatal maternal anxiety shapes caregiver and infant behavior. Yet, the relationship with infant brain function remains unclear. We examine the relation of maternal anxiety with infant resting state functional connectivity (rsFC). To evaluate the clinical significance of the rsFC networks identified, exploratory analyses tested whether the rsFC associated with maternal anxiety moderates risk trajectories from infant behavioral inhibition (BI) to childhood anxiety/depression symptoms. Four-month-old infants (N = 60) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and mothers completed the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI). Analyses included 49 infants with high-quality imaging and maternal anxiety data. In the longitudinal subsample (n = 21), BI was observed at 14 months, and anxiety/depression symptoms were assessed at 4-6 years using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Using whole-brain network enrichment analyses, we identified cortical network pairs that were significantly associated with maternal anxiety. Connectivity estimates from significant network pairs were averaged and tested as moderators of infant BI and childhood anxiety/depression association. Infants exposed to higher maternal anxiety showed an altered limbic-dorsal attention network (DAN) and default mode (DMN)-DAN. In both network pairs, negative and positive node-to-node pairs were identified, indicating that some regional connections exhibited stronger coupling, while others exhibited weaker coupling. Results demonstrated that DMN-DAN rsFC moderated developmental pathways: greater BI was associated with higher early-childhood anxiety/depression among infants with stronger DMN-DAN connectivity. Maternal anxiety is related to infant brain connectivity, and these neural differences moderate BI-related risk for anxiety/depression. DMN-DAN coupling may serve as an early marker of infants at risk for anxiety/depression. Given the small longitudinal sample, the moderation finding should be considered exploratory and requires replication in a larger, independent cohort.

title: Acquired cytomegalovirus in children: pathogen, bystander, or immune trainer?
abstract: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is one of the most common infections worldwide, with acquisition occurring predominantly in early childhood (younger than 5 years). Although congenital CMV is a recognised cause of neurodevelopmental impairment, the consequences of postnatally acquired CMV in children remain poorly defined and are often assumed to be benign. However, accumulating evidence suggests that acquired CMV infection is biologically active even when clinically silent, with the capacity to shape immune ontogeny, influence immune responses to other pathogens and vaccines, and alter health trajectories across the life course. In this Review, we examine the epidemiology, transmission pathways, immune responses, and clinical consequences of acquired CMV infection in childhood. We synthesise evidence to evaluate whether acquired CMV acts as a driver of pathology, a neutral bystander, or a beneficial immune trainer. The effects of CMV are highly context-dependent, determined by the timing of acquisition, host immune maturity, maternal health, co-infections, and broader social and environmental factors. Evidence of harm is strongest in infants with heightened biological or contextual risk, such as infants born preterm and those living with or exposed to HIV, whereas effects in children who are immunocompetent are heterogeneous and often clinically silent. Acquired CMV should be understood as a context-dependent immune modifier rather than a uniformly benign or pathogenic infection. This reframing of acquired CMV has important implications for policy and research. Universal intervention is unlikely to be appropriate; instead, targeted CMV prevention and treatment strategies for populations at high risk of CMV infection and severe disease integrated into maternal and child health programmes could offer the greatest benefit. Defining high-risk populations and critical windows for intervention should be prioritised to translate emerging evidence into improvements in childhood morbidity and equity.

title: Parent Comfort With Artificial Intelligence-Led Behavioral Therapy for Their Child
abstract:
This survey study assesses the comfort of parents with pediatric behavioral therapy led by artificial intelligence (AI) by evaluating results from a cross-sectional survey of US adults with at least 1 child aged 5 to 17 years.

Shortages in pediatric behavioral health services have increased interest in leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) for support, and platforms that offer to deliver these services are increasingly accessible to children and adolescents. In a 2025 national survey, 19.2% of US youth aged 12 to 21 years reported using AI chatbots for mental health advice, often without disclosure to parents or clinicians. Pediatric behavioral therapy requires clinical evaluation, family involvement, safety planning, and clear escalation procedures. The American Psychological Association has cautioned that adolescent AI use raises concerns about developmental vulnerability, inaccurate health information, and privacy. Parents’ views may inform how AI-led behavioral therapy is governed for children, yet parent comfort with this approach is unknown. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of US adults in November 2025 through the OutbreaksNearMe participatory surveillance platform using a nonprobability end-page river sample on SurveyMonkey, with survey weights approximating US Census demographic targets for age, gender, race and ethnicity, education, and income. The analytic sample included adults with at least 1 child aged 5 to 17 years. The Boston Children’s Hospital institutional review board approved the study, which followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guideline. Participants provided electronic informed consent. Participants self-selected race and ethnicity from survey categories for weighting and adjustment. The primary outcome was an ordered 4-level response to “How comfortable would you be with a therapy session led by an AI for your children?” Options were “not comfortable at all,” “not too comfortable,” “somewhat comfortable,” and “very comfortable.” Parallel items asked about therapy and primary care for themselves. Associations with higher comfort were estimated using survey-weighted cumulative-logit ordinal logistic regression among parents with complete data. Models adjusted for parent age, gender, race and ethnicity, educational attainment, household income, chronic illness, health care satisfaction, household child age groups, and the AI-related measures reported in the Figure and Table . The proportional-odds assumption was assessed qualitatively using threshold-specific estimates and graphical summaries. Weighted proportions and 95% CIs used logit-transformed Taylor-linearized standard errors. Analyses used R version 4.6.0 (R Foundation). Results Among 3102 respondents, 584 had at least 1 child aged 5 to 17 years, and 572 responded to the primary outcome regarding comfort level with AI-led behavioral therapy for their child. After weighting, the sample was 53.3% female, 45.7% male, and 1.0% not listed or nonconforming; 6.2% were Asian or Pacific Islander, 12.0% Black, 23.6% Hispanic, 54.2% White, and 3.9% other. Weighted comfort levels were 47.2% not comfortable at all (95% CI, 42.1%-52.3%), 28.8% not too comfortable (95% CI, 24.5%-33.6%), 16.2% somewhat comfortable (95% CI, 12.7%-20.5%), and 7.8% very comfortable (95% CI, 5.3%-11.3%). In the multivariable ordinal regression model (n = 554), higher comfort was associated with parents’ own comfort with AI-led behavioral therapy for themselves (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 20.94; 95% CI, 9.78-44.86) and AI-led primary care for themselves (aOR, 3.78; 95% CI, 2.16-6.59). Higher comfort was also associated with expectations that AI would perform better than (aOR, 10.12; 95% CI, 4.38-23.38) or about the same as (aOR, 3.31; 95% CI, 1.95-5.61) medical professionals for pediatric behavioral therapy. Child receipt of behavioral therapy in the past year was also associated with higher comfort (aOR, 2.07; 95% CI, 1.22-3.50). General AI use by parents and children was not associated with comfort. When asked which factors would matter most in deciding about AI-led behavioral therapy for their child, parents (n = 546) most frequently selected accuracy of diagnosis (58.5%), level of empathy (49.4%), recommendation from a medical professional (46.8%), and confidentiality and privacy (43.7%); cost (32.8%), scheduling flexibility (29.5%), and appointment wait time (27.7%) were selected less often. Discussion In this cross-sectional survey of US parents, approximately three-quarters were not comfortable at all or not too comfortable with AI-led behavioral therapy for their child. Higher comfort was most strongly associated with parents’ own comfort with AI-led health care and expectations that AI would perform similarly to or better than medical professionals, with prior child behavioral therapy also associated. These findings add the parent perspective to prior work on youth AI chatbot use. Parent acceptance may depend more on AI-related health care trust than on convenience or familiarity alone; general AI use was unrelated to comfort. Diagnostic accuracy, empathy, professional recommendation, and privacy were selected as priorities more often than cost, scheduling flexibility, or wait time. Clinician recommendations may be a modifiable lever for acceptance yet remain uncharacterized for pediatric AI-led therapy. Limitations Limitations include the nonprobability sample, modest sample size limiting precision and assessment of subgroup heterogeneity, and unmeasured familiarity with health care AI. Comfort may not reflect actual use, appropriateness, or safety. Cross-sectional data preclude causal inference, and parent comfort for self and child may reflect the same underlying construct. Conclusions This study found that most parents reported low comfort with AI-led behavioral therapy for their children. As these tools scale, policy should emphasize rigorous clinical evaluation, privacy protections, clinician and family oversight, and escalation pathways to earn parental trust.

title: SARS-CoV-2 mRNA Vaccination in Pregnancy and Child Neurodevelopment at 18 to 30 Months
abstract:
This study evaluates whether there is an association between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or shortly before pregnancy and offspring neurodevelopmental measures.

Key Points Question Is maternal SARS-CoV-2 messenger RNA vaccination during pregnancy associated with offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes at 18 to 30 months of age? Findings In this cohort study of 217 matched pairs, median Ages and Stages Questionnaire, Third Edition (ASQ-3) total scores were similar between children of vaccinated and unvaccinated participants. No significant differences were observed in secondary neurodevelopmental measures. Meaning These findings support continued recommendations for SARS-CoV-2 messenger RNA vaccination during pregnancy.

Importance Little is known about neurodevelopmental outcomes of children exposed to SARS-CoV-2 messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccine during pregnancy. Evidence on long-term offspring outcomes after in utero exposure to SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination is needed to inform vaccine recommendations in pregnancy. Objective To evaluate whether there is an association between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or shortly before pregnancy and offspring neurodevelopmental measures. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, prospective, cohort study of 18- to 30-month-old children was conducted at 14 centers of the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units Network from 2024 through 2025. Women who received a SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine during or within 30 days prior to pregnancy (exposed) were matched with women who did not (unexposed) by delivery site, delivery date, insurance status, and race and ethnicity. These data were analyzed from June 2025 to May 2026. Exposures Maternal receipt of at least 1 dose of an mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccine during, or within 30 days prior to, the index pregnancy vs no SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during pregnancy or within 30 days prior. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was Ages and Stages Questionnaire version 3 (ASQ-3) total score, which was deemed to be equivalent between the exposed and unexposed groups if the 90% CI of the median difference was between −10 and 10. Secondary outcomes included domain-specific ASQ-3 scores, the Child Behavior Checklist, Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, and Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire scores. Results Of 3956 screened, 271 exposed and 240 unexposed children were enrolled. Matching on all characteristics was possible in 217 pairs. Of the 434 children enrolled, 258 (59.4%) were Non-Hispanic White, 96 (22.1%) Non-Hispanic Black, 52 (12.0%) Hispanic, and 28 (6.5%) were not represented by any of the above racial or ethnic groups. Median age at assessment was 25.8 [24.6 to 28.3] months, 221 were female (50.9%), and 213 were male (49.1%). Exposed mothers were more likely to be nulliparous; their children were slightly younger at assessment and more likely to have been vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2. The primary outcome of ASQ-3 score was equivalent between the exposed and unexposed groups (255 vs 260, adjusted median difference, −3.4; 90% CI, −9.8 to 3.0). There were no significant differences in secondary outcomes. Conclusions and Relevance In this multicenter cohort study, ASQ-3 scores were equivalent between 18- to 30-month-old children whose mothers did or did not receive mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or immediately prior to pregnancy. These findings support continued recommendations for SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination during pregnancy.

title: Mindfulness-Based Intervention Improves Cognitive Function in Patients With Schizophrenia in Remitted: A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
ABSTRACT Background Patients with schizophrenia exhibit deficits in facial emotion recognition (FER), attention, P300, and quality of life (QoL), which severely hinder functional recovery. This study aims to explore the effects of mindfulness‐based intervention (MBI) on these outcomes and the potential mediating mechanisms. Methods In this 8‐week randomized, single‐blind, controlled study, a total of 70 remitted patients with schizophrenia were randomly assigned to the MBI group or the control group. The Five‐Factor Mindfulness Scale (FFMQ), FER, P300 indices, Continuous Performance Test‐Identical Pairs (CPT‐IP), and Schizophrenia Quality of Life Scale (SQLS) were measured at baseline and week 8 to assess mindfulness levels, cognitive function, neurophysiological parameters, and QoL. Linear mixed models evaluated intervention effects. Mediation analyses used pre‐post change scores with bootstrap resampling. Results For the primary outcome, MBI significantly improved FFMQ ( β = 16.750, 95% CI [7.769, 25.731], p < 0.001). For the exploratory outcomes, significant improvements were observed for P300 latency ( β = −63.602, 95% CI [−88.651, −38.554], p < 0.001) and CPT‐IP ( β = 8.219, 95% CI [4.004, 12.433], p < 0.001). FER and P300 amplitude showed nominal improvements only, and SQLS showed a non‐significant trend. A significant indirect effect through FER change was observed for change in SQLS (indirect effect = −6.343, 95% CI [−11.467, −2.288]), but CPT‐IP change did not mediate P300 amplitude improvement. Conclusion MBI significantly improved the primary outcome of mindfulness (FFMQ) and showed promising exploratory improvements in processing speed (P300 latency) and sustained attention (CPT‐IP). FER change may represent a potential indirect pathway associated with change in SQLS. These findings support MBI as a promising cognitive rehabilitation intervention. Trial Registration https://www.chictr.org.cn , identifier ChiCTR 2500106735, registered on: 29/07/2025

1 Introduction Schizophrenia is a severe psychiatric disorder, with its global age‐standardized point prevalence estimated at 0.29% (GBD 2019 Mental Disorders Collaborators 2022 ), while in China, this figure stood at 0.31% (Huang et al. 2019 ). The impact of schizophrenia on patients extends beyond positive symptoms (e.g., hallucinations, delusions). Cognitive deficits including impairments in attention and facial emotion recognition (FER), and social functional impairments particularly reduced quality of life (QoL), constitute more persistent burdens that impede patients' reintegration into society even after clinical stability is achieved (M. Dong et al. 2019 ; Owen et al. 2016 ). Deficits in FER and attention may lead to poorer social functioning and QoL (Kohler et al. 2010 ; Pavlova et al. 2023 ; Rocca et al. 2018 ). For instance, attentional distraction frequently undermines patients' ability to complete daily tasks, while difficulties in FER precipitate failures in social interaction. These challenges ultimately contribute to a decline in QoL (M. Dong et al. 2019 ). Currently, while antipsychotic medications are available for the treatment of schizophrenia, their side effects frequently result in medication discontinuation and distress. Additionally, these medications do not consistently improve cognitive and social functions (Wykes et al. 2017 ). Furthermore, a number of patients with schizophrenia exhibit either non‐response to antipsychotic medications or persistent residual symptoms (such as blunted affect, social withdrawal, cognitive impairment) throughout the course of their illness (Javed and Charles 2018 ). Consequently, social rehabilitation for patients with schizophrenia confronts considerable challenges. Fortunately, international guidelines recommend combining psychosocial interventions with antipsychotic medications for the treatment of schizophrenia (Gaebel et al. 2021 ; Galderisi et al. 2021 ). As highly effective supplementary approaches, common psychosocial interventions include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and mindfulness‐based intervention (MBI). Originating from meditation, mindfulness centers on “non‐judgmental awareness of present‐moment experiences.” Recent studies have demonstrated that MBI improves emotion regulation (Vancampfort et al. 2021 ), positive and negative symptoms (Böge et al. 2021 ; K. H. Lee 2019 ; Shen et al. 2023 ), neurocognitive functions (Shen et al. 2023 ), and QoL (Xue et al. 2024 ) in patients with schizophrenia. FER is a core component of social cognition in schizophrenia and a key factor influencing social functioning (Lyu et al. 2024 ). Patients with schizophrenia rely on FER to communicate with the general public, and this ability is crucial for effective communication and social interaction because it allows individuals to understand others' emotional states and respond appropriately (Faghel‐Soubeyrand et al. 2020 ; Gao et al. 2021 ; Martínez‐Cao et al. 2024 ). Impaired FER in these patients hinders their ability to identify others' diverse emotional states (Kohler et al. 2010 ), and they exhibit particularly notable deficits in recognizing negative emotions (anger, fear, sadness) (Barkhof et al. 2015 ). This impairment causes misunderstandings, social isolation, and deterioration of interpersonal relationships, which exacerbates the social withdrawal common in these patients, severely disrupts their social functioning, and may even triggers inappropriate social reactions (e.g., aggressive behavior), thereby making their social interactions more challenging (Bulgari et al. 2020 ; X. Dong et al. 2024 ; S. C. Lee et al. 2020 ). The research results show that attention‐based mindfulness is beneficial to FER in healthy individuals (Giannou et al. 2023 ). However, research on the effect of MBI on FER in patients with schizophrenia remains limited, and the relationship among mindfulness, FER, and QoL also lacks clarity. Therefore, further in‐depth research is warranted to address these gaps. Attention is one of the cores of neurocognition. A large multi‐site study using the CPT‐IP neuropsychological test to measure sustained attention or vigilance found that attention deficits exist in schizophrenia, are independent of symptom severity, and are related to functional capacity of daily living (Rocca et al. 2018 ). P300, as a component of event‐related potential (ERP), is closely related to cognitive activity. Perrottelli et al. found reduced auditory and visual P300 amplitudes in first‐episode schizophrenia (FES) patients and high‐risk psychiatric populations (Perrottelli et al. 2021 ), suggesting that P300 abnormalities may already be present before the full onset of psychosis. P300 deficits are considered an endophenotype of schizophrenia and are used to measure neurobiological susceptibility to this disorder (Chun et al. 2013 ). Recently, a study found that patients with opioid use disorder exhibited significant changes in P300 following an 8‐week MBI (Garland et al. 2025 ). However, the effect of mindfulness on P300 in schizophrenia patients remains unclear, as does the relationship among mindfulness, attention, and QoL. This study aimed to investigate the effects of a MBI on mindfulness levels, FER, attention, QoL, and P300 in remitted patients with schizophrenia through an 8‐week randomized clinical trial, and to clarify the underlying mechanisms among these variables. We proposed the following hypotheses: (1) MBI improves patients' mindfulness levels, cognitive functions (FER, attention), QoL, and P300; (2) changes in FER would mediate the effect of group assignment on changes in QoL; and (3) changes in sustained attention (CPT‐IP) would mediate the effect of group assignment on changes in P300 amplitude. 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design and Setting To evaluate the impact of MBI on FER, attention, and QoL in remitted patients with schizophrenia, as well as the interrelationships among these three factors, we conducted an 8‐week, parallel‐group, randomized controlled trial (RCT) with assessor blinding. This study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University (2022‐KY‐0002). All participants provided written informed consent before enrollment in the study. This clinical trial has been registered at https://www.chictr.org.cn (No. ChiCTR2500106735, dated:29/07/2025). Inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Aged 18–60 years; (2) Diagnosis of schizophrenia in accordance with the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM‐5); (3) Stable or recovering condition, defined as a Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) score ≤ 60 or a PANSS reduction rate ≥ 50%; (4) Receiving a stable therapeutic dose of antipsychotic medication; (5) Educational level above primary school. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Presence of serious physical disorders; (2) History of substance abuse or dependence; (3) Diagnosis of mental retardation; (4) Exhibiting impulsive, excitable behaviors, or being uncooperative with the study procedures; (5) Presence of audio‐visual disorders; (6) Having received four or more MBI trainings prior to enrollment; (7) Being pregnant. 2.2 Measures 2.2.1 General Information Questionnaire This questionnaire collected baseline information of participants, including name, gender, age, educational level, duration of schizophrenia, and family history of mental illness. 2.2.2 Five‐Factor Mindfulness Scale (FFMQ) The FFMQ (Baer et al. 2006 ) is a 39‐item self‐report scale designed to assess mindfulness levels in patients with schizophrenia. It comprises five dimensions: Observing, Describing, Acting with Awareness, Nonjudging of Inner Experience, and Nonreacting to Inner Experience. Each item is scored from 1 to 5. It has strong construct validity and reliability (Cronbach's α = 0.79–0.86). 2.2.3 Facial Emotion Recognition (FER) Stimuli were selected from the Chinese Facial Affective Picture System (CFAPS) (Gong et al. 2011 ), with two phases: practice and formal test. A total of 90 facial pictures (45 male/45 female) were categorized into positive, neutral, negative (30 each). The practice phase included 5 pictures per category (15 trials) for task familiarization. The formal phase had two rounds (90 random pictures/round, 180 total trials), lasting∼ 20 minutes. In each trial, a fixation cross (“+”) was presented first, followed by a facial picture. Subjects classified emotions via keyboard: “D” (positive), “G” (neutral), “L” (negative). Response within 3000 ms triggered the next trial; no response = incorrect, auto‐proceeding. Stimulus presentation and data collection were controlled via E‐Prime software. The FER outcome was the accuracy rate (percentage of correctly classified formal trials). 2.2.4 P300 Visual P300 (Karoumi et al. 2000 ) was tested via the Guangdong Runjie WJ‐1A ERP system. According to the 10–20 International Electrode Allocation Method, the recording electrode was grounded in the Central zero (Cz), and the reference electrodes were placed in the bilateral mastoid regions. A visual “oddball” paradigm was used: deviant stimuli (20% probability, 40 total) and standard stimuli (80% probability) were randomly presented (stimulus onset asynchrony [SOA] = 1200 ms, presentation time = 600 ms). Subjects responded only to deviant stimuli. Electrical activity was recorded with alternating current (AC) sampling (1000 Hz), bandpass‐filtered (0.1–70 Hz), and electrode impedance was kept < 5kΩ. P300 amplitude and latency were analyzed using Cz electrode signals. 2.2.5 Continuous Performance Test‐Identical Pairs (CPT‐IP) CPT‐IP (Cornblatt et al. 1988 ) is commonly used to assess attention maintenance and alertness. Subjects sustain attention to rapidly flashing numbers on a computer screen, pressing the left mouse button when two identical numbers appear consecutively. The test includes 3 groups (2‐digit, 3‐digit, 4‐digit numbers). Main evaluation indexes: number of correct responses, incorrect responses, and reaction time. The primary indicator is d‐prime. For subsequent statistical analysis, the raw scores of d‐prime will be converted to T‐scores based on healthy population norms. 2.2.6 Schizophrenia Quality of Life Scale (SQLS) The Chinese version (Kuo et al. 2007 ) was adapted from the original SQLS (Wilkinson et al. 2000 ). This 30‐item scale assesses QoL in schizophrenia patients, covering three factors: psychosocial function, motivation and energy, and symptoms and side effects. The total scale uses reverse scoring, and higher scores indicate poorer QoL. It has strong construct validity and reliability (Cronbach's α = 0.78–0.93). 2.3 Outcomes The primary outcome was FFMQ total score, selected as the primary indicator of mindfulness level. The exploratory outcomes included P300 latency, CPT‐IP, FER accuracy, P300 amplitude, and SQLS (total score and its three subdomains: Psychosocial, Motivation and energy, and Symptoms and side effects). 2.4 Assessment The random allocation sequence was generated by an independent researcher who was not involved in participant recruitment or outcome assessment, using a computer‐generated random number sequence in SPSS software. Participants were allocated to the intervention or control group at a 1:1 ratio. Allocation concealment was ensured using sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes. The envelopes were prepared by the independent researcher and opened sequentially by the enrolling researcher only after each participant had met eligibility criteria and provided written informed consent. This procedure ensured that the allocation sequence remained unpredictable to both the enrolling researcher and the participants before group assignment. All outcome assessors and the researcher managing the assessment schedule were blinded to group allocation. Assessors were independent of intervention delivery, signed a written blinding protocol before the trial, and were reminded at each assessment session not to inquire about or be informed of participants' group allocation. Participants and therapists were not blinded to the intervention type but were explicitly instructed not to disclose group assignment to assessors. To further protect blinding, the two groups received interventions at staggered times to minimize interaction between participants, and all participants were repeatedly reminded throughout the study that the content of their intervention program was confidential and should not be discussed with others. Two separate teams of therapists each delivered only one program (MBI or general rehabilitation); no therapist delivered both. All participants were assessed at baseline (pre‐intervention) and post‐intervention (after 8 weeks) using the FFMQ, FER task, P300 measurement, CPT‐IP, and SQLS.
