title: [Confidential enquiry into maternal suicide: lessons for clinical practice]
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In the Netherlands, suicide is the leading cause of maternal death up to one year postpartum. Understanding underlying causes and care processes is essential to reduce maternal mortality. Structured case analysis can help identify factors contributing to deaths in the perinatal period.

AIM: To identify gaps in care for peripartum women experiencing suicidality and to formulate recommendations.

METHOD: Retrospective qualitative analysis of five cases reviewed in 2021 and 2024 by the Dutch Audit Committee Maternal Mortality and Morbidity. Information was available from primary care and/or mental health services. Additional committee documentation was used to formulate lessons learned, and a vignette was derived from discussed case histories.

RESULTS: The analysis yielded lessons in five themes: 1. identification of non-medical risk factors and suicidality, 2. regional network agreements for perinatal mental healthcare, 3. safety-planning in peripartum suicidality, 4. reporting and 5. peer-support.

CONCLUSION: The analysis highlighted important lessons for the care of peripartum women with suicidality, particularly in the areas of recognition, multidisciplinary collaboration, and access to specialized perinatal psychiatric care. Limitations include incomplete documentation and underreporting.

title: Claustrum Transcriptome Alterations in Schizophrenia
abstract:
Key Points Question Is the transcriptome of the dorsal claustrum (dCLA) altered in schizophrenia? Findings In this case-control study, transcriptome profiling of the dCLA revealed numerous alterations in schizophrenia, including upregulation of immune response and transcription regulation genes and downregulation of mitochondrial activity and oxidative phosphorylation genes, and the number of differentially expressed genes detected was larger than in the anterior cingulate or prefrontal cortices. The pattern of alterations was highly concordant across these 3 regions but less concordant with altered gene expression in striatal regions. Meaning These findings suggest a molecular disease process in schizophrenia that is conserved across interconnected brain regions but more pronounced in the dCLA.

Importance Schizophrenia (SZ) is associated with transcriptome alterations in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), key regions in a distributed network that mediates cognitive functions impaired in the illness. The subcortical dorsal claustrum (dCLA) is structurally densely interconnected with the ACC and dlPFC and functionally coactivated with these regions during certain cognitive tasks. Objective To identify SZ-associated transcriptome alterations in the dCLA. Design, Settings, and Participants This case-control study used RNA sequencing data for dCLA homogenates from postmortem human brain of individuals with SZ and unaffected comparison (UC) individuals. Brain donations were obtained from the Allegheny County Office of the Medical Examiner, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Data analysis was performed from January 12, 2024, through May 22, 2026. Exposure Schizophrenia. Main Outcomes and Measures Gene expression differences in the dCLA between individuals with SZ and UC individuals were the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included gene set enrichment in the dCLA and comparisons of gene expression differences across the dCLA, ACC, dlPFC, putamen, and caudate between individuals with SZ and UC individuals, including rank-rank hypergeometric overlap (RRHO) analyses. Results In the final dCLA samples from 96 individuals, including 47 individuals with SZ (10 [21.3%] female; mean [SD] age, 49.0 [13.3] years) and 49 UC individuals (10 [20.4%] female; mean [SD] age, 49.9 [14.2] years), there were 1717 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between individuals with SZ and UC individuals, with 1149 (66.9%) of the DEGs upregulated in SZ. Many upregulated DEGs were associated with immune response or transcription regulation, and many downregulated DEGs were associated with mitochondrial activity or oxidative phosphorylation. In comparisons between individuals with SZ and UC individuals with data from the dCLA, ACC, and dlPFC, the number of DEGs detected was 4 to 12 times greater in the dCLA (1242 DEGs) than in the ACC (289 DEGs) or dlPFC (102 DEGs). However, threshold-free RRHO analyses revealed a conserved pattern of SZ-associated gene expression alterations across all 3 regions. In comparison, concordance of gene expression alterations was lower with the putamen and caudate, subcortical regions with weaker connections to the dCLA. Conclusions and Relevance The results of this case-control study suggest that the dCLA is a prominent site of molecular alterations in SZ. These alterations might reflect the dCLA’s extensive connectivity with affected cortical regions, distinctive intrinsic circuitry, and/or enrichment of vulnerable cell types.

This case-control study investigates schizophrenia-associated transcriptome alterations in the dorsal claustrum.

title: Targeted Use of Kudzu for Binge Drinking Among Adults With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Phase 2b Randomized Trial
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to determine the efficacy and acceptability of targeted use of kudzu, an herbal supplement, in adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD) who binge drink.

METHODS: In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with AUD who binge drink were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to targeted (as-needed) use of oral kudzu extract (2 grams taken on days when binge drinking was anticipated) or matching placebo, plus weekly counseling for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was number of binge-drinking days in the past week. Prespecified secondary outcomes included number of self-reported binge-drinking weeks, number of drinks, and measurements of changes in alcohol use using biomarkers, including ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and phosphatidylethanol (PEth).

RESULTS: Retention was high: 88% completed the trial, and 86% of weekly follow-up visits were completed. In the primary intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, assignment to kudzu versus placebo reduced number of binge-drinking days (incidence rate ratio [IRR]=0.73, 95% CI=0.54, 0.99); as-treated (taking medication ≥2.7 days per week) analysis estimated a stronger effect (IRR=0.58, 95% CI=0.38, 0.89). Secondary outcomes showed lower number of binge-drinking weeks in ITT analysis (relative risk [RR]=0.79, 95% CI=0.62, 0.99). In as-treated analyses, reductions in number of binge-drinking weeks (RR=0.68, 95% CI=0.47, 0.98) and PEth positivity (RR=0.82, 95% CI=0.67, 0.99) were also significant. The number of binge-drinking days showed significant sustained reductions at the 3-month posttreatment visit (RR=0.68, 95% CI=0.47, 0.97). The overall frequency of adverse events was similar between groups. No serious adverse events related to kudzu occurred during follow-up.

CONCLUSIONS: Targeted use of kudzu reduced self-reported binge-drinking outcomes among adults with AUD during treatment compared to placebo. Greater reductions in binge drinking and PEth were observed among those who took medication more frequently. Reductions in self-reported binge drinking persisted at the posttreatment visit. Kudzu may be a helpful pharmacologic treatment for binge drinking among people with AUD.

title: Deficient Monetary Reward Processing in Schizophrenia: A Meta-Analysis and Computational Modeling of a Monetary Incentive Delay Task
abstract: Abstract Background and Hypothesis Evidence regarding monetary incentive-processing deficits in schizophrenia (SZ) remains inconsistent. Clarifying how Monetary Incentive Delay (MID) task performance relates to model-derived learning indices may help characterize motivational and incentive-processing abnormalities in SZ. We hypothesized that patients with SZ would show altered behavioral performance and model-derived expected-value and prediction-error (PE) indices associated with clinical symptom severity. Study Design We integrated a meta-analysis of MID studies (30 studies; SZ/healthy controls (HCs), n = 785/755) with an independent subject-level MID task (SZ/HCs, n = 60/74). A Rescorla–Wagner model with a fixed learning rate was used to derive group-comparable mean absolute PE values and expected-value (Q) indices. Study Results The meta-analysis showed small-to-moderate behavioral differences in SZ including prolonged reaction times (RT) and reduced reward-trial correct rate (CR). In an independent subject-level computational study, patients with SZ showed prolonged RT, lower reward- and loss-trial CR, and higher neutral-trial CR than HCs, consistent with reduced cue-specific modulation. Model-derived analyses showed higher absolute reward PE and absolute loss PE (ABSLPE), lower Reward-Q, and more negative Loss-Q in SZ under the current Rescorla–Wagner framework. Loss-related indices, particularly ABSLPE and Loss-Q, were associated with Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale-Negative scores. Trial-level logistic regression analyses further indicated weaker cue-related modulation of hit probability in SZ. Conclusions These findings suggest that SZ is associated with altered MID task performance and model-derived PE- and Q-related indices. These indices may help characterize incentive-processing abnormalities in SZ, but their clinical and neurobiological significance requires validation in future longitudinal and multimodal studies.

title: Primary care exploration of suicidal ideation by general practitioners before suicidal acts: a national observational study of the French Sentinelles Network
abstract:
Background The exploration of suicidal ideation (SI) during primary care consultations with general practitioners (GPs) is crucial for suicide prevention. We performed a retrospective assessment of the prevalence of SI exploration by GPs during the six months preceding suicidal acts with the aim of identifying associated factors, such as the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods We performed bivariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses on data from weekly questionnaires completed by 459 GPs from the French Sentinelles Network (2013–2023) regarding 1,156 suicidal acts: 928 suicide attempts (SA) and 205 suicides (S). Results GPs had explored SI during the six months before a suicidal act for 54.9% (95%CI 52.0–57.8) of patients. The prevalence of SI exploration was higher after 2020 (post-COVID period) than before 2020 (61.8% [95%CI: 57.6; 65.8] versus 48.2% [95%CI: 44.0; 52.3], p < 0.001). Factors positively associated with SI exploration were: post-COVID period (OR = 2.25, 95%CI [1.5–3.4], p < 0.001), spontaneous expression of SI (OR = 20.52, 95%CI [9.1–55.7], p < 0.001), consultation for psychological reasons (OR = 3.37, 95%CI [1.9–6.0], p < 0.001), history of SA (OR = 2.10, 95%CI [1.4–3.2], p < 0.001), depression (OR = 1.92, 95%CI [1.3–2.9], p = 0.001), SD versus SA (OR = 1.86, 95%CI [1.1–3.3], p = 0.024), substance misuse (OR = 1.82, 95%CI [1.1–3.0], p = 0.020), consultation within the last month (OR = 1.63, 95%CI [1.1–2.4], p = 0.010). Limitations The findings may be subject to a social desirability bias. Conclusion The exploration of SI needs to be improved, particularly for patients consulting for somatic conditions. GPs may have become more aware of SI since the COVID-19 pandemic. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-026-03465-5 .

Highlights • The COVID pandemic may have increased GPs’ awareness of suicidal ideation • Suicidal ideation is insufficiently explored by GPs when patients have somatic comorbid conditions • Most suicide risk factors influence the exploration of suicidal ideation by GPs Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-026-03465-5 .

Introduction Suicide is a major global health issue. In France, 250,000 suicide attempts (SA) and 9,000 deaths from suicide (SD) are reported annually (13.4/100,000 inhabitants), with suicide constituting the second leading cause of death in the15-24 years age group [ 1 ]. During a suicidal crisis, suicidal ideation (SI) emerges and becomes increasingly invasive, eventually leading to a suicidal act (SD ou SA). 82.7% of patients displaying suicidal behavior report suicidal ideation or planning [ 2 ]. SI is the third most important predictor of suicide [ 3 ]. In primary care, the goal is to provide care and allow patients to express their suffering, thereby helping them to overcome the crisis and prevent a suicidal act [ 4 ]. General practitioners (GPs) play a key role in suicide prevention, as they often manage common mental disorders, as instance mood and anxiety disorders [ 5 – 7 ], particularly in certain areas of France in which access to psychiatrists is very limited. About 45% of patients who died by SD suicide [ 8 , 9 ] or made a SA [ 10 ] consulted a primary care physician during the month preceding the suicidal act. However, a significant proportion of patients do not openly express their suicidal thoughts or behaviors [ 11 ]. For example, in a Dutch sentinel network study [ 12 ], the practitioner considered suicidal behavior a matter of concern at the last consultation in only about 30% of cases. There were, therefore, missed opportunities to prevent suicide in those patients whose suicidal behavior was not detected. General practitioners frequently report difficulties exploring SI with their patients, which they attribute to a lack of training or time constraints [ 13 ], further contributing to these missed opportunities. Improving the recognition of SI is, therefore, essential to improve suicide prevention. This aspect has become all the more important since the recent COVID-19 pandemic, which contributed to a deterioration of mental health in the general population and an increase in the risk of suicidal ideation [ 14 , 15 ]. The exploration of suicidal ideation is particularly challenging for GPs because suicide risk can increase rapidly in primary care patients [ 2 ], and individuals experiencing SI may be less engaged in care [ 16 ]. Patients may also choose not to discuss their suicidal ideation with their GP [ 17 , 18 ]. More frequent consultations, allowing the GP to build a trust relationship, could help. Previous studies in diverse primary care settings populations showed that about 8% of primary care patients had experienced SI during the month preceding the consultation [ 19 , 20 ]. Some of these patients consulted for somatic conditions, making it harder for the GP to identify the suicide risk [ 21 ]. Studies on depressed patients have shown that SI is explored in 40% to 66% cases [ 22 , 23 ]. However, the frequency of SI exploration by GPs in patients who attempt or die by suicide has never been evaluated. Patients could also self-disclose suicidal ideations to the practitioner, which can be limited for several reasons. Patients could limit the expression of SI: for example because they don’t have it at the time of the consultation, or because they feared the outcome of disclosure, including stigma, overreaction, and loss of autonomy [ 11 ]. In depressed patients, the severity of depression [ 23 ] and the patient’s age and sex [ 22 ] have already been shown to be associated with the likelihood of SI being explored by the GP. The influence of other risk factors for suicide on the likelihood of GPs exploring SI remains unknown. These factors include previous SA [ 24 ], alcohol misuse [ 25 ], long-term unemployment [ 26 ], and the diagnosis of a chronic disease [ 27 ]. The influence of other factors associated with an increase in SI, such as the COVID-19 pandemic [ 14 , 28 ], on the likelihood of GPs exploring SI has also been little studied. Furthermore, the influence of other characteristics of the suicidal act — such as the violent or non-violent nature of the act, as defined in previous studies [ 28 , 29 ] — is also unknown. There is some evidence to suggest that SD and SA define two different populations SD [ 30 ]. We therefore forced this variable into the multivariate model, as it has been shown that a variable non-significant in bivariate logistic regression can be significant in a multivariate model [ 31 ]. The characteristics of the GPs have also been shown to be associated with the likelihood of detecting SI in a population with clinical anxiety or depression. Key GP characteristics include the recent participation of the GP in training programs on depression [ 23 ], the duration of the consultation [ 23 ], GP age, and having undergone psychotherapy [ 32 ]. The factors influencing the exploration of suicidal ideation by GPs may partly reflect their knowledge of the risk factors associated with suicide risk, shedding light on areas in which training is required to improve the detection and prevention of suicidal behavior. This approach could help to identify profiles for which SI is underexplored, including patients for which GPs do not even consider evaluating SI despite the existence of a real risk. In this context, the objectives of our study were: 1) to evaluate the prevalence of the exploration of suicidal ideation by GPs in the six months preceding a suicidal act in primary care patients and to assess the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on this prevalence and 2) to identify factors patient and GP characteristics associated with the exploration of SI. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational study in mainland France, using data reported by GPs to the Sentinelles Network between 2013 and 2023. The Sentinelles Network is a population-based surveillance system operated by volunteer GPs. It comprises about 500 French GPs throughout mainland France (1.2% of the French GP population) who report health-related events on an unpaid voluntary basis. Age is comparable between the Sentinelles Network GPs and those of the general French GP population, and the network covers all regions of France [ 28 ]. Sentinelles Network GPs differ from the general French GP population in terms of sex and geographical distribution [ 33 ]. The Sentinelles Network contains a lower proportion of women (19% in the Sentinelles Network vs. 29% for the general French GP population), and 47% of from the doctors in the Sentinelles Network are located in South-East France (vs. 27% for the general French GP population). Each week, GPs report the number of suicidal acts among their patients and their characteristics on an online questionnaire. The definition proposed to doctors since 1999 was based on the definition of acts with suicidal intent. It excludes acts without suicidal intent, such as self-harm, according to the WHO/EURO multicentre study on parasuicide [ 34 ]. A suicidal act is defined as “an act of self-inflicted injury (for example, phlebotomy, jumping from high places, hanging, gun shots, asphyxiation) or self-poisoning with drugs in excess of the generally recognized therapeutic dose”, with intent to die. Study population We aimed to investigate the exploration of SI during the six months preceding a suicidal act. We therefore considered all suicidal acts reported between January 2013 and December 2023 by GPs for patients over 15 years of age who had been in contact with their GP during the preceding six months. We did not restrict our population to adults, but instead included all individuals over the age of 15, in line with the UN definition of “youth” as corresponding to the population aged from 15 to 24 years [ 35 ]. Data collected For each suicidal act reported, the GP completes a questionnaire with the following information: An evaluation of the GPs’ exploration of suicidal ideation through the question “have you already explored suicidal ideation in previous consultations?”. Other data: Patient sociodemographic data (age, gender, professional activity: employed, student, retired, unemployed), history of SA SD or SA Chosen method: self-poisoning, self-cutting, firearm, hanging, other/multiple; non-violent suicidal acts were defined as voluntary overmedication and poisoning with gas or toxic substances. All other types of suicidal act were considered to be violent, as in a previous study [ 29 ]). Contact with the GP, or an absence of such contact, before the suicidal act. If the patient had been in contact with the GP, the timing of this contact relative to the suicidal act (< 1 week, < 1 month, 1- 6 months before). For consultations since January 2016, the reason for the consultation was also noted as somatic only, psychological and somatic or exclusively psychological. Diagnosis of depression or alcohol misuse by the GP in the last year and, for data collected since 2020, diagnosis of depression, anxiety, substance misuse, personality disorder, or another condition in the last three months. The questionnaire was modified in 2020. The “depression” variable was therefore created by merging the two methods of assessing depression status (diagnosis during the last year for data before 2020, diagnosis during the last three months since 2020). The “substance misuse” variable was created by merging “alcohol” before 2020 and the detection of substance misuse after 2020. Spontaneous expression of SI by the patient GP characteristics: When registering with the network, general practitioners provide demographic information about themselves and their location (urban/rural). Statistical analysis All analyses were performed with R version 4.3.2 software (2023–10–31). Descriptive statistical analyses were first performed on the study population and the sample of GPs. The annual prevalence of the exploration of suicidal ideation by GPs during the six months preceding a suicidal act was calculated from 2013 to 2023. The Cochran–Armitage test for trends was used to evaluate the linear trend between the prevalence of the exploration of suicidal ideation and year. A bivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify significant differences between the cases for which SI was (exploration of suicidal ideation +) and was not (exploration of suicidal ideation -) explored by GPs during previous consultations. The variables included in the analysis were patient age and gender, employment status, depression and substance misuse during the previous month to the GP’s knowledge, a history of prior SA known to the GP, the reason the consultation, the date of the last consultation, the violent or non-violent nature of the suicidal act, outcome of suicidal act (SD or SA), spontaneous expression of SI by the patient, and the period of declaration (before 2020 vs. 2020 and after), and the GP’s age, gender, and type of practice. A multivariable logistic regression (GLM) including all explanatory factors with p < 0.2 in bivariate analyses was then performed. We tested whether patient sex or vital outcome of the suicidal act (SA vs. SD) modified the associations by adding interaction terms to the model and comparing model fit using likelihood ratio tests. Interaction terms with p < 0.05 were retained; if interactions were non- significant, the variables were included in the model without interaction. We included 809 suicidal acts in this analysis, the others being excluded due to missing values. Outcome of the suicidal act appeared to be important because SD and SA identified two different populations in a previous study [ 30 ]. We therefore forced this variable into the multivariate model, as previous studies have shown that variables non-significant in bivariate logistic regression may become significant in a multivariate mode [ 31 ]. We also assessed the differential effects of sex and suicidal act outcome on the relationship between other factors and the exploration of suicidal ideation, by including these variables as interaction terms in subsequent models (supplementary tables S1 and S2). In cases of a non-significant interaction, the variable was forced into the model as the interaction could be significant. Interactions were included for p -values < 0.05 in the likelihood ratio test. We have computed variance inflation factor (supplementary table S3). We also tested a random effect on the identification of a suicidal act by the GP because many GPs declared several suicidal acts. The percentage of missing values for each variable is indicated in Table 3 . We considered values of p < 0.05 to be significant. Ethics statement The protocol was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Helsinki Declaration. The Sentinelles Network has been approved by the French data

title: Mobile Units for Integrated Addiction and HIV Prevention Services for People Who Inject Drugs: The HPTN 094 Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
Key Points Question Does providing 26 weeks of integrated HIV prevention and addiction services for people who inject drugs using peer navigation delivered in a mobile unit produce superior outcomes compared to peer navigation to existing standard-of-care community-based services alone? Findings In this randomized clinical trial, HIV prevention and addiction outcomes were similar between study arms, though the intervention showed a greater reduction in all-cause mortality compared with standard of care. Meaning The findings suggest that integrated mobile service delivery models may reduce all-cause mortality for people who inject drugs.

This randomized clinical trial evaluates the use of preexposure prophylaxis for HIV and medications for opioid use disorder among individuals who inject drugs.

Importance Integrated models to deliver HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) for people who inject drugs are needed. Objective To determine whether integrated PrEP and MOUD services delivered on a mobile unit with manualized peer navigation improved PrEP and MOUD use compared with peer navigation to existing community-based services. Design, Setting, and Participants This 2-group, open-label, randomized clinical trial was conducted between May 2021 and September 2024 in Houston, Texas; Los Angeles, California; New York, New York; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; and Washington, DC, among people aged 18 years and older currently injecting drugs, without HIV, with OUD, and not taking MOUD but willing to consider MOUD. Interventions The intervention arm (n = 203) consisted of 26 weeks of manualized peer navigation plus integrated PrEP, MOUD, and limited clinical and supportive services delivered on a mobile unit. The active control arm (n = 206) consisted of 26 weeks of manualized peer navigation to available community-based PrEP, MOUD, harm reduction, and supportive services. Main Outcomes and Measures The co–primary outcomes were PrEP use and MOUD use at 26 weeks. Secondary outcomes included PrEP and MOUD use at 52 weeks, HIV incidence, and all-cause mortality. Results Of 842 people who inject drugs who were screened, 409 were randomized: 134 (32.8%) female; 146 (11.2%) aged 30 years and younger vs older than 30 years. At the 26-week visit, the intervention and active control arms were similar for confirmed PrEP use: 11/203 (5.4%) vs 6/206 (2.9%) and MOUD use: 30/203 (14.8%) vs 22/206 (10.7%), respectively. At the 52-week visit, intervention and active control arms were similar for confirmed PrEP and MOUD: 4/203 (2.0%) vs 4/206 (1.9%) and MOUD use: 27/203 (13.3%) vs 29/206 (14.1%). One HIV acquisition occurred in the intervention and 2 in the active control arms; HIV incidence rate of 0.9 per 100 person-years (95% CI, 0.2-2.6). Four deaths were confirmed in the intervention arm and 13 in the active control arm (hazard ratio, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.1-0.9; P = .03). Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, mobile delivery of integrated HIV prevention, addiction, and navigation services did not improve primary outcomes beyond peer navigation alone. The significantly lower all-cause death rate at 52 weeks in the intervention arm bears replication for delivering integrated PrEP and MOUD services to people who inject drugs. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04804072

Introduction Opioid use disorder (OUD) is a major driver of HIV acquisition in the US and a leading contributor to mortality among people who use opioids, whether alone or in combination with stimulants. Beyond HIV acquisition and overdose, people who inject drugs experience elevated risks of comorbid conditions, including hepatitis C, bacterial infections related to nonsterile injection practices, injection-related wounds, and other sexually transmitted infections. People who inject drugs face substantial barriers to accessing key services and support necessary for consistent engagement in HIV prevention and addiction treatment. These barriers include poverty, unstable housing, food insecurity, and limited access to health care, all of which impede regular use of HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and medication for OUD (MOUD). Siloed medical and addiction treatment systems further restrict access by fragmenting care for primary health services, HIV PrEP, and MOUD. Mobile units offer a way to address multiple barriers faced by people who inject drugs in accessing integrated services, including HIV prevention, MOUD, primary care, and social services. Mobile unit-based care differs from care based in conventional brick-and-mortar settings for people who inject drugs along key features of location, integration, immediacy, and service proximity. Yet, rigorous evaluation of mobile unit-based interventions for people who inject drugs remains limited. This study tests whether advantages of integrated HIV and MOUD services using a mobile unit combined with peer navigation would produce statistically significant improvements in primary outcomes of PrEP and MOUD compared to peer navigation to existing standard of care, community-based services alone for people who inject drugs in 5 US cities. Methods Trial Design and Oversight HPTN 094 was a 2-arm, individually randomized, controlled, open-label study that evaluated whether an integrated intervention delivered in a mobile unit improved use of HIV PrEP and MOUD at 26 and 52 weeks ( Figure 1 ). The trial protocol and statistical analysis plan are in Supplement 1 . A single institutional review board, Advarra, provided oversight of the research. Biannual data monitoring oversight was provided by an independent study monitoring committee at the HPTN. All participants provided written informed consent. The study followed the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials ( CONSORT ) reporting guideline. Participants Eligibility criteria included current injection drug use, being aged 18 years and older, the ability to provide informed consent, not currently using but willing to use MOUD, self-reported sharing injection equipment, or having condomless sex in the last 3 months with people with HIV or persons of unknown HIV serostatus, and being able and willing to provide adequate contact information of a person or persons who could help locate participants for follow-up visits. Participants were excluded from the study if they self-reported MOUD in the past 30 days as part of a treatment program or if they were enrolled in another interventional study. Although people with HIV were recruited and randomized, enrollment numbers were insufficient to support rigorous analysis in that group. Study Sites HPTN 094 was conducted in Houston, Texas; Los Angeles, California; New York, New York; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; and Washington, DC. The cities represented diverse large urban contexts with substantial HIV and overdose risks among people who inject drugs. Study sites were selected based on prior experience conducting research on HIV prevention and addiction for people who inject drugs, on geographic diversity, and on HIV prevalence in people who inject drugs. Mobile Units Los Angeles, Houston, and New York chose identical 33-ft medical units that contained an examination table, space for processing laboratory samples, and a toilet; Philadelphia and Washington, DC, chose 26-ft, similarly equipped medical units. Data collection during screening, enrollment, week 26, and week 52 occurred in the mobile unit for all participants. Mobile Unit Placement Preimplementation activities prior to study start-up were conducted by the research team in each city to develop data-driven, community-focused maps using HIV and overdose data, and the location of available community health care services to identify geographic locations where people who inject drugs might best access the mobile units. Locations were intended to facilitate access for actively injecting people who use drugs who lacked a source of care. Recruitment Participants were recruited through street-based outreach at mobile unit locations, community-based recruitment events, incentivized peer referral, and social media. Purposive methods were used to compile a sample with preset target percentages of 25% women and 25% younger (<30 years) participants. Total compensation for completing all research visits was $175 in Houston; $200 in New York, $210 in Philadelphia, $350 in Los Angeles, and $360 in Washington, DC. Screening Screening involved assessments to determine eligibility, including confirmation of OUD diagnosis (clinical interview and DSM-5 checklist), active drug injection activity (recent injection marks), HIV status (rapid antibody point-of-care tests and laboratory-based confirmation), and recent opioid use (urine point-of-care test for opioids; laboratory-based test for fentanyl). Intervention Arm Participants assigned to the intervention arm received 26 weeks of integrated HIV, addiction, and supportive services with peer navigation facilitation of these services, all delivered in a mobile unit (eTable 1 in Supplement 2 ). Peer navigation sessions linked participants to available community services if desired. Medical services delivered on the unit were (1) access to oral PrEP for people without HIV with persons assigned female sex at birth receiving emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate; persons assigned male sex at birth receiving emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (eAppendix 1 in Supplement 2 ). Long-acting cabotegravir for PrEP was not provided by the study; long-acting cabotegravir use was assessed at each study visit and (2) immediate access to MOUD (sublingual buprenorphine provided on-unit or by prescription; facilitated referral to methadone clinic). In addition to facilitated access to MOUD, people who inject drugs with polysubstance use involving stimulants (methamphetamine, amphetamine, cocaine) were referred to local stimulant treatment and 12-step programs. Active Control Arm Because a uniform standard for delivering integrated PrEP and MOUD to people who inject drugs who are out of treatment is not consistently available, the active control arm received 26 weeks of manualized peer navigation to facilitate linking participants to available services at brick-and-mortar agencies. The scope of services identified and referred in the active control arm paralleled services provided to the intervention arm in the mobile unit. The active control arm provided an ethically acceptable and clinically beneficial comparison condition to no navigation or to no referrals Peer navigation services were delivered virtually or in community spaces away from the mobile unit, such as in parks or near food banks and fast food restaurants. Peer Navigation Peer navigators were hired locally and had personal lived experience of OUD, including injection drug use, or had shared community background involving addiction and recovery with people who inject drugs. The published peer navigation model was informed by systems, self-determination, empowerment, shared decision-making, and social support theories of behavior change (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 2 ). A reference manual for supervisors based on the model-guided navigation sessions aided implementation across sites. Fidelity-supporting procedures for using the navigation model included peer navigators completing 2 weeks of online and in-person training on the model and the study prior to delivering services. Peer navigators provided services to participants in both arms and were supervised by a senior staff member at each site. Peer navigation supervisors from each site met monthly with an expert with extensive experience in training and supervising peer navigators to monitor adherence to the peer navigation model and to support navigators in monitoring their own recovery journeys. Peer navigators met with participants, established rapport, conducted needs assessments, and made referrals to and assisted in accessing services. All participants completed 5 required sessions: (1) MOUD and harm reduction; (2) HIV PrEP; (3) barriers and facilitators to integrated health care; (4) housing, food security, hygiene; and (5) sexual risk behaviors. Additional sessions included these topics: (1) injection risk reduction/drug splitting; (2) stimulants and other substances; (3) alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other downers; and (4) depression and stigma. Dose of peer navigation was measured by number of sessions completed (required and elective), session length (in minutes), and session topics. After 26 weeks, no peer navigation services were provided for either arm. Study Assessments Self-reported demographic characteristics (age, sex assigned at birth, race, ethnicity) and behavioral variables (housing status, access to health care, mental health, criminal justice engagement, drug and alcohol use, overdose experiences, drug treatment experience, and personal connections and support) were captured on case report forms at enrollment, week 26, and week 52. Sensitive information was collected via computer-assisted self-interview, including sexual behavior, medication adherence, stigma, violence, and sexual abuse. Reported deaths were verified by death certificate or medical examiner report, when feasible. Laboratory Methods Biomarkers of recent drug use at screening and follow-ups were measured via antibody-based urine dipsticks that assessed organic and synthetic opioids, oxycodone, cocaine, methamphetamine, amphetamine, and benzodiazepines. Urine screens for fentanyl were conducted via local laboratories. Blood specimens were collected at weeks 0, 26, and 52 and tested in local laboratories. Plasma, urine, and dried blood spots were collected at study visits for HIV confirmatory testing, PrEP, and detection of illicit or nonprescribed drugs. A biomarker confirmed methadone testing was determined using HPTN Laboratory Center–derived urine measurements. Plasma samples were used to assess adherence to buprenorphine. Testing was performed at the HPTN Laboratory Center (Johns Hopkins University) and described in detail in eAppendix 1 in Supplement 2 . Statistical Analysis The study had 2 co–primary outcomes. The primary HIV prevention outcome was the proportion of enrolled participants who returned for the week 26 visit and had biomarker-verified evidence of PrEP use. The primary drug use outcome was the proportion of enrolled participants who attended the week 26 visit and had biomarker-verified evidence of MOUD use (buprenorphine or methadone) and a current prescription for buprenorphine or proof of attendance at a methadone clinic. Secondary outcomes included PrEP and MOUD use at 52-week visits, HIV incidence, overdose-related mortality, and all-cause mortality. title: Cost-Effectiveness of Early Dose Reduction or Discontinuation Versus Antipsychotic Maintenance After First-Episode Psychosis: Results From the HAMLETT Study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: After remission from a first episode psychosis (FEP), international clinical guidelines recommend continuation of antipsychotic medication for at least 1 year, although many patients wish to reduce or discontinue medication due to side effects or long-term health concerns. Evidence on the cost-effectiveness of early dose reduction or discontinuation compared to continuation remains limited.

METHODS: A trial-based cost-utility analysis was conducted alongside the ongoing HAMLETT study, in which 347 remitted FEP participants were randomized to either early guided dose reduction or discontinuation or maintenance treatment for 1 year. Both healthcare and societal perspectives over a 24-month time horizon were considered. Health outcomes were expressed as quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) derived from the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire using Dutch valuation tariffs. Costs were estimated using patient reported healthcare utilization and administrative pharmacy data. Incremental costs and effects were analysed using seemingly unrelated regression with uncertainty assessed through nonparametric bootstrapping and multiple sensitivity analyses.

RESULTS: Early dose reduction or discontinuation was associated with lower quality-adjusted life years and higher or comparable costs compared with maintenance treatment over the 2-year analysis period. In the base-case societal perspective analysis, incremental costs were €23,563 and incremental effects were -0.077 QALYs, resulting in an incremental net monetary benefit of -€27,430 at a willingness-to-pay threshold of €50,000 per QALY at 24 months. Results were consistent across several scenarios with only approximately 9% probability that early dose reduction or discontinuation was cost-effective at the assumed willingness-to-pay threshold. However, a sex-at-birth subgroup analysis suggested a small and uncertain positive incremental net monetary benefit among female participants.

CONCLUSION: Over a 24-month period, early dose reduction or discontinuation of antipsychotic medication after remission from a FEP is unlikely to be cost-effective compared with maintenance treatment from both healthcare and societal perspectives. Whether longer term functional improvements associated with early dose reduction translate into cost-effective benefits remains uncertain and requires follow-up.

title: Quality of media reporting of suicidal behaviour in India
abstract:
BACKGROUND: India has a suicide rate of 18-21 fatalities per 100,000 people (compared to a global rate of 11 per 100,000), constituting around 28% of all suicides worldwide. Conscientious media coverage of suicide is one of the pillars of the World Health Organization's (WHO) life framework for suicide prevention. Media reporting of suicide events has thus far gone without sufficient scrutiny in India.

METHODS: A scholarly content analysis study was carried out on news articles reporting on suicide attempts and deaths in 6 daily newspapers in India between 1st January 2023, and 31st January 2023. The quality of suicide reporting against the WHO guidelines and the Press Council of India (PCI) 2022 recommendation was assessed. Descriptive statistics were used.

RESULTS: A total of 117 articles were analysed. The average number of suicide articles per newspaper per week was 3.9 (range 0.4-13.2). The names, occupation, and method of suicide were mentioned in 93 (79.5%), 58 (49.6%), and 97 (82.9%) of articles, respectively. 58.1% offered a single cause for the suicide event, whereas negative life events were mentioned for 63.2% of the news. All news articles included at least one harmful information according to the WHO media reporting guidelines. 84 (71.8%) news articles violated the recommendation provided in the guideline by not including any helpful information. The reporting of suicide violated the PCI 2022 guidelines in every domain.

CONCLUSION: Media coverage of suicidal behaviour is often suboptimal and fails to meet the standards set by the WHO suicide reporting guidelines and PCI edition 2022 guidelines.

title: Suicide reporting in a changing media landscape: perspectives from Nepali media professionals
abstract:
Background Responsible media reporting of suicide is an evidence-based population-level suicide prevention intervention. To devise programs to engage with the media, it is imperative to understand the experiences and perspectives of media professionals. Suicides are highly newsworthy in Nepal and deeply shaped by socio-cultural factors such as gender roles, caste, and ethnicity. Yet little is known about media professionals’ practices and experiences in reporting on suicide. This study examines Nepali media professionals’ perspectives and experiences of suicide reporting, and the contextual forces shaping their work. Methods In 2025, semi-structured qualitative interviews with 22 diverse media professionals with experience reporting on suicide-related news were undertaken across different regions in Nepal. Semi-structured interviews explored why suicide incidents are reported, how suicide news is sourced and produced, and perceived challenges and responsibilities in reporting. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed and translated, and analysed using a thematic approach that combined deductive and inductive coding. Results Commercial pressures, audience demands, and socio-cultural factors were seen to drive decisions about which suicides become news (e.g. female suicides), how they are framed, and whose deaths are overlooked. While not allocated to one beat, suicides were often treated as crime news, with brief and graphic reports. A demand-supply logic was used to explain the high level of coverage of suicide news, with a high degree of audience interest in these stories. Participants described how organisational pressures, changing media environments, and sociocultural factors such as gender norms, stigma, and cultural narratives shaped suicide reporting. Conclusions Our findings shed light on how media professionals in Nepal understand and enact suicide reporting in a rapidly changing environment. By foregrounding media professionals’ own accounts of news values, routines and constraints, this study provides a contextual foundation for future work on media, suicide and public communication in Nepal. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-28891-z .

Background Globally, suicide accounts for around 720,000 deaths per year, with three-quarters of these deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) [ 1 ]. Suicide rates in Nepal are among the highest globally, with recent estimates indicating approximately 20–24 deaths per 100,000 population per year, and males experiencing higher suicide mortality than females [ 2 ]. These figures should be interpreted with caution, in the absence of a national suicide registry [ 3 ]. Suicide data in Nepal are also filtered through reporting systems shaped by social, cultural, legal, and medical factors, making them less reliable [ 4 ]. Suicide research in Nepal is understood through culturally shared explanations shaped by gender roles, family relationships, social expectations and structural inequalities. Emerging qualitative evidence has attempted to examine what people think and believe about suicide which is often a part of their gendered cultural scripts [ 5 ]. These narratives may also influence which suicide incidents are considered newsworthy. For example, our previous study in South Asia found that suicides among females were substantially more likely to be reported in the news than suicides among males due to cultural framings around judgement and blame [ 6 ]. Female suicide is frequently explained as a response to persistent oppression, domestic violence, marital conflict, dowry-related abuse, restricted autonomy, and threats to family honour [ 5 , 7 , 8 ]. In contrast, male suicide is commonly explained through narratives of financial hardship, unemployment, migration, alcohol use, and the inability to fulfil socially prescribed roles as providers, alongside expectations regarding suppressing emotional distress [ 5 , 7 ]. Across both males and females, suicide is often interpreted through interpersonal and moral frameworks involving shame ( ijjat ), family conflict, social exclusion, and societal expectations [ 5 , 7 ]. Suicide patterns among males and females are shaped by the intersection of multiple socio-demographic factors, including age, marital status, employment, education, socioeconomic status, and health conditions, resulting in differences in suicide methods, profiles, and underlying contributing factors [ 9 ]. Therefore, suicide is often framed as the culmination of several socio-cultural constraints rather than individual psychopathology. These culturally embedded narratives shape not only public understandings of suicide but also the broader environment in which suicide is communicated, interpreted, and represented. A public health approach to suicide prevention that addresses broader social determinants has recently gained increasing global momentum, including in low- and middle-income countries [ 10 , 11 ]. Responsible media reporting has been recognised as one of the few effective, population level strategies for preventing suicides [ 12 – 14 ]. A substantial body of evidence demonstrates that media reporting can shape suicide-related behaviours. While sensationalised and graphic reporting has been associated with increased suicide risk through the “Werther effect”, responsible reporting and portrayals of hope, recovery, and alternatives to suicide have been linked to reduced suicide rates through the “Papageno effect" [ 15 ]. Importantly, efforts to curtail irresponsible media reporting have been linked to reductions in suicide rates [ 16 , 17 ] and have also been found to shape audience experiences of suicide reporting [ 18 ]. Accordingly, the WHO has issued guidelines to promote responsible media reporting [ 14 ]. While this represents an important step toward addressing the issue, much of the existing evidence on media reporting comes from high-income countries (HICs). Evidence on suicide and media in LMICs is expanding but remains concentrated in a few countries and dominated by newspaper analyses [ 19 ]. Research examining the lived experiences and perspectives of media professionals demonstrates that suicide reporting is shaped by an interplay between professional judgement, ethical responsibilities and broader socio-cultural contexts rather than media guidelines alone [ 20 – 22 ]. Media professionals frequently report balancing between competing imperatives such as informing the public, meeting audience expectations and producing news within a commercial and time pressed environment[ 20 , 21 ]. Consequently, responsible reporting guidelines represent only one influence among many, with their implementation often constrained by newsroom practices, local media environments, and professional norms [ 21 , 22 ]. This may partly explain the inconsistent implementation of WHO media guidelines across countries, particularly in LMICs which are often viewed as recipients of strategies and guidelines developed in HICs [ 23 ]. Media professionals have also highlighted their limited involvement in guideline development, scepticism regarding the evidence linking reporting styles with imitative suicide, and concerns that reporting restrictions may constitute censorship or reinforce taboos around suicide [ 21 , 22 ]. Additional challenges identified in India include fatalistic attitudes towards suicide, limited confidence in crisis support services, and the influential role of senior editorial leadership in shaping reporting practices [ 20 ]. At the same time, media professionals’ central roles in agenda-setting, framing, and priming public responses underscore their potential as important partners in suicide prevention efforts [ 20 ]. Notably, the limited literature on Nepal’s media landscape indicates that it is shaped by both significant change and persistent structural challenges that affect how news is produced, reported, and consumed. Since the 1990s, Nepal has seen rapid quantitative growth in media outlets across print, broadcast, and online platforms; however, this proliferation has not necessarily translated into high journalistic quality or accountability [ 24 ]. The Press Council has been largely ineffective in fulfilling a regulatory role due to limited resources and political interference [ 25 ]. Economic pressures have weakened “traditional” media with declining revenues leading to layoffs, reduced editorial capacity, and a narrowing focus on political and economic stories at the expense of broader social issues, undermining independent reporting [ 25 ]. Simultaneously, digital and online media offer expanded reach, audience engagement, and opportunities for innovative, public-oriented journalism. However, challenges related to media literacy, accountability, access, and regulatory debates continue to shape the balance between press freedom, state control, and responsible reporting across platforms [ 26 ]. Media professionals operate within professional environments governed by editorial policies and regulatory frameworks. They also work within broader sociocultural and political contexts that shape what is considered newsworthy, how suicide is interpreted, and the narratives through which it is communicated. These intersecting influences inevitably shape suicide reporting practices. In Nepal, multiple initiatives such as the adaptation of the WHO media guidelines by the National Health Education Information and Communication Centre (NHEICC), Department of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Population (MoHP) and WHO supported media training workshops have been undertaken to promote responsible reporting [ 27 ]. However, little is known and documented about Nepali media professionals’ perspectives and day-to-day experiences in relation to suicide reporting. Evidence from Nepal is needed to help inform future collaborative work that is sensitive to local media realities. Building on a similar qualitative study in India [ 20 ], this study aims to examine media professionals’ perspectives on suicide reporting in Nepal, including perceptions of newsworthiness, reporting processes, and the challenges involved. Methods We conducted semi‑structured interviews (February – September 2025) with media professionals in Nepal who had previously reported on suicide‑related news. We conducted semi‑structured interviews to gather in‑depth data on specific media practices, perceptions, and experiences of these media professionals in reporting suicide. Ethical approval (ref:2025-31439-62503-3) was obtained from the Human Research Ethics Committee at The University of Melbourne and the Ethical Review Board of Nepal Health Research Council (ref:1535). Informed consent to participate in the study was obtained from all study participants. The study was conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations prescribed by the above mentioned ethical boards. The Consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research (COREQ [ 28 ]) checklist was followed (Supplementary material 1). Study setting Media professionals were recruited from Kathmandu and other regions including Jhapa, Ilam, Janakpur, Banke, and Sindhupalchowk. These locations include both the capital and smaller urban centres, reflecting variations in media infrastructure and reach. Kathmandu was the primary recruitment site due to the high concentration of media professionals in the city. Participants from other regions were accessed through existing professional networks, using Kathmandu as the base for outreach. The official language in all these cities is Nepali. Study participants We interviewed 22 media professionals (February-September 2025) from different media outlets. Eligible participants were media professionals from any media sector or content area and from any media format (e.g., print, television, radio, and online media). We specifically sought to include participants with experience reporting on suicide. We used purposive and snowball sampling employing multiple complementary strategies for recruitment. Our first contact with a media professional was established in 2022 during a series of workshops. This individual subsequently acted as a key informant, facilitating introductions to other eligible media professionals through their professional network. We also reached out to key individuals in media research, the Press Council, the Health Journalists’ Federation, and the Nepal Police. To broaden the sample and include experiences from alternative platforms, participants were also recruited from prominent YouTube channels, fact-checking organisations, FM radio stations, and television outlets. Furthermore, we searched online e-papers for media professionals working in suicide reporting in Nepal and invited them for interviews. Information about the study was shared through emails with the recruitment advertisement and contact details of the interviewer (PS). Through a snowball approach, existing participants helped identify more participants for the study. Appointments at a convenient time were sought from the participants. The sample size was guided by the concept of information power [ 29 ], which proposes that sampling must be guided by factors such as objectives of the study; characteristics of the sample relevant to their involvement in suicide reporting; quality of the interview process; and the spread of experiences across regions, areas of reporting and media types. As data collection progressed, the sample generated sufficient information to address the study objectives. Recruitment ceased when the research team judged that the study had achieved sufficient information power. Practical considerations, including time and resource constraints, also informed this decision. After 22 interviews, the research team determined that a sufficient range of responses had been obtained, since no new issues emerged in the discussion. Recruitment was therefore ceased following discussion with senior members of the team (GA and KG). No repeat interviews were carried out. Data collection The interviewer (PS; Nepali female from the Newar community: Janajati ) undertook a 45‑minute to one-hour, audio‑recorded, semi‑structured qualitative interview to discuss media professionals’ perspectives and experiences in relation to suicide reporting in Nepal. A semi‑structured guide was used to guide the discussion with participants, which had been prepared by adapting a guide used in similar research in India [ 20 ]. The guide (Supplementary Material 2) focused on media professionals’ experiences with suicide reporting; their views on current reporting practices in Nepal; challenges encountered; recommendations for responsible reporting guidelines and reflections on the media’s role in suicide prevention (examined in a separate manuscript).
