title: Serum selenium, iron and rubidium are altered in treatment-resistant schizophrenia
abstract: The molecular basis of schizophrenia is complex, involving an interplay of genetic and environmental factors. In recent postmortem and imaging studies, we identified disturbances in iron homeostasis in cortical and subcortical regions of individuals with schizophrenia. These may be relevant to neuropathology identified in the disorder and could relate to mechanisms of oxidative stress and inflammation. Recent work has proposed that there is a dysregulation of brain metals and other elements in schizophrenia that might impact on oxidative stress. Using a metallomics approach, we report robust changes in serum levels of pro-oxidant iron, anti-oxidant selenium, and the potassium-marker, rubidium, in a cohort of people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS). The cohort also expressed elevated levels of serum pro-inflammatory cytokines and hepcidin, and lower levels of anti-oxidant selenoproteins, selenoprotein-P1 (SEPP1) and glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3). The changes in serum iron, rubidium and selenium discriminate between control individuals and TRS cases, and they were not affected by age or clozapine serum levels. We propose that the changes in selenium and cytokines might drive the expression of hepcidin, resulting in reduced serum iron levels. Further research should investigate the relationship between peripheral and central measures of these elements and their metabolism, and further explore the relevance of pro-oxidant stress to the neuropathology of schizophrenia.

title: A Crh-defined insular cortex-brainstem-thalamic circuit regulates anxiety-related behavioral states
abstract: Anxiety disorders are among the most prevalent and debilitating psychiatric conditions, yet the neural circuits underlying anxiety-related states remain incompletely understood. Here we identify a cortical-brainstem-thalamic pathway in which Crh-expressing neurons in the anterior and middle insular cortex (a/mIC) engage the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), which in turn recruits the posterior paraventricular thalamic nucleus (pPVT) to contribute to anxiety-related behavior. Single-cell calcium imaging reveals that the predator odorant 2-methyl-2-thiazoline (2-MT) and footshock recruit partially overlapping populations of PBN-projecting a/mIC neurons; neurons activated by both stimuli exhibit increased activity during open-arm approach in the elevated plus maze. Exposure to 2-MT increases corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) signals in the PBN, where CRF enhances PBN neuronal excitability and CRF receptor 1 (CRFR1) signaling facilitates a/mIC-terminal-evoked firing. Inhibition of Crh⁺ a/mIC-PBN projections, Crh knockdown in the a/mIC, or blockade of CRFR1 signaling within the PBN attenuates 2-MT-induced anxiety-like behavior. Human neuroimaging further reveals stronger functional coupling within a putative homologous aIC-PBN-pPVT network in individuals with anxiety symptoms, and the strength of this coupling correlates with anxiety severity. Together, these findings define a molecularly specified insular circuit that contributes to anxiety-related behavioral states.

title: A preconceptional stress model identifies thalamostriatal substrates of intergenerational vulnerability
abstract: Antenatal depression affects up to 20% of pregnancies worldwide and is associated with increased neuropsychiatric vulnerability in offspring, yet the enduring behavioural, neuroanatomical, and molecular features associated with maternal mood disturbance remain incompletely characterized. To model depression that begins before conception, female mice were subjected to social-isolation rearing (SIR) from weaning through gestation and lactation, and behavioural, neuroanatomical, and molecular outcomes were assessed in adult offspring of both sexes. Offspring of SIR dams exhibited robust anxiety-like behaviours across multiple paradigms. High-resolution ex vivo structural magnetic resonance imaging revealed reduced relative volumes of the thalamus and striatum, together with relative expansion of gustatory/visceral and visual cortices. Multivariate analyses identified a pattern of thalamostriatal and other regional volume differences that covaried with behavioural impairment. Diffusion tensor imaging further identified region-specific elevations in fractional anisotropy, consistent with persistent differences in brain microstructure. Transcriptomic profiling of the thalamus revealed widespread, sex-dependent differences in gene expression, implicating pathways related to synaptic organization, protein synthesis, neuronal plasticity, and myelination. Exploratory DNA-methylation analyses identified nominal, sex-dependent pathway enrichments that did not survive false-discovery-rate correction. Together, these findings show that maternal stress beginning before pregnancy leaves a persistent imprint on offspring brain structure, microstructure, and epigenetic regulation, converging on the thalamus as a central hub of intergenerational vulnerability. This work establishes SIR as a translationally relevant model of depression that predates conception and provides integrated MRI- and molecular-level biomarkers for dissecting mechanisms and informing early preventive strategies.

title: Dynamic epigenetic changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy in major depressive disorder
abstract: Although antidepressants remain the main pharmacological treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), therapeutic response varies, highlighting the need for molecular markers that predict treatment response, as well as insights into the biological processes underlying antidepressant efficacy. Candidate-gene and cross-sectional epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have reported DNA methylation signatures associated with antidepressant response; however, findings remain inconsistent. To date, no longitudinal EWAS has examined methylation trajectories across multiple time points during antidepressant treatment in MDD. Within the Early Medication Change trial, DNA methylation data was generated for 162 patients with MDD (81 responders, 81 non-responders) and 48 matched healthy controls. Patients were assessed at four times across eight-weeks of standardized antidepressant treatment, while controls were assessed twice. Differentially methylated positions (DMPs) and regions (DMRs) were identified using longitudinal EWAS models and the comb-p algorithm. Baseline methylation levels were associated with depressive symptom severity at day 28 and day 56 through two and six DMRs, respectively (e.g., TNRC6C, CAT), whereas no single DMP reached significance. Longitudinal analyses identified one DMP associated with improvement in depressive symptoms (YLMP1) and three DMRs showing methylation changes over time (e.g., GPR126, PM20D1). Combined patient-control analyses revealed additional DMPs and DMRs associated with diagnosis and temporal effects. This study provides first longitudinal evidence of regionally coordinated DNA methylation changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy, revealing alterations in genes involved in neuroplasticity and inflammatory processes that are associated with clinical response. Replication and functional validation will be essential to determine their relevance for personalized antidepressant treatment.

title: Immune-Microbiome Crosstalk in the Developmental Origins of Neurodevelopmental Disorders
abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) arise from genetic and environmental factors converging across development, from embryogenesis through adulthood. Two systems central to brain development, the immune system and the microbiome, are incompletely formed at birth. Development of these immune and microbiome systems is shaped by factors transferred across prenatal and postnatal maternal-offspring interfaces including the placenta, birth canal, and breast. Despite literature linking each system independently to NDD risk, these fields have largely proceeded in parallel, rarely interrogating their interactions. This siloed approach constrains mechanistic understanding and progress. Here, we present evidence that the immune system and microbiome are interacting, not independent, influences on neurodevelopmental programming. Preclinical evidence from germ-free, antibiotic depletion, and maternal immune activation models demonstrates that perturbation of either system alters the other; human cohort evidence remains largely associational. Across each maternal-offspring interface, immune and microbial signals converge on the developing brain, acting on peripheral and neuroimmune populations. Microglia emerge as a recurring cellular mediator. Resolving mechanisms of NDD risk requires experimental designs that treat immune and microbial variables as interactive and that span prenatal through postnatal development. The field must move beyond disciplinary silos to integrate these systems across the full neurodevelopmental time course they jointly shape.

title: Age-dependent structural brain aging in medication-free major depressive disorder: A multi-site analysis from COORDINATE-MDD consortium
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with altered brain structure and accelerated brain aging. However, previous studies have been limited by clinical samples with mixed medication status and multiple mood states, modest sample sizes, underrepresentation of older adults with MDD, and/or reliance on summary-level data.

METHODS: Harmonized T1-weighted MRI from MDD (n = 645), all medication-free and in a current depressive episode, and matched healthy controls (n = 645), segmented into 145 regional volumes, from 11 sites in COORDINATE-MDD consortium. Brain age gap (BAG) was estimated cross-sectionally using gradient boosting regression with nested cross-validation. Group differences in BAG (and age-corrected BAG [cBAG]) were examined across age strata. Regional contributions were evaluated using SHAP values.

RESULTS: MDD was associated with significantly elevated cBAG compared with healthy controls (mean difference + 2.0 years [95% CI 1.251, 2.774], Cohen's d -0.289 [95% CI -0.399, -0.179]). Age-stratified analyses showed no differences before mid-30s, with progressively larger gaps thereafter, reaching +6.8 years in MDD aged 55 and older in unadjusted analyses (4.3 years after accounting for site). cBAG differed across neuroanatomical phenotypes previously identified using COORDINATE-MDD data. Key contributing regions included lateral and medial prefrontal regions, middle temporal gyrus, putamen, supplementary motor cortex, central operculum, and cerebellum.

CONCLUSIONS: Structural brain aging in MDD is age-dependent and most pronounced in a neuroanatomical phenotype associated with poorer key clinical outcomes. The findings are consistent with, but do not establish, neuroprogression models of MDD and demonstrate that cBAG is not a uniform feature of MDD, being more strongly expressed in a specifically clinically vulnerable disease phenotype.

title: Harmonization of transdiagnostic psychiatric phenotypes across a large multi-site study reveals high burden of neuropsychiatric multimorbidity in 16p11.2 and 22q11.2 copy number variant carriers
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Modern psychiatric research is increasingly collaborative, but significant differences in recruitment and assessment methods across cohorts present major methodological challenges when integrating data.

METHODS: The Core Psychiatric Phenotype Summary (C2PS) tool was developed to harmonize data on psychiatric/neurodevelopmental diagnoses and subthreshold symptoms from multiple sources. Demonstrating its reliability, and breadth and depth, we report findings in the largest cohort to date of individuals with reciprocal copy number variants (CNVs) at 22q11.2 or 16p11.2, collected across 14 international sites in the Genes to Mental Health (G2MH) Network.

RESULTS: Neuropsychiatric phenotypes were harmonized for 1,325 G2MH participants (22qdel: n=752, 22qdup: 219, 16pdel: 227, 16pdup: 127, median age 16.0 years [IQR 11.0, 27.0], 52% female). Inter-rater reliability indicated fair-to-excellent agreement across C2PS domains (Light's Kappa: 0.48 to 1). Completion was feasible, with an average of 4% missingness (range 1% to 13%). Multimorbidity (> 2 disorders) affected 57%, with a median of 3 (IQR: 2 to 5) disorders per individual. Of those without any neuropsychiatric diagnosis (n= 244, 18%), subthreshold symptoms were common (82% in >1 domain, 57% > 2 domains). Higher multimorbidity was associated with lower adaptive functioning on the Vineland Adaptative Behavior Scales [-5.5 points per additional impacted domain (95% CI: -7.5, -3.6; p=5x10 -8 ].

CONCLUSIONS: The C2PS is a pragmatic and reliable tool to harmonize heterogeneous neuropsychiatric phenotypic data for large multi-national studies. Observations in 1,325 individuals with CNVs at 16p11.2 or 22q11.2 reveal variant-specific psychiatric profiles, emphasize burden and impact of psychiatric multimorbidity, and provide insights beyond categorical diagnoses.

title: A Dynamic Model of Amygdala Circuits in Threat and Reward: Implications for Affective Disorders
abstract: Animals must continuously evaluate their surroundings and select adaptive responses to survive in ever-changing environments. Central to this capacity is the assignment of importance to environmental cues, which guides motivated behavior toward rewarding opportunities and away from potential threats. Here we propose a theoretical framework, a dynamic motivational model based on threat and reward imminence, in which motivational states evolve continuously as a function of imminence rather than shifting between discrete stages. Within this framework, three interacting dimensions define the stimulus relevance of an environmental cue: salience, valence, and value. We leverage the amygdala as a substrate to illustrate the circuit mechanisms underlying importance assignment and examine how stimulus imminence drives motivational state transitions to promote adaptive behavior. Applied to affective disorders, it reframes amygdala dysfunction as projection- and circuit-specific stress adaptation rather than uniform regional hyperactivity, providing a common language for comparing major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorders. By integrating animal circuit studies with human neuroimaging and clinical evidence, this framework positions amygdala-centered networks as candidate biomarkers for biologically informed subtyping and targets for personalized treatment in depression and related affective disorders.

title: Efficacy of Lumateperone 42 mg in Major Depressive Disorder: Subgroup Analysis of a Phase 3 Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective:  Lumateperone is an FDA-approved atypical antipsychotic to treat schizophrenia, bipolar I or II depression, and major depressive disorder (MDD). Post hoc analyses of a randomized, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Study 501) evaluated the efficacy of lumateperone 42 mg adjunctive to antidepressant therapy (ADT) in demographic and clinical subgroups of patients with MDD with inadequate ADT response.  Methods:  Adults with  DSM-5  criteria for MDD with inadequate response to 1-2 courses of ADT, Montgomery- Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) Total score ≥24, Clinical Global Impression Scale-Severity (CGI-S) score ≥4, and Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology-Self-Report 16-item (QIDS-SR-16) score ≥14 were randomized 1:1 to 6-week oral lumateperone 42 mg+ADT or placebo+ADT. Efficacy was evaluated in the overall population and patient subgroups by demographic (age, sex, race, ethnicity, and region) and baseline disease characteristics (MADRS Total score, ADT type, number of ADT failures [in current episode and lifetime], and presence of anxious distress).  Results:  The modified intent-to-treat population comprised 481 patients (lumateperone+ADT, n = 239; placebo+ADT, n = 242). Lumateperone+ADT significantly improved MADRS Total score (least squares mean difference [LSMD], -4.9;  P  < .0001), CGI-S score (LSMD, -0.7;  P  < .0001), and QIDS-SR-16 Total score (LSMD, -2.4;  P  < .0001) at Day 43 versus placebo+ADT. Lumateperone+ADT significantly improved MADRS Total score ( P  < .01) across all demographic subgroups and baseline disease severity versus placebo+ADT. Significant improvements ( P  < .05) in CGI-S, QIDS-SR-16 Total scores, and MADRS response and remission rates were also observed across most subgroups.  Conclusion:  Lumateperone+ADT demonstrated robust efficacy over placebo+ADT across a broad range of demographic and clinical subgroups of patients with MDD.  Clinical Trials Registration . ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04985942.  Prim Care Companion CNS Disord   2026;28(6):26m04289 .  Author affiliations are listed at the end of this article.

title: Identifying expanded adverse childhood experiences and examining their relationship with health outcomes: a systematic review protocol
abstract:
Abstract Introduction Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with poor health outcomes, with higher cumulative exposure conveying more risk. Although earlier ACE studies focus on household-level adversities, growing evidence explores traumatic childhood experiences originating outside the home (expanded ACEs). Expanded ACEs may co-occur with household-level ACEs, causing misclassification bias if not measured. A comprehensive list of expanded ACEs has not been identified, and no unified framework exists to consider their impacts. This systematic review will identify expanded ACEs published in peer-reviewed literature and examine their associations with physical and mental health outcomes and behaviours by demographic subgroups, offering the first unified framework for expanded ACEs’ impacts on health. Methods and analysis Six databases were systematically searched in February 2026 for global, peer-reviewed studies published in English since database inception: PubMed/Medline, Embase, CINAHL, PsycInfo, CENTRAL and Scopus. Eligibility includes studies involving humans without restriction to date, setting, population or location; studies with ACEs originating outside the home as the exposure; and studies with outcomes including physical or mental health outcomes anchored to International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision or Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition codes or behaviours. Researchers (RAs) screen titles/abstracts using pre-established eligibility criteria on training batches of 30–50 articles with faculty oversight. Once agreement consistently reaches 80%, RAs may use a hybrid screening process that prioritises independent, dual screening, relying on single-screening with fidelity checks to stay within budget and timeline, while maintaining rigour. Title/abstract screening is followed by full-text review and extraction. Study quality will be assessed using validated tools, with limitations reported. Data will be summarised via quantitative synthesis or narrative summary as appropriate. Ethics and dissemination The University of Pennsylvania #26-7542 determined this work is not human subjects research. Dissemination will occur through peer-reviewed presentations and publications. PROSPERO registration number CRD420261432925.

STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY This review systematically catalogues the expanded adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) that appear in the literature. The review will report effect sizes between expanded ACEs and physical and mental health outcomes and behaviours. Subgroup analyses will identify relationships across demographic subgroups by age, race and sex. Articles are limited to those published in English. Grey literature is excluded. Introduction In a landmark study published in 1998, researchers from Kaiser Permanente and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) demonstrated the negative life course impact of childhood exposure to abuse, neglect and various household stressors, termed adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). 1 ACEs are defined broadly by the CDC as ‘potentially traumatic events that occur in childhood (age 18 years and younger)’. 2 In the more than 25 years following publication of the original Kaiser-CDC ACE study, the association between childhood exposure to adversities and poor health outcomes (health risk behaviours and mental and physical health conditions) has been repeatedly substantiated, recognising that higher cumulative exposure conveys more risk. 3 – 8 The original Kaiser-CDC ACE study 1 focused predominantly on traumatic events occurring within the home or within the context of families (ie, household ACEs) and included participants who were mostly white, upper-middle class and medically insured. Subsequent research measured adversity in other geographic and demographic subgroups and specifically measured adversities occurring outside the home, seeking a more wholistic understanding of childhood adversity. 9 Between 2013 and 2015, two independent research teams reported on childhood traumatic events occurring outside the home (ie, expanded ACEs): The Philadelphia ACE Task Force and The Crimes Against Children Research Center. Findings from these studies uncovered important connections between health outcomes and stressful encounters occurring outside the home (ie, neighbourhood violence, racial discrimination, peer victimisation). 10 – 14 Since their publication 10 years ago, these papers have been heavily referenced with more than 4300 combined citations, indicating strong interest in expanded ACEs. Substantial additional evidence now exists to show that various community ACEs are associated with health outcomes. 15 – 20 With considerable overlap between expanded ACEs and household-level ACEs, 10 recent work has highlighted the importance of measuring household and community ACEs in tandem to avoid misclassification bias and overestimated effect sizes for household-level adversities. 21 Prior work highlights the need to better understand the types of community-level ACEs youth experience and their relationship to health outcomes. While there has been rapid expansion of studies exploring expanded ACEs, a comprehensive list of expanded ACEs has not been identified, nor is there a unified framework to consider their impacts on health, creating a significant barrier to advancing this work. Studies continuously reflect the importance of cumulative trauma on health outcomes, and expanded ACEs comprise a critical part of that equation. The proposed study has the potential to improve trauma-informed research and practice by collating a list of expanded ACEs and describing their associations with physical and mental health outcomes and behaviours. Our objectives are to (1) complete a systematic review of existing peer-reviewed, primary research to identify what ACEs originating outside the home have been studied; (2) examine the associations between ACEs originating outside the home with physical and mental health outcomes and behaviours; and (3) identify if these relationships differ across specific demographic subgroups, such as age, race, sex and socioeconomic indicators. Methods and analysis Protocol and registration This protocol was created using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Protocols checklist ( online supplemental appendix A ). 22 The protocol is registered on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO Registration CRD420261432925). 23 Timeline The study start date is February 2026; given the iterative nature of systematic reviews, the projected completion date may change as the review progresses. Therefore, we refer readers to the living PROSPERO record for the most current timeline, which will be updated throughout the review process. Review team Three members of the research team have ACE content expertise (CMF, RW, PFC), and two have methods expertise in systematic reviews (JL and YZ-I). A team of research assistants (RAs) will receive orientation to the study topic and methods to provide foundational knowledge about conventional ACEs, expanded ACEs and systematic reviews. After the initial orientation, RAs will receive more in-depth training on conducting systematic reviews and Covidence to ensure rigour of the review. Patient and public involvement Patients and the public will not be involved in this review. Eligibility Eligibility criteria are described below using the standard Population, Intervention/Exposure, Comparator and Outcome format. 24 Inclusion Population : we will include full-text studies published in peer-reviewed journals with human participants of all ages, without restriction to the setting, population, date or location of study. We include a broad mix of study designs, including descriptive, observational, qualitative and mixed-methods studies, as the primary goal of this review is to develop a comprehensive catalogue of expanded ACEs identified in the literature. We will focus on full-text reports to ensure sufficient data are available to consistently and rigorously evaluate all studies. Intervention(s), exposure(s ): for this study, expanded ACEs are defined as potentially traumatic childhood events (age 18 years and younger) originating outside the home. All exposures to expanded ACEs will be considered, including acute (eg, single experiences like sexual assault, school shooting or an accident), chronic (eg, repeated experiences, such as abuse) or complex (eg, severe, prolonged, relational experiences such as racial discrimination, kidnapping or trafficking) traumas. 25 26 Other examples include, but are not limited to, community, neighbourhood or peer-related traumas; school-related, institutional-related or system-related trauma; and other harms originating outside the household. Some factors which may be relevant at both the household and community levels (eg, food insecurity and housing instability) will only be included when measured specifically at the community level as indicated by the study authors to avoid misclassification bias; for example, housing instability measured as insufficient housing availability per capita within the community would be included, whereas eviction or repeated moves, measured at the household level, would not. ACEs must be presented descriptively (ie, prevalence, qualitatively) or as an exposure to be included. Comparator(s)/control : given the context, we expect many of the published studies to be observational, comparing those who were and were not exposed to one or more expanded ACE(s) (ie, exposed group(s) and unexposed control group). However, there is no requirement for studies to include a comparator (eg, qualitative and descriptive studies are included). Outcomes: primary outcomes of interest include physical and mental health outcomes and behaviours, regardless of the measurement tool used or whether outcome data were measured objectively or subjectively. International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision 27 and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth edition 28 codes will be used to qualify outcomes. Outcomes describing symptomatology that aligns with diagnosis codes will be included (eg, restlessness, excessive worrying, difficulty concentration as a function of generalised anxiety disorder). Exclusion Population : animal studies are excluded. To align with our objective of identifying primary scientific studies of expanded ACEs that are published in the peer-reviewed literature, grey literature is excluded, along with the following media types and study designs: abstract only, books or chapters of books, book reviews, case studies, case reports, case series, commentaries/editorials/opinion pieces, datasets, intervention studies, newsletters, notes, preprints, policy statements, randomised controlled trials, reports, retractions, reviews, social media content, surveys, unpublished clinical trials. Importantly, we would expect relevant empirical findings discussed in grey sources to be captured via our search of the primary literature. While we anticipate being able to access all published scientific articles, when full-text articles cannot be accessed after exhausting all available means (eg, interlibrary loan, contacting authors, etc.), those articles will be excluded to ensure all studies are assessed using the same standards. Intervention/exposure : we also will exclude studies of human participants whose traumatic experience under study occurred beyond childhood (18 years of age or older). Additionally, any studies solely exploring stressors originating at the household level are excluded. Furthermore, articles centred exclusively on exposures of structural hardships that are framed in the context of the household (eg, food insecurity, housing instability) will be excluded. Studies where ACEs are not the exposure of interest (eg, mediator, moderator, other covariate, etc.) will be excluded. Outcomes : we will exclude studies with outcomes that focus on care models and resilience. Search strategy A study team member who is a medical research librarian searched the following bibliographic databases for global, peer-reviewed studies published in English since database inception through February 2026: PubMed/Medline via NIH, Embase via embase.com, CINAHL via EBSCO, PsycInfo via ProQuest, CENTRAL via Cochrane Library and Scopus via scopus.com. These are the sole information sources. Because of resource limitations and lack of translation capability among team members, articles were restricted to those published in English to ensure accuracy of translation. Near the end of the review, the librarian will repeat the search to ensure eligible articles published since February 2026 are screened for inclusion/exclusion criteria. The following components are included in the search strings: controlled terms: (MeSH, EMTREE), keywords and search filters. The search strategy was constructed through consensus methods between study team members who include a medical research librarian, primary care clinicians and researchers with expertise in childhood adversity and health outcomes. The search strategy was finalised through peer review by a second medical research librarian, and any indicated adaptations were made until consensus was reached. See online supplemental appendix B for finalised search strategies. Search results will be uploaded, deduplicated and screened in Covidence, which will be used for data management and review. Study selection/screening process RAs will begin pilot screening titles and abstracts with batches of 30–50 training articles that are randomly chosen from those generated by the search. RAs will review articles using established eligibility criteria. Screening concordance will be assessed, and faculty members (CMF, RW) will facilitate discussions after each batch is screened to clarify eligibility concerns and generate consensus. Pilot training will continue in batches until RAs achieve a minimum level of agreement of 80%, after which they will continue to review independently with supervision by a senior team member. To accommodate screening for more than 13 000 records, we anticipate needing to balance methodological rigour with the practical realities of staffing, budget and timeline constraints. Therefore, we will use a hybrid screening process that prioritises independent, dual screening, while reserving the option to transition to single screening with fidelity checks to ensure that the project can be completed within budget and on schedule, consistent with established guidance. 29 30 As long as screening agreement remains high, we may transition to single screening with routine random fidelity checks, bounded by predefined constraints and conducted on a subset of excluded records. If drift occurs, we will provide booster trainings and return to dual screening until agreement retur

title: Sensory hyper- and hyporeactivity at age 3 as transdiagnostic prospective markers of neurodevelopmental, emotional, and behavioral difficulties at age 8: A population-based cohort study in the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort Study (MoBa)
abstract: Atypical sensory reactivity is a core feature of autism but has mostly been studied in small, clinical, cross-sectional samples. We examined whether early sensory atypicalities are transdiagnostic or unique to autism and whether sensory modality and persistence matter. This study is based on the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort Study (MoBa), a Norwegian population-based cohort in which race/ethnicity is not recorded. In a subsample ( N  = 113,785; 51.0% boys, 49.0% girls; child age at the age-8 assessment M = 97.6 months, SD = 2.0; analytic samples  n  ≈ 31,000-33,000), three parent-reported markers at age 3 (auditory hypersensitivity, reduced pain sensitivity, and unusual sensory interest) predicted seven age-8 outcomes: autism traits, ADHD inattention and hyperactivity, oppositional and conduct problems, anxiety, and depressed mood. In robust regressions and a three-wave persistence analysis, sensory atypicality predicted all domains (standardized β). Autism traits were most strongly predicted ( β  = 0.18 composite; 0.42 persistent), yet not uniquely (autism-ADHD difference = 0.05 SD). Auditory hypersensitivity was related to internalizing problems, reduced pain sensitivity to externalizing problems, and lower anxiety. Cumulative load showed a graded dose-response. Effects were small, indicating population-level rather than individual predictive value.

title: Prenatal Vitamin C supplementation mediates the association between prenatal distress and infant negative affect: A prospective cohort study
abstract:
Negative affect (NA) is a temperament trait reflecting the propensity to feel and express negative emotions. High NA in infancy is an early risk factor for future psychopathology and clinical diagnoses. Prenatal maternal depression, anxiety, and stress are linked to elevated infant NA, suggesting developmental programming effects. Given its anti-oxidative and stress-regulating properties, we investigated whether prenatal vitamin C mediates the association between maternal prenatal distress and infant NA. Pregnant participants ( N =302; 73.2% White, non-Hispanic; M age =31.94 years, SD =4.23 years) reported their prenatal vitamin C supplementation and completed three 24-hour dietary recalls from which dietary vitamin C intake was derived. Participants also completed assessments for prenatal depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies-Depression [CES-D], Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS]), anxiety (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory [STAI], Beck Anxiety Inventory [BAI]), and stress (Perceived Stress Scale [PSS]). Six months following delivery, infant NA was assessed via the Infant Behavior Questionnaire-Revised. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a latent prenatal maternal distress variable, using prenatal CES-D, EPDS, STAI, BAI, and PSS as indicators. Higher prenatal maternal distress predicted higher infant NA at six months ( β =0.21, p =.001). Adjusting for covariates, structural equation modeling showed that prenatal vitamin C supplementation, but not dietary vitamin C intake, mediated the association between maternal prenatal distress and infant NA (indirect β =.02, bootstrapped 95% CI [0.01, 0.05]). As such, lower vitamin C intake during pregnancy may influence fetal neurodevelopment via altering the intrauterine environment. These findings point to prenatal vitamin C supplementation’s potential as a modifiable and scalable intervention to promote healthy early socioemotional development.

Pregnancy is a time of increased vulnerability for mental health conditions ( Howard & Khalifeh, 2020 ). Mounting evidence suggests that in utero exposures to elevated maternal distress (anxiety, depression, and stress) exerts programming effects on infant temperament ( Beijers et al., 2010 ; Blair et al., 2011 ; McGrath et al., 2008 ; Thiel et al., 2021 ), predisposing infants to future psychopathology, with effects persisting into adolescence and beyond ( Rogers et al., 2020 ). High negative affect (NA), or temperamental tendencies for elevated sadness and irritability ( Gartstein & Rothbart, 2003 ), is an early risk marker for adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes and later mental health concerns ( Grant et al., 2009 ; Kostyrka-Allchorne et al., 2020 ). It is of great interest, therefore, to identify factors involved in the mechanism by which prenatal maternal distress influences the developing brain. Adequate maternal nutrient intake during pregnancy is critical for fetal development ( Christian et al., 2015 ). Stress is a well-established contributor to unhealthy dietary patterns in the general population ( Hill et al., 2022 ). Prenatal depression, stress, and anxiety are similarly linked to poor dietary quality in pregnancy ( Avalos et al., 2020 ; Baskin et al., 2015 ). Preclinical evidence ( Mitchell et al., 2022 ; Sullivan et al., 2010 ) and emerging evidence from human studies ( Brunst et al., 2014 ; Gustafsson et al., 2016 ; Wood et al., 2025 ), links maternal perinatal nutrition to infant behavioral health and temperament, with diets high in fats and simple sugars, or with low omega-3:omega-6 ratios, associated with offspring psychopathology risk, including greater NA. While maternal prenatal nutrition is increasingly considered as a modifiable factor in programming infant temperament ( Gartstein & Skinner, 2018 ), key nutritional targets remain poorly defined. Here, we examine the association between maternal prenatal vitamin C intake and infant NA. Vitamin C, L-ascorbic acid, is an essential, water-soluble micronutrient with critical roles supporting fetal development. Pregnancy involves increased vitamin C demands, reflected in higher recommended daily allowances (85 mg/day vs. 75 mg/day for non-pregnant adults) ( Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Dietary Antioxidants and Related Compounds, 2000 ). Maternal vitamin C intake is reflected in maternal plasma concentrations of vitamin C ( Scaife et al., 2006 ), with newborns reportedly exhibiting higher cord blood concentrations of vitamin C compared to the vitamin C concentrations in maternal circulation, impacts of maternal vitamin C intake on the fetal environment. Indeed, vitamin C is preferentially transferred to the fetus under typical conditions; however, this does not occur in instances of maternal vitamin C insufficiency ( Schjoldager et al., 2013 ). Because humans cannot endogenously synthesize vitamin C, the fetus relies completely on adequate maternal vitamin C supply to meet developmental demands, including protection from oxidative stress ( Padayatty et al., 2003 ), facilitation of collagen synthesis and iron metabolism ( Lane & Richardson, 2014 ), and placental support ( Schjoldager et al., 2015 ). Vitamin C has immunomodulatory properties ( Carr & Maggini, 2017 ; Jafarnejad et al., 2018 ), which may be relevant to fetal development because, while inflammatory signaling is a normal and necessary part of pregnancy, excessive or dysregulated maternal inflammation has been linked to altered fetal neurodevelopment and later child behavioral outcomes, including elevated infant NA ( Gumusoglu & Stevens, 2019 ; Gustafsson et al., 2019 ). Importantly, vitamin C is highly concentrated in the brain ( Rice & Russo-Menna, 1997 ), and vitamin C transport into neural tissue is actively regulated, suggesting specific functional roles in central nervous system development ( Hansen et al., 2014 ). Preclinical work further suggests that vitamin C supports neurodevelopmental processes relevant to neuronal differentiation and myelination, including dopaminergic differentiation in fetal midbrain stem cells and oligodendrocyte differentiation and remyelination in experimental models ( Guo et al., 2018 ; He et al., 2015 ). Vitamin C also supports redox homeostasis ( Lykkesfeldt & Moos, 2005 ), catecholaminergic neurotransmitter system modulation ( May et al., 2013 ), and iron- and collagen-related processes relevant to vascular and tissue integrity ( Lane & Richardson, 2014 ). Preclinical work further supports the role of vitamin C exposure may influence fetal brain development, with vitamin C transporter knockout mice exhibiting perinatal mortality, cerebral hemorrhage, and increased neural oxidative stress ( Harrison et al., 2010 ; Sotiriou et al., 2002 ), while guinea pig models show that prenatal vitamin C deficiency increases markers of oxidative stress in the fetal brain during late gestation ( Paidi et al., 2014 ) and reduces postnatal hippocampal volume and disrupts hippocampal development ( Tveden-Nyborg et al., 2012 ). Early postnatal vitamin C deficiency reduces hippocampal neuron counts and impairs spatial memory ( Tveden-Nyborg et al., 2009 ). Although direct human evidence linking prenatal vitamin C intake specifically to infant NA is limited, available human and preclinical literatures support vitamin C as a biologically plausible prenatal exposure relevant to fetal brain development and infant behavioral outcomes, including NA. Despite vitamin C’s potential to program infant temperament, no prior studies have examined whether vitamin C intake helps explain the association between maternal prenatal distress and infant NA. Vitamin C can be consumed through dietary intake and supplementation. While numerous studies show comparable bioavailability between natural vs. synthetic vitamin C sources ( Carr & Vissers, 2013 ), social and psychological differences influence their intake. Dietary vitamin C, primarily obtained from fruits and vegetables, comes with additional bioactive compounds, enhancing its nutritional impact. Access to vitamin C-rich foods, however, may be limited by features of the built environment ( Morland et al., 2002 ), psychological functioning ( Avalos et al., 2020 ; Baskin et al., 2015 ), and financial constraints ( Lee, 2022 ). In contrast, vitamin C supplements provide concentrated ascorbic acid doses and may offer a more convenient alternative for those seeking to fill dietary gaps. Supplement usage may reflect differences in personal resources ( Jun et al., 2020 ), educational attainment ( Marques-Vidal et al., 2009 ), underlying psychological states ( Kessler et al., 2001 ; Marques-Vidal et al., 2009 ), and overall health ( Bailey et al., 2013 ). While there is growing recognition of prenatal nutrition’s importance for infant neurodevelopment, studies do not typically differentiate between dietary and supplemental sources of specific nutrients. Discerning their impact on infant development is a critical next step for improving clinical guidance and policy recommendations. Maternal prenatal distress may also plausibly relate to prenatal vitamin C intake. In the general population, depressive, anxious, and stress symptoms have been linked to poorer overall dietary quality ( Gibson-Smith et al., 2018 ; Schweren et al., 2021 ), including increased intake of foods with negative health effects (e.g., sugar-sweetened beverages, trans fats), which may in turn affect the intake of micronutrient-rich foods, including those high in vitamin C. In perinatal populations specifically, evidence from prior studies suggest that distress symptoms are associated with lower-quality diets overall ( Barker et al., 2013 ; Baskin et al., 2015 ), supporting the possibility that maternal distress may shape prenatal nutrient exposure through behavioral pathways such as food choice and adherence to health recommendations. Prenatal distress may also be related to supplement-taking behavior, as psychological symptoms can affect health behaviors, such as increased smoking, higher caffeine consumption, increased alcohol and drug use, and unhealthy eating ( Lobel et al., 2008 ; Mora et al., 2009 ; Zuckerman et al., 1989 ). Conversely, studies also suggest that depression and anxiety symptoms ( Kessler et al., 2001 ; Marques-Vidal et al., 2009 ) as well as higher psychosocial stress ( Shi et al., 2005 ) may be associated with higher supplementation. Thus, maternal mood may impact nutritional intake through behavioral pathways; however, mediation models are necessary to disentangle how prenatal distress may alter vitamin C intake during pregnancy and result in differences in infant development. Despite calls for examining the influence of prenatal maternal distress and nutrition on infant development ( Monk et al., 2013 ), few studies examine these exposures simultaneously ( Barker et al., 2013 ). When maternal distress and nutrition are considered, most studies assess their independent or interacting effects ( Brunst et al., 2014 ; Lipton et al., 2017 ), or adjust for one while examining the other ( Gustafsson et al., 2016 ; Wood et al., 2025 ), rather than testing whether nutrition mediates the association between maternal distress and child development. Only one study of which we are aware examines whether prenatal antioxidants moderate maternal stress effects on infant temperament ( Lipton et al., 2017 ), finding that lower dietary vitamin C intake is associated with lower effortful control and surgency/extraversion at 30 months. Knowledge gaps remain, however, including whether prenatal vitamin C intake is a mechanistic pathway by which maternal distress influences infant temperament, and whether effects are detectable at earlier stages. Identifying key nutrients that mediate the effects of prenatal distress on infant temperament would result in critical insight into modifiable intervention targets that may disrupt pathways to adverse developmental trajectories. Here, we examine maternal prenatal vitamin C intake as a potential pathway through which prenatal maternal distress influences infant NA. We address three related questions: Does prenatal maternal distress predict infant NA ? Based on prior work, we predicted that higher prenatal distress would be associated with higher infant NA. Does prenatal vitamin C intake predict infant NA ? We predicted that higher prenatal vitamin C intake would be associated with lower infant NA. Independent dietary and supplemental vitamin C effects were examined to identify which source has a stronger association with infant NA. Does prenatal vitamin C intake mediate the association between prenatal maternal distress and infant NA ? We predicted that greater prenatal distress would be associated with lower prenatal vitamin C intake (both dietary and supplemental) and that vitamin C intake would mediate the prenatal-distress-to-infant-NA association. Method Data came from a prospective, longitudinal cohort study investigating how maternal perinatal nutrition, adiposity, and metabolic state influence offspring neurodevelopment. Detailed study recruitment information is described elsewhere ( Wood et al., 2025 ; Wood et al., 2023 ). The current study focused on prenatal data during the third trimester (target data collection range: 37-39 weeks) and six months postpartum, including maternal dietary intake, supplement use, mental health questionnaires, demographic surveys, body composition assessments, medical record review, and infant temperament questionnaires. The study was approved by Oregon Health & Science University’s Institutional Review Board (IRB #18759), adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki guidelines, and written consent was obtained from all participants. Participants The sample included 302 pregnant women, who delivered between 2019-2021. Exclusionary criteria are described in detail elsewhere ( Wood et al., 2025 ; Wood et al., 2023 ) and included multiple gestation, recurrent pregnancy loss, fetal anomalies, genetic conditions affecting neurodevelopment, substance use (including nicotine), teratogenic medications or those affecting inflammation, and inflammation-linked medical conditions. The study originally enrolled N =310 participants; however, five participants were determined post-enrollment to have exclusionary medical conditions and three participants experienced fetal loss. Five participants were followed across two pregnancies, and non-independence of siblings was addressed statistically. Maternal Psychological Distress Maternal prenatal distress was assessed between 37-39 weeks using standardized measures of depression (Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale [CES-D] ( Radloff, 1977 ); Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS] ( Cox et al., 1987 )), anxiety (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory [STAI] State Scale ( Spielberger, 1983 ); Beck Anxiety Inventory [BAI] ( Beck et al., 1993 )), and stress (Perceived Stress Scale [PSS] ( Cohen et al., 1983 )). title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Adolescent Substance Use: School Connectedness as a Moderator of Risk
abstract: Although the link between adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and adolescent substance use is well established, it remains unclear how factors such as school connectedness might moderate this relationship. This study addressed this gap by examining whether the relationship between ACEs and substance use varies by levels of school connectedness among a large sample of adolescents. Data from 23,078 students in grades 9 through 12, collected via the 2022 Florida Youth Substance Abuse Survey, were analyzed using negative binomial regression models adjusting for a range of potential confounding influences. Results indicated that each additional ACE was associated with a 17% higher incidence rate of substance use (IRR = 1.17,  p  < .001). Greater school connectedness was strongly protective (IRR = 0.71,  p  < .001), which corresponds to a 29% reduction in the expected rate of substance use. Although the positive interaction term (IRR = 1.04,  p  < .001) indicates slight relative attenuation, school connectedness remained significantly associated with lower predicted substance use across all levels of ACE exposure.

title: Incorporating Childhood Identity-Based Discrimination into the Adverse Childhood Experiences Framework
abstract: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are prevalent stressors that can have lasting negative impacts on well-being. However, ACEs research has historically excluded childhood discrimination, which is an important contributor to health disparities. The goal of this study was to identify the frequency of discrimination-related ACEs in childhood and examine their effects on young adult mental health, accounting for other ACEs. This study recruited 160 18-25-year-olds who identified as members of US racial or ethnic minority groups (n = 99), as members of the LGBTQIA+ community (n = 107), or as both (n = 46). Participants were recruited to complete an online survey both through a subject pool enrolled in college-level Psychology courses as well as through community and online flyering in the Northeast US. The anonymous survey assessed history of Sexual and Gender Minority ACEs (SGM-ACEs), Racial and Ethnic Minority ACEs (REM-ACEs), traditionally assessed ACEs, and current depression and anxiety. In several models, the inclusion of SGM-ACEs alongside traditionally assessed ACEs explained significant variance in outcomes. Results demonstrated that experiencing more SGM-ACEs uniquely predicted higher anxiety (b = 1.39, SE = 0.39, β = 0.40, p < 0.001) as well as depression (b = 1.69, SE = 0.47, β = 0.41, p < 0.001), accounting for the effects of traditionally assessed ACEs and socioeconomic status. REM-ACEs were not uniquely associated with mental health. These findings highlight how larger cultural, systemic, and political influences need to be better accounted for in ACEs measures and can contribute to long-term adjustment.

title: Resiliency as a Protective Factor Against the Negative Impact of Adverse Childhood Experiences on Suicidality
abstract:
Suicide is a leading cause of death in the United States. Suicide risk is higher among those who have experienced more adverse childhood events (ACEs). Yet the impact of ACEs on suicide risk could potentially be buffered by individual-level psychological characteristics. The purpose of this study was to test whether resiliency moderated the association between ACEs and suicide attempts. Using prospective data from a large, nationally representative sample of 8,671 respondents surveyed over 30 years, we found that although each additional ACE increased the odds for making a suicide attempt by 56%, these odds were significantly lower when resilience was high. Post hoc probing of the significant interaction term indicated that when ACEs were high, but resiliency was low, the probability that a participant had made a suicide attempt was 4.4%, compared to 1.6% when ACEs were high, but resiliency was also high. Our findings on the importance of resiliency in promoting mental health indicate the need for programs designed to promote resiliency across different settings.

Suicide as a Public Health Problem Suicide is a significant public health problem and has been a leading cause of death in the United States for the past 70years (2008 (Vital and Health Statistics; CDC, 2026 ). Rates of suicide increased 37% between 2000 and 2018, then decreased 5% between 2018 and 2020 before increasing again to their peak in 2022, with an age-adjusted rate per 100,000 of 14.2 (CDC, 2025 ). In 2023, there was a suicide death every 11 min in the United States, resulting in over 49,000 deaths (CDC, 2025 ). Suicide deaths represent the tip of the iceberg. Data from 2023 indicate that in addition to the 49,316 suicides, there were 1.5 million attempts, 3.7 million who made a suicide plan, and 12.8 million people who had serious thoughts about suicide (CDC, 2026 ). Thus, for every death by suicide, there are approximately 31 suicide attempts and 234 serious suicide ideations. One of the most significant predictors of suicide is a prior attempt (Coon et al., 2024 ). Although most people (approximately 90%) who attempt suicide do not eventually die by suicide (Owens et al., 2002 ), over half of those who die by suicide have made a prior attempt (Ribeiro et al., 2016 ). These findings reveal the importance of understanding risk and protective factors for nonfatal suicidal attempts. Risk Factors of Suicide Behaviors An extensive body of literature has identified many risk factors for suicidal behaviors, including mental health issues such as depression and anxiety, as well as stressful and traumatic life events (Franklin et al., 2017 ; Werbart et al., 2021 ). Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) have also specifically been linked to an increased risk for suicidal behaviors (Choi et al., 2017 ; Dube et al., 2001 ; Ng et al., 2018 ; Thompson & Kingree, 2022 ). The various types of ACEs that have been shown to increase risk for suicidal behaviors include experiencing physical, sexual, and/or emotional abuse and neglect (Devries et al., 2014 ; Miller et al., 2013 ; Thompson & Kingree, 2022 ), having a parent with alcohol problems (Thompson et al., 2017 ; Thompson & Kingree, 2022 ), having a parental in jail during childhood (Dube et al., 2001 ; Thompson & Kingree, 2022 ), losing a parent to death (Guldin et al., 2015 ; Rostila et al., 2016 ; Thompson & Kingree, 2022 ), as well as having a family history of suicide (Brent et al., 2015 ; Feigelman et al., 2016 ; Thompson & Kingree, 2022 ). Further, research indicates that the accumulation of ACEs is associated with an increased risk for suicide attempts, such that those who experienced three or more ACEs were three times more likely to have attempted suicide than those who did not experience any ACEs (Thompson et al., 2019 ). Resiliency as a Protective Factor Research has revealed several important risk factors for suicidality, including ACES, yet less research has focused on protective factors. One protective factor that this study seeks to investigate is resiliency. The term resilience refers to the ability to recover from or adjust easily to misfortune or change (Merriam- Webster, n.d. ). This definition implies that resiliency can be conceptualized as a buffer against traumatic life experiences, thereby reducing their negative impact. A meta-analysis of 60 studies on the role of resiliency indicated that it was associated with better mental health outcomes, such as depression and anxiety (Hu et al., 2015 ). Although less attention has focused on the moderating or stress-buffering role of resilience in the presence of adversity, studies suggest that an individual’s level of resiliency can impact how they respond to adverse or traumatic events (Johnson et al., 2011 ). That is, a traumatic event may not have the same impact on everyone who experiences it. Rather, an individual’s degree of resiliency can buffer against some of the negative consequences of an adverse experience. In the Hu et al. ( 2015 ) meta-analysis, the effect sizes between resilience and mental health were significantly stronger for those experiencing adversity compared to those not experiencing adversities. The purpose of our study was to determine if the prospective association between ACEs and suicide attempts was moderated by resiliency. We hypothesized that higher levels of ACEs would be prospectively associated with a higher likelihood of suicide attempts, and that suicide risk would be attenuated when resiliency was high. We used a nationally representative sample to generalize the results to the US population. We also took advantage of a longitudinal research design, such that we could examine the long-term protective impact of resiliency in the face of childhood trauma. Although the primary (i.e., universal) prevention of ACEs is ideal, this study can help inform secondary (i.e., selective) and tertiary (i.e., treatment) prevention efforts to reduce the negative sequelae of ACEs. Method Data Source and Sampling Procedures We used restricted data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health, Harris, 2018 ; Harris et al., 2019 ). The Add Health study has followed a nationally representative sample of adolescents for approximately 30 years, from adolescence through emerging adulthood, to middle adulthood. The Add Health study was approved by the University of North Carolina School of Public Health Institutional Review Board using guidelines based on the Code of Federal Regulations on the Protection of Human Subjects 45CFR46. Local IRB approval for the secondary analysis of the restricted data was also obtained. Add Health participants provided written informed consent for participation in all aspects of the study. Participants were surveyed for the first time in 1994–1995, and then re-surveyed five additional times, 1, 7, 14, 22, and 30 years later, for a total of six waves of data collection. Details about study design, sampling, and survey procedures, and response rates are available on the Add Health website ( http://www.cpc.unc.edu/addhealth ). The Add Health research design entailed multistage sampling and clustering of students withing schools. Thus, we needed to account for this in order to obtain unbiased variance estimates and to generalize our findings to the population. Thus, we restricted our sample to individuals with valid sampling weights to ensure our findings were nationally representative. The weight variable we used was recommended for longitudinal data with Wave 1 in-home survey participants who also completed surveys at Waves 4, 5, and 6 (Chen & Harris, 2020 ). This resulted in an analytic sample of 8,671 participants. The sample was evenly divided by sex at birth, with 50% males and 50% females. At Wave 5, participants were 33–43 years old, and at Wave 6, they were 39–51 years old. Measures Dependent Variables Respondents were asked at Waves 5 and 6 “During the past 12 months, how many times have you actually attempted suicide?” A dichotomous variable was created that reflected whether a respondent had attempted suicide at least once in the past year at either Wave 5 or Wave 6. Predictor Variables We created a cumulative measure of ACEs by summing the number of eight different retrospectively reported adverse childhood experiences. In Add Health, these ACE items were reported at different times across the prospective study. However, we were able to ensure that incidents counted as an ACE occurred before the respondent was 18 years of age. Physical abuse, assessed at Wave 4, measured if respondents had been hit with a fist, kicked, or thrown on the floor, into a wall, or downstairs by a parent or adult caregiver more than once before they were 18 years of age (Brumley et al., 2017 ; Smith et al., 2018 ). Sexual abuse, assessed at Wave 4, measured if a parent or other adult caregiver had touched them in a sexual way, forced them to touch him or her in a sexual way, or forced them to have sexual relations before the age of 18. Emotional abuse, assessed at Wave 4, measured if a parent or other adult caregiver had said things that hurt their feelings or made them feel unwanted or unloved six or more times before their 18th birthday. We used a cut point of six or more times to increase the measure’s specificity in reflecting moderate-to‐severe emotional abuse (Scheidell et al., 2017 ; Smith et al., 2018 ). Neglect, assessed at Wave 3, measured if a parent or other adult caregiver had not taken care of their basic needs before sixth grade (Brumley et al., 2017 ). Parental death, assessed at Waves 1 and 2, measured if respondents had experienced the death of either parent during childhood. Parental incarceration, assessed at Wave 4, measured if a respondent’s biological mother or father had spent time in jail or prison before the youth was 18 years of age. Parental alcoholism, assessed at Wave 1 when the respondents were 12 to 17 years of age, measured if the child’s biological mother and/or biological father had alcoholism. Family history of suicide attempts, assessed at Waves 1 and 2, measured if a family member had tried to kill themselves during the past 12 months. Moderator: Resilience We used the 13-item Adolescent to Adult Health Resilience Instrument (Montoya-Williams et al., 2020 ) to assess resiliency at Wave 4 when the respondents were on average 24–32 years old. The scale developers selected questions in Add Health that that were similar to items on other validated resilience scale (e.g., Connor Davidson Resilience Scale). The scale showed good psychometric properties and good construct validity, as indicated by its correlation with the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale, which has been used to validate other resilience scales (Montoya-Williams et al., 2020 ). Items assess personal competence (e.g., “there is little I can do to change the important things in my life”), coping and isolation (e.g., “I often feel isolated from others;” “in the last 30 days, I have often felt unable to control the important things in my life”), and optimism (e.g., “overall, I expect more good things to happen to me than bad”). Items were transformed into z-scores prior to computing a mean score, since the response formats varied across items. Higher scores indicate greater resiliency (alpha = 0.79). Data Analytic Strategy We computed weighted descriptive statistics to examine the prevalence of our study variables. We used SPSS (Version 29) Complex Samples to conduct logistic regressions that tested the moderating role of resiliency in the association between ACEs and suicide attempts. We first ran a model with measures of ACEs and resiliency, while controlling for sex and age. Then, we added an interaction term between resiliency and the respective ACE to the model to determine if resiliency buffered the association of ACEs with suicide attempts. Variance estimates were adjusted to account for the complex sample design. As noted previously, we applied sample weights so we could generalize our findings to the population. We used SPSS PROCESS (version 4.2) to conduct post hoc probing of significant interactions. Results Descriptive Statistics Weighted frequencies indicated that 2.5% of the sample had attempted suicide at Waves 5 or 6. The number of ACEs reported by the sample ranged from 0 to 6. Based on weighted frequencies, a little over half of the sample (54.3%) reported no ACEs, and approximately one-quarter (25.4%) reported one ACE. Of the remaining respondents, 11.9% experienced two ACEs, 5.8% experienced three ACEs, 1.9% experienced four ACEs, 0.6% experienced five ACEs, and 0.1% reported six ACEs. The most common ACEs were experiencing emotional abuse (16.0%), having a parent with an alcohol problem (14.1%), experiencing physical abuse (12.9%), having a parent in jail (10.1%), experiencing neglect (7.2%), having someone in the family attempt or complete suicide (7.1%), experiencing sexual abuse (5.2%), and losing a parent to death as a child (4.9%). Logistic Regressions Accounting for the complex sample design, weighting the data, and controlling for age and sex, results revealed that respondents higher in resiliency had a significantly lower odds of attempting suicide (AOR = 0.31; 95% CI = 0.24–0.41). This finding indicates that the odds of someone making a suicide attempt decreased by 69% for each unit increase in resiliency. The higher the number of ACEs, the higher the odds of attempting suicide in middle adulthood (AOR = 1.56; 95% CI = 1.33–1.83). This finding indicates that the odds of making a suicide attempt increased 56% for each additional ACE experienced. Of relevance to our study’s aims, resiliency significantly moderated the association between ACEs and the odds of a suicide attempt, indicating that the association between ACEs and suicide risk varied depending on a participant’s level of self-reported resiliency (parameter coefficient = 0.21; SE = 0.10, p =.04). As shown in Table 1 and in Fig. 1 , post hoc probing of the significant interaction conducted using SPSS PROCESs (Hayes, 2018 ), indicated that when ACEs were high but resiliency was low, the probability that a participant had made a suicide attempt was 4.4%, compared to 1.6% when ACEs were high but resiliency was also high. When ACEs were low, but resilience was also low, the probability of a suicide attempt was 2.5%. Discussion This study found that higher levels of ACEs were associated with a higher likelihood of suicide attempts up to 22–30 years later. The suicide risk was attenuated when resiliency was high. In fact, the probability of a suicide attempt when ACEs were high, yet resiliency was also high, was lower than when ACEs were low, but resilience was also low. The greatest odds of a suicide attempt were when ACEs were high, and resiliency was low. title: Caregiving-related early adversities and parental context effects on adolescents' momentary emotion differentiation
abstract: Emotion differentiation - the ability to identify specific experienced emotions - correlates with psychological health. Although theorized to develop through caregiving experiences, contextual effects on emotion differentiation in developmental populations have rarely been investigated, particularly among youth who have experienced disruptions in early caregiving. Here, we examined how adolescents' momentary emotion differentiation varies across socio-emotional contexts and whether these patterns differ following exposure to severe caregiving-related early adversities (crEAs). Adolescents aged 10-17 years with or without crEAs ( N  = 81; mean age = 13.49, SD = 1.97; 53% male/47% female; 9%-Asian American, 28%-Black/African American, 34%-White/European American, 28%-Other) completed a 7-day ecological momentary assessment protocol (4-5 surveys/day), reporting emotions and social contexts. At the trait level (spanning all contexts), after controlling for covariates, there were no significant group differences in emotion differentiation. At the momentary level, negative momentary emotion differentiation decreased following negative parent-related contexts compared to other contexts. However, the momentary emotions' standard deviation indicated more differentiated phasic intensification of a few negative emotions. Importantly, exposure to crEAs attenuated these contextual effects,  F (3, 2,317) = 3.06/3.75,  p  = .027/.011. These findings provide initial evidence linking severe crEAs to affective dynamic processes and raise the hypothesis that early caregiving disruptions attenuate momentary parental modulation effects on emotion differentiation.

title: Preadolescent psychosocial maladjustment in children who exhibited different developmental patterns of co-occurring externalizing behaviors during the preschool years
abstract: The co-occurrence of externalizing behaviors (EBs) in school-aged children is associated with long-term homotypic (similar) and heterotypic (diverse) psychosocial difficulties. It is unknown whether this developmental process begins with the first manifestations of EBs in the early preschool years. This population-based cohort study examined psychosocial maladjustment at ages 10-12-including externalizing problems, addictive behaviors, internalizing problems, and socialization difficulties-among children who followed distinct patterns of single or co-occurring EBs across the preschool years. EBs included parent-rated hyperactivity-impulsivity, noncompliance, and physical aggression. Six high-trajectory classes, identified with latent growth modeling, were used as longitudinal indicators of EBs and compared to a reference class of children with low or moderate trajectories across all EBs, controlling for internalizing problems and other confounders. Results indicated that all trajectories characterized by high levels of single or co-occurring EBs showed homotypic continuity, and most exhibited heterotypic continuity, at ages 10-12. Preschoolers with a high co-occurrence pattern encompassing all three EBs showed the poorest psychosocial adjustment across all 14 outcomes in the four maladjustment domains. Differences between the other trajectories with high levels of single-EB and co-occurring EBs, relative to the reference class, were more mixed. Results suggest that high and stable levels of a single EB or co-occurring EBs in preschool are associated with significant homotypic and heterotypic continuity into preadolescence. They underscore the importance of early manifestations of EBs and highlight that the multiple co-occurring EBs observed in preadolescents originate from similar patterns observable during the preschool years.
