title: Top-Down Self-Regulation: Bidirectional Associations Between Vagal Regulation and Cool and Hot Executive Functions in Adolescents
abstract: Vagal regulation and executive functions both reflect top-down self-regulation. However, how vagal regulation and executive functions are interconnected with each other during adolescence remains an open question. This study investigated bidirectional associations between vagal regulation and cool and hot executive functions in adolescents using a two-wave data collection (T1: November 2021, T2: May 2023). At both waves, 163 Chinese adolescents (M age  = 12.92, SD age  = 0.82; 47.24% females) underwent a speech task during which their baseline respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) and RSA suppression were obtained, assessing vagal regulation, and completed a Flanker task and an Emotional Stroop task, assessing cool and hot executive functions, respectively, indexed by intra-individual reaction time variability. Results showed that baseline RSA was not significantly associated with either cool or hot executive functions at T1 or T2. Additionally, RSA suppression to the impromptu speech task was bidirectionally associated with hot executive functions across timepoints, while unidirectionally associated with cool executive functions, with only the predicted direction from RSA suppression to cool executive functions being found. Findings revealed distinct prospective associations between vagal regulation and hot and cool EFs, providing a possibility for further investigation of longitudinal co-development of different aspects of top-down self-regulation during adolescence. SUMMARY: This study is the first to explore the bidirectional associations between vagal regulation and executive functions (EFs) as two aspects of top-down self-regulation. No significant associations between baseline respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) and cool and hot EFs were found. RSA suppression to the impromptu speech task was bidirectionally associated with hot EFs and unidirectionally associated with cool EFs during adolescence. Findings revealed distinct prospective associations between vagal regulation and hot and cool EFs.

title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Disordered Eating Behaviors in Adolescence: Differences by Gender
abstract:
Eating disorders often develop during adolescence. Disordered eating behaviors (DEBs) such as skipping meals, binging, and purging are less severe but still lead to significant health problems. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are linked to various maladaptive behaviors, including DEBs, but gender-specific relationships are less understood. The purpose of this study is to explore the link between various types and measurements of ACEs and DEBs among adolescents, examining gender-specific differences. Data from the 2022 National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH), involving a nationally representative sample of 21,573 adolescents aged 11 to 17, was used. DEBs were assessed based on parent reports of binge eating, purging, and use of diet pills. Fourteen ACEs were measured in a variety of ways, including categorized into economic hardships, violence exposure, family hardships, and discrimination. Logistic regressions modeled DEBs by ACE measures, controlling for covariates. Bivariate and multivariate analyses were stratified by gender. Each additional ACE increased odds of DEBs by 33% (OR = 1.33, p < .01), with no significant gender differences in cumulative effects. However, specific ACEs had gender-differentiated impacts: food insecurity increased odds among females (OR = 2.55, p < .01), while violence increased odds for males (OR = 3.14, p < .01). Body image concerns and obesity were more strongly associated with DEBs in females, whereas higher family income was significant for males. Findings highlight the need for gender-sensitive prevention and intervention strategies, addressing household stressors and promoting healthy family dynamics for females, and focusing on coping mechanisms and emotional expression for males.

Atypical eating patterns commonly develop during adolescence (Volpe et al., 2016 ). Eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge eating share key characteristics: severe disruptions in eating behaviors, distressing thoughts and emotions, and significant physical, psychological, and social impairments (Vanderlinden & Palmisano, 2018 ). Disordered eating behaviors (DEB), though less severe, can include meal skipping, binging, purging, restrictive dieting, and the use of diet pills to control weight (Dunn et al., 2022 ). Globally, around 1 in 5 children and adolescents engage in DEBs (Hart et al., 2020 ; Lopez-Gile et al., 2023 ). While not everyone with DEBs will develop an eating disorder, DEBs share risk factors and outcomes with more severe disorders, including long-term consequences like health problems, self-harm, poor mental health, and impaired functioning (Kärkkäinen et al., 2018 ; Micali et al., 2016 ; Warne et al., 2021 ). Both males and females engage in DEBs, but prevalence, symptoms, and impacts vary by gender (Chen et al., 2022 ; Massaldjieva et al., 2017 ). Females are more likely to restrict diets, binge eat, and purge (López-Gile et al., 2023 ), while DEBs in males have been increasing, especially related to body dissatisfaction, muscularity concerns, and pursuit of a lean physique (Gorrell & Murray, 2019 ; Mitchison & Mond, 2015 ). Outcomes also differ in that females may experience low body weight, amenorrhea, and osteoporosis (Barrack et al., 2021 ), while males are at risk of muscle dysmorphia, steroid use, and excessive exercise (Badenes-Ribera et al., 2019 ; Nagata et al., 2019 ). Gender differences in DEB etiology and consequences highlight the need for further research into how these behaviors manifest in adolescents across genders. Various factors contribute to DEB onset and maintenance, including psychological, interpersonal, sociocultural, and biological factors. Psychological traits such as low self-esteem, negative affect, perfectionism, neuroticism, poor body image, and difficulty regulating emotions are linked to DEBs (Russon et al., 2019 ). These vulnerabilities often interact with environmental stressors, leading to maladaptive coping mechanisms, such as using food to manage distress. Additionally, interpersonal relationships, especially family and peer dynamics, shape attitudes toward food and body image, influencing DEB development (Haynos et al., 2016 ; Keel & Forney, 2013 ). DEBs also share risk factors with obesity, including sociocultural pressures and interpersonal dynamics (Barakat et al., 2023 ; Jabeile et al., 2021 ). Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) have emerged as significant risk factors for various adverse outcomes, including mental health disorders and DEBs. First studied by Felitti et al. ( 1998 ), ACEs encompass abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction, including parental incarceration, domestic violence, household mental illness or suicide, and substance abuse. Additional adversities such as neighborhood violence, bullying, and parental death are also commonly included in ACE measures. ACEs are often studied using a cumulative risk framework, with research showing a dose-response relationship: the more ACEs, the higher the likelihood of adverse outcomes (Grummitt et al., 2022 ; Liming et al., 2018 ). Some studies suggest not all ACEs are equal, with certain ACEs forming natural clusters (Lee et al., 2020 ), while others highlight gender differences in the association between ACEs and adverse outcomes (Grigsby et al., 2020 ; Jones et al., 2022 ; Machado et al., 2024 ). ACEs are consistently linked to the development of eating disorders. Studies have shown that individuals who experience childhood adversities such as household violence, household mental illness, or neglect are more likely to develop eating disorders (Chu et al., 2022 ; Kovács-Tóth et al., 2022 ; Pop et al., 2020 ). The cumulative impact of ACEs also increases the likelihood of an eating disorder diagnosis (Chu et al., 2022 ; Guillaume et al., 2016 ; Kovács-Tóth et al., 2022 ). Specific ACEs, such as household mental illness, household violence, and criminal household members, have been found to have particularly strong associations with binge-eating disorder in younger age groups (Chu et al., 2022 ). Thus, childhood adversities increase the risk of developing eating disorders, and the type and number of adversities are important considerations in understanding these risks. Fewer studies have investigated the connection between ACEs and the broader spectrum of DEBs, but some research has begun to explore these relationships. Weight-based teasing, for instance, has been linked to dietary restraint and bulimic behaviors (Menzel et al., 2010 ), while individual studies have identified links between physical, sexual, and emotional abuse, bullying, discrimination, and various DEBs (Dunn et al., 2022 ; Fuemmeler et al., 2009 ; Isohookanaa et al., 2016 ; Nelson et al., 2023 ). However, Morrison ( 2021 ) emphasizes the need for more research to understand how different types and numbers of ACEs relate to DEBs. While much research has focused on the association between ACEs and eating disorders, especially in adult populations, the relationship between specific ACEs and DEBs in adolescents remains underexplored. Given that DEBs can severely impact physical and psychological well-being and increase the risk of developing clinically diagnosed eating disorders, this study aims to fill a critical gap in the literature. We will examine the relationship between multiple types of ACEs and DEBs, focusing on both individual ACE items and cumulative measures of ACEs by domain clusters. Additionally, given gender differences in DEB prevalence and emotional outcomes, the study will stratify results by gender to assess whether certain ACE items or clusters disproportionately affect adolescent females compared to males. Methods Data from the 2022 National Surveys of Children’s Health (NSCH) were used for this study. The NSCH is a cross-sectional survey designed to measure child physical and mental health, as well as access to health care services and socio-environmental contexts of families. The survey employs a complex sampling methodology that draws on the US Census Bureau’s Master Address File, which spans all 50 states and the District of Columbia. NSCH data were collected using a two-stage paper survey instrument and a single-stage web-based survey instrument to ensure adequate representation across geographic regions, racial/ethnic groups, and socioeconomic status. Sample weights were calculated to account for nonresponse, align the sample distribution with the known population distribution, adjust for potential coverage error, and provide reliable estimates at the national level and for specific demographic groups. Parents or guardians responded on behalf of their children regardless of their age (CAHMI, 2024). Our sample was truncated to adolescents ages 11 to 17, resulting in n = 21,573. Measures Disordered Eating Parents were asked if their child engaged in several behaviors related to eating in the last year. These included (1) binge eating, (2) purging or vomiting after eating, or (3) using diet pills, laxative, or diuretics to lose or maintain weight without a doctor’s orders. If parents responded ‘yes’ to individual disordered eating behaviors, they were coded 1, and ‘no’ was coded as 0. If parents answered ‘yes’ to any of the three behaviors, they were coded as 1 (any disordered eating), while ‘no’ responses to any of the three items were coded as 0 (no disordered eating). Adverse Childhood Experiences Parents were asked a series of questions on household poverty, child violence exposure, family hardships, and different forms of discrimination. Each item listed below was dummy coded (yes = 1, no = 0). Four clusters of ACEs were identified: economic hardships, violence exposure, family hardships, and discrimination. Economic Hardships : (1) basic needs : reports that it was sometimes or often hard to cover basic needs like food or housing since the child was born; (2) food scarcity : reports that sometimes or often household was not able to afford enough food to eat in the previous year; and (3) housing : reports of a parent being worried about being evicted from their home in the previous year. Violence Exposure included: (1) the child witnessed violence in the home in their lifetime; (2) the child was a victim or witnessed violence in the neighborhood in their lifetime; and (3) the child was bullied or picked on by other children in the previous year. Family Hardship included: (1) parental separation or divorce; (2) parent death , (3) parent incarceration , (4) household member with severe mental illness , and (5) household member with alcohol or drug problems . Finally, Discrimination included: (1) racial discrimination: child treated or judged unfairly due to their race or ethnicity; (2) gender discrimination: child treated or judged unfairly due to their sexual orientation or gender identity; and (3) disability discrimination: child treated or judged unfairly due to health condition or disability. These 14 items were added together to create a continuous measure ranging from 0 ACEs to 14. Additionally, each of the clusters were coded as ordinal measures: 0 = no ACEs, 1 = single ACE, and 2 = multiple ACEs per cluster. Covariates Important variables related to DEBs and ACEs as identified in the literature review were included in multivariate models. These included child age in years, child sex (female or male), and race and ethnicity (Non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, Asian, multiple race/ethnicities, Other (including American Indian or Alaskan Native, Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander, and other race/ethnicity not listed), and Non-Hispanic White. Family poverty was measured by calculating the family’s income-to-needs ratio, which was estimated by dividing family income by its corresponding poverty threshold in 2022. The poverty threshold varies by family size and is based on the money necessary for the minimally accepted amounts of food. It ranged from 50% of the Federal poverty line (FPL) to 400% of the FPL. Parents were asked how concerned their child was about their weight, body shape, or body size in the last year. If parents responded “very much” or “somewhat,” they were coded as 1 ( body image concern ), and “not at all” was coded as 0 (no body image concern). Parents were asked to report child’s height and weight. Body Mass Index (BMI) was then calculated as obese (= 1) if they were at or above the 95th percentile based on standardized growth curves published by the CDC (Kuczmarski, 2000 ). For family functioning, parents were asked how often all family members who live in the household ate a meal together in the previous week. Ordinal responses included never (zero days), some days (one-to-three days), most days (four-to-six days), and every day (seven days). This measure was dichotomized to family mealtimes every day = 1 and all else = 0. Analytic Plan All analyses were performed using STATA Statistical Software Release 16. STATA survey commands were applied to obtain unbiased estimates of population parameters. The differences in DEBs by individual ACE items and ordinal cluster measures were examined using the Pearson χ 2 test. Mean score differences in the number of total ACEs by DEB were performed using independent t-test analysis. Analyses also included logistic regressions, which modeled DEB by various measures of ACEs – including individual items, ordinal clusters, and overall mean number of items - while controlling for covariates. All analyses were also stratified by gender. Odds ratios were calculated for logistic regression models. This study was reviewed by the first author’s University institutional review board and was determined not to constitute human subjects research due to data being publicly available. Results As shown in Tables 1 , 6% of youth engaged in DEBs in the previous year: 0.5% purged, 5.5% binged, and 0.2% used diet pills. Regarding ACEs, 15% of families faced basic needs and housing issues, while 6% had low food security. Seven percent of children witnessed violence, 6% were victims, and 34% were bullied. 32% experienced family separation, 5% dealt with a family death, 8% had an incarcerated family member, and 12% were impacted by mental illness or substance abuse. Discrimination was reported by 7% for race, 4% for health, and 3% for gender. Youth averaged 14 years of age, with just under half being female. Racial composition was 46% non-Hispanic White, 26% Hispanic, 14% non-Hispanic Black, 9% other races, and 5% Asian. The average income-to-needs ratio was 2.5 times the poverty threshold. Body image concerns were reported by 32% of youth, with 16% classified as obese. About 33% of families ate meals together daily. T-test analysis (not reported in tables) showed that youth exhibiting a DEB had on average 3.1 ACEs (SD = 2.5) compared to 1.4 ACEs (SD = 1.7) for youth not exhibiting a DEB, t(19,593) = 30.4, p <.0001. There were no differences in direction, effect size, or significance when stratifying by gender. Table

title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Associated Health-Risk Behaviors Among University Students in Turkey: A Cross-Sectional Analysis
abstract: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are potentially traumatic events occurring before the age of 18 that may have long-term consequences for health and well-being. This study aimed to examine the association between ACEs and health-risk behaviors (HRBs) among university students in Turkey. A cross-sectional web-based survey was conducted between April and June 2024 with 1,115 university students aged 18–27 years. Data were collected using a structured self-report questionnaire assessing exposure to ACEs, including child maltreatment and household dysfunction, as well as a range of HRBs in young adulthood. Overall, 97.7% of participants reported experiencing at least one ACE, while 47.8% reported exposure to four or more ACEs. The most frequently reported ACEs were community violence (81.1%), emotional neglect (74.0%), emotional abuse (49.9%), witnessing violence against household members (39.2%), bullying (33.2%), and physical abuse (27.9%). A higher number of ACEs was significantly associated with several HRBs, including tobacco use, alcohol consumption, sedentary behavior, overweight and obesity, suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, interpersonal violence, and early sexual initiation (before age 16). These findings indicate a strong association between cumulative exposure to childhood adversity and multiple health-risk behaviors in young adulthood. The results highlight the need for trauma-informed public health strategies aimed at preventing ACEs and promoting resilience to reduce the long-term health consequences of childhood adversity.

title: Opposing excitatory and inhibitory synaptic pathologies drive ZC4H2-associated intellectual disability
abstract: Understanding genotype-phenotype correlations is critical for precision medicine, yet patients carrying mutations in the same gene are often classified under one disorder and treated alike, despite potentially opposite responses to therapy. ZC4H2-associated rare disorder (ZARD) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental condition caused by diverse mutations across ZC4H2. Here, we show that distinct ZC4H2 mutations drive intellectual disability through opposing synaptic mechanisms. The gain-of-function mutation ZC4H2 L66H  enhances GABA A  receptor (GABA A R) degradation, impairing inhibitory synaptic transmission and plasticity. By contrast, the loss-of-function mutation ZC4H2 R213W  increases AMPA receptor (AMPAR) stability and dysregulates excitatory synaptic activity. Despite these diametrically opposed synaptic pathologies, ZC4H2 L66H/y  and ZC4H2 R213W/y  knockin mice exhibit comparable cognitive deficits. Importantly, muscimol, a GABA A R agonist, specifically rescues deficits in ZC4H2 L66H/y  mice, whereas the AMPAR antagonist perampanel rescues ZC4H2 R213W/y  mice. These findings demonstrate that opposing synaptic etiologies can underlie a single genetic disorder and highlight pathomechanism-based stratification for targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Hypothalamus-driven brain health through metabolic flexibility
abstract: Organismal physiology depends on continuous, non-hierarchical communication among cells, tissues, and organs. We argue that this communication rests on metabolic flexibility-the capacity of cells and tissues to adapt substrate use to changing energetic demands-and that the hypothalamus serves as the central hub coordinating this flexibility across the body. Using hypothalamic agouti-related protein (AgRP) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons as a model, we show these melanocortin neurons do more than regulate hunger and satiety: by integrating metabolic, hormonal, and immune signals, they shape reward, learning, executive function, and social behavior, while imposing coordinated metabolic states on peripheral tissues. When this flexibility is lost, as with aging or overnutrition, body-brain communication becomes rigid, driving cognitive decline, chronic inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease. We propose that signals from the body are not peripheral modifiers of brain function but fundamental determinants of it, with direct implications for hypothalamus-centered strategies to preserve brain health across the lifespan.

title: Cell-specific transcription dysregulation in human Huntington's disease-positive developing striatum
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG-repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Progressive loss of striatal projection neurons leads to cognitive, psychiatric, and motor impairments that typically manifest in midlife, despite the expansion being present from conception. Increasing evidence supports a neurodevelopmental component to HD; however, authentic human developing HD-positive striatal tissue has not previously been characterised. We used single-cell RNA sequencing to compare an HD-positive human fetal striatal sample to an age- and sex-matched control, with CAG-repeat lengths of 16, 49 and 16, 17 respectively. We also compared the fetal HD-positive transcriptional signature with publicly available datasets from postmortem adult HD-positive brain tissue. We identified 2,032 differentially expressed genes and defined nine cellular clusters.. Gene enrichment analysis revealed alteration of key biological processes across the developing HD-positive striatum, with pathway-level dysregulation varying between clusters. There was substantial overlap in gene expression changes between fetal and adult HD-positive striatal tissues, although not in all transcriptional profiles, and some were reversed. Together, these findings demonstrate that molecular features of HD pathology are present during early human striatal development, supporting the concept that disease mechanisms are established decades prior to clinical onset.

title: Cell-type- and subregion-specific basolateral amygdala inputs to ventral CA1-subiculum
authors: Li 李明华 M et al.
abstract: The hippocampus is essential for learning and memory and interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions. Although the heterogeneity of intrinsic connectivity of hippocampal neurons is well established, the diversity of its extrahippocampal connectivity remains less understood. Such differential connectivity may contribute to functional diversity of hippocampal neurons in specific positions. Ventral CA1 (vCA1) and ventral subiculum (vSub) form strong reciprocal connections with the basolateral amygdala (BLA), a region critical for emotional and social regulation. Consequently, BLA-vCA1-vSub circuits have been implicated in anxiety-related and social behaviors. However, the functional connectivity from BLA to vCA1-vSub at the cellular and circuit levels is underexplored. To address this, we combined viral tracing with Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)-assisted slice electrophysiology to examine BLA projections to vCA1-vSub in mice of either sex. We found that BLA inputs are not uniformly distributed along the transverse axis in vCA1-vSub. Instead, BLA selectively excites pyramidal neurons in distal vCA1-vSub while largely avoiding proximal vCA1 near CA2. BLA terminals strongly excited parvalbumin-expressing interneurons but only weakly recruited a small subset of somatostatin-expressing interneurons, generating robust disynaptic inhibitory synaptic currents in pyramidal neurons. Additionally, the same distal pyramidal neurons that receive BLA excitation also project back to the BLA. These findings reveal that BLA establishes cell-type- and subregion-specific excitatory connections within vCA1-vSub, highlighting a circuit architecture that may underlie functional heterogeneity in ventral hippocampal processing. Significance statement  The hippocampus interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions, yet how long-range extrahippocampal inputs are organized across hippocampal subregions remains poorly understood. We examined projections from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to the ventral hippocampus and found that BLA inputs selectively excite pyramidal neurons in distal ventral CA1 and ventral subiculum while largely avoiding proximal ventral CA1. BLA projections preferentially excite parvalbumin-expressing interneurons, provide disynaptic inhibition onto pyramidal neurons, and are reciprocally connected with the same pyramidal neurons in ventral CA1 and subiculum they excite. These findings reveal a highly selective connectivity pattern of amygdala-hippocampal circuits, providing a circuit framework for understanding how emotional information is routed through distinct ventral hippocampal pathways.

title: A multi-institutional investigation of psilocybin's effects on mouse behavior
abstract: Studies reporting the effects of psychedelic drugs on mouse behavior are rapidly emerging. However, the reproducibility and reliability of these effects remain uncertain. Here we implemented a multi-institutional collaborative approach to assess which effects of psilocybin on mouse behavior are robust and replicable. Five independent laboratories performed the same experiments to test the acute and persistent effects of psilocybin (2 mg kg -1 , intraperitoneally) on various behaviors. Psilocybin acutely increased anxiety- and avoidance-related behaviors and decreased fear expression in a robust and replicable manner. Surprisingly, however, psilocybin did not have replicable effects 24 h after administration in terms of reducing anxiety- and depression-like behaviors or facilitating fear extinction learning. Additionally, we did not observe psilocybin-induced alterations in social preference or social reward learning. Our characterization of psilocybin's behavioral effects, using ~200 male and female mice per experiment across five laboratories, demonstrates several robust acute effects and suggests that some of psilocybin's reported persistent effects in mice may be modest and/or inconsistent.

title: Redox-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial nucleoids contributes to bioenergetic decline during neuronal aging
abstract:
Summary Why mitochondria progressively fail in aging neurons remains a fundamental question in neurobiology. Although bioenergetic decline and oxidative stress are hallmarks of aging, whether redox signaling remodels mitochondrial nucleoids (mt-nucleoids) to impair neuronal bioenergetics remains unclear. Using aged mouse neurons and human iPSC-derived neurons, we demonstrate that redox-driven mt-nucleoid remodeling underlies reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and bioenergetic decline. Combining MINFLUX nanoscopy with single-molecule transcription mapping, we identify distinct mt-nucleoid architectures governed by TFAM-mediated mtDNA compaction. Aging-associated oxidative stress drives mt-nucleoid remodeling from compact, transcriptionally active structures toward decompacted forms with reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and impaired mitochondrial ATP production. This remodeling involves species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms: cysteine oxidation promotes human TFAM polymerization, whereas methionine oxidation weakens mouse TFAM-mtDNA interactions. Notably, expressing an oxidation-resistant TFAM variant restores mt-nucleoid organization, mtDNA transcript abundance, and ATP production in aged neurons, identifying mt-nucleoid architecture as a potential target for preserving neuronal bioenergetics during aging.

Graphical Abstract

eTOC blurb Cheng and Gao et al. reveal that oxidative stress remodels mitochondrial DNA organization in aging neurons, disrupting mitochondrial gene expression and bioenergetics. Species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms converge on mt-nucleoid decompaction. Expression of redox-resistant TFAM restores mt-nucleoid compaction and ATP production, revealing a conserved mechanism linking oxidative stress to mitochondrial dysfunction.

Introduction A central challenge in aging research is understanding why mitochondria—the primary source of cellular energy—progressively fail in long-lived tissues. This question is especially important for neurons, which are uniquely vulnerable to bioenergetic deficits because of their high metabolic demands, elaborate morphologies, and postmitotic longevity. 1 , 2 Recent advances underscore this problem: (i) mitochondrial transcripts encoding electron transport chain (ETC) subunits decline broadly with age, 3 , 4 (ii) mitochondrial dysfunction accelerates aging, 5 , 6 whereas preserving mitochondrial integrity delays functional decline, 7 and (iii) brain-wide respiration atlases identify aging as a major determinant of mitochondrial performance. 8 Together, these findings highlight a fundamental gap in understanding how age-associated changes in mitochondrial genome organization and regulation—beyond mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) mutations 9 , 10 —drive bioenergetic decline. Although mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are defining hallmarks of aging, 11 – 13 how redox imbalance disrupts mitochondrial genome organization over the lifespan remain largely unknown. The mtDNA, which encodes 13 essential ETC subunits, 14 is packaged with its transcriptional machinery into ~100-nm mt-nucleoids. 15 – 17 Mitochondrial Transcription Factor A (TFAM), the principal nucleoid-associated protein, binds, bends, loops, and compacts mtDNA through dimerization, thereby organizing the genome for transcription. 18 – 20 Disruption of TFAM-dependent mtDNA packaging and transcription has been implicated in aging and neurodegeneration. 21 Individual mt-nucleoids can exist in transcriptionally active or quiescent states, 22 but how these structural states are regulated and affect mitochondrial gene expression and bioenergetics remains poorly understood. Because mitochondria are a major source of reactive oxygen species (ROS), 23 , 24 mt-nucleoids are chronically exposed to oxidative stress, which increases in aging neurons. 25 Although reversible protein oxidation contributes to physiological redox signaling, persistent oxidative stress disrupts redox homeostasis and promotes protein dysfunction and tissue aging. 26 Whether age-associated oxidative stress remodels mt-nucleoid architecture to impair mitochondrial transcription and bioenergetic function, and whether these changes can be reversed, remains unknown. Addressing this question has been limited by the lack of mammalian neuronal aging models that integrate nanoscale mt-nucleoid analysis with measurements of mitochondrial ATP production, redox homeostasis, and mtDNA transcript abundance at single-organelle and single-molecule resolution. Here, using dorsal root ganglion neurons (DRGNs) from young adult and aged mice, we combine MINFLUX nanoscopy with live ATP and redox imaging, in situ transcription mapping, biomolecular phase-separation assays, and machine-learning modeling to define a mitochondrial aging signature. Aged neurons exhibit disorganized mt-nucleoids, reduced mitochondrial respiration and ATP production, elevated oxidative stress, and reduced mtDNA transcript abundance. Similar remodeling occurs in aged mouse hippocampal neurons. MINFLUX imaging (~3-nm localization precision) reveals an aging-associated mt-nucleoid architecture characterized by decompacted mtDNA and reduced TFAM localization density. Mechanistically, oxidative stress drives this transition through species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms: disulfide-mediated polymerization of human TFAM and methionine oxidation–dependent weakening of mouse TFAM–mtDNA interactions. Despite these distinct mechanisms, both converge on mt-nucleoid decompaction. These redox-dependent changes are reproduced in human iPSC-derived cortical neurons exposed to oxidative stress, whereas expression of a redox-resistant, mtDNA-packaging-competent TFAM variant restores mt-nucleoid compaction, mtDNA transcript abundance, and ATP production in aged neurons. Together, our findings establish redox-dependent mt-nucleoid remodeling as a conserved mechanism linking oxidative stress to mitochondrial dysfunction during neuronal aging and identify TFAM redox regulation as a potential therapeutic target for age-associated neurodegeneration. Results Establishing an aging mouse neuron model To investigate how aging remodels mt-nucleoids, we established a primary neuronal aging model using DRGNs isolated from young adult and aged mice. Because postmitotic neurons do not divide, DRGNs from aged mice provide a tractable system for investigating age-dependent remodeling of mt-nucleoids and mitochondrial bioenergetics. Unlike intact aged brain tissue, cultured DRGNs enable nanoscale visualization of individual mt-nucleoids together with measurements of mitochondrial ATP production, redox dynamics, and mtDNA transcripts. Although many neuronal populations from aged animals exhibit poor survival in culture, 27 , 28 DRGNs are unusually resilient and retain key physiological properties. 29 – 35 We therefore compared DRGNs from young adult (1 month, P1M) and aged (24 months, P24M) mice. Neurons from both age groups extended elaborate axonal arbors and maintained dense mitochondrial networks throughout the soma and distal processes ( Figure S1A ). Thus, this preparation provides a tractable model for examining mt-nucleoid architecture, mitochondrial bioenergetics, redox homeostasis, and mtDNA transcript abundance during neuronal aging. Aging-associated mt-nucleoid decompaction occurs in peripheral and central neurons Mitochondrial genome instability contributes to aging, 13 , 36 yet whether mt-nucleoid architecture is preserved during neuronal aging remains unknown. Aberrant mt-nucleoid morphology has been reported in skin fibroblasts from individuals with Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS), a premature aging disorder, 18 suggesting that mt-nucleoid disorganization may contribute to age-associated mitochondrial dysfunction. Because TFAM is the principal organizer of mt-nucleoids and is required for mtDNA compaction and transcription, 19 we asked whether physiological aging disrupts TFAM-dependent mtDNA packaging in neurons. We first examined mt-nucleoid organization in DRGNs from young adult (P1M) and aged (P24M) mice. In young adult neurons, mt-nucleoids appeared as compact, sharply defined circular puncta, with extensive colocalization of mtDNA and TFAM ( Figure 1A ). In contrast, aged neurons exhibited enlarged, dispersed, and irregular mtDNA- and TFAM-positive structures. Despite these morphological changes, overall mt-nucleoid density did not differ significantly between young adult and aged neurons ( Figure S1B ). Consistent with these observations, while young adult neurons contained compact, well-defined mt-nucleoids within the mitochondrial network in the soma, aged neurons displayed enlarged and decondensed mt-nucleoids, with increased mtDNA- and TFAM-positive area, reduced circularity, and lower fluorescence intensity ( Figures 1B – 1E ). We next asked whether neuronal aging similarly affects other mitochondrial biomolecular condensates, including mitochondrial RNA granules (MRGs), which mediate mitochondrial RNA processing. Using GRSF1 as an MRG marker, 37 we found that, in contrast to the pronounced mt-nucleoid decompaction in aged neurons, MRG morphology was largely preserved, with no significant age-associated changes in granule area, circularity, or fluorescence intensity ( Figures S1C and S1D ). These findings indicate that aging-associated remodeling selectively affects mt-nucleoids rather than reflecting a generalized reorganization of mitochondrial biomolecular condensates. To determine whether this remodeling extends beyond peripheral neurons, we examined hippocampal sections from adult (P3M) and aged (P24M) mice. The soma-enriched pyramidal cell layer and the adjacent neurite-enriched stratum radiatum were identified based on nuclear staining ( Figure S2A ). Compared with adult mice, aged hippocampal neurons exhibited enlarged and decompacted mtDNA and TFAM signals in both somatic and neuritic compartments ( Figures S2B and S2C ), consistent with the mt-nucleoid remodeling observed in aged DRGNs ( Figure 1 ). TFAM signals were confirmed to localize to mitochondria ( Figure S2D ). Thus, aging-associated mt-nucleoid remodeling occurs in both neuronal somata and neurites, supporting the conclusion that mt-nucleoid decompaction is a conserved feature of neuronal aging in both peripheral and central neurons. Machine-learning segmentation identifies a decompacted mt-nucleoid population in aged neurons To distinguish compact from decompacted mt-nucleoid populations, we developed a machine-learning semantic segmentation framework integrating an InceptionV3 backbone 38 into a U-Net architecture (iUNet). Trained on manually annotated confocal images ( Figures S3A and S3B ), iUNet outperformed conventional threshold-based segmentation and showed high concordance with expert annotations ( Figures S3C – S3H ). Quantitative analysis revealed that the age-associated increase in mt-nucleoid area arose predominantly from expansion of the decompacted population ( Figures 1F and S3I ), whereas reduced circularity was most pronounced among compact nucleoids ( Figures 1G and S3J ). Both mtDNA and TFAM fluorescence intensities were reduced in aged neurons ( Figures 1H and S3K ), consistent with decreased TFAM-mtDNA packing density. Thus, young adult neurons were dominated by compact, TFAM-enriched mt-nucleoids, whereas aged neurons exhibited an expanded population of decompacted, TFAM-reduced mt-nucleoids. These findings prompted nanoscale interrogation of mt-nucleoid architecture using MINFLUX nanoscopy. MINFLUX nanoscopy reveals aging-associated mt-nucleoid remodeling Conventional super-resolution methods, including STED and PALM/STORM, provide ~20-nm resolution, limiting their ability to resolve nanoscale structural transitions within individual mt-nucleoids and quantify TFAM-mtDNA packaging at the single-molecule level. We therefore employed MINFLUX (Minimal Photon Fluxes) nanoscopy, which provides 1–3 nm localization precision and resolves fluorophores separated by ~6 nm. 39 , 40 Two-dimensional MINFLUX imaging revealed striking age-associated remodeling of mt-nucleoid architecture. Individual mt-nucleoids, selected from confocal fields (5 × 5 μm 2 ), were resolved into distinct nanoscale structures. In young adult (P1M) neurons, mt-nucleoids predominantly exhibited compact, TFAM-enriched condensates, whereas aged (P24M) neurons displayed decompacted, irregular TFAM organization ( Figures 2A and 2B ). Although TFAM localization density spanned a continuous distribution in both age groups, consistent with previous observations using confocal and STED microscopy in human fibroblasts and Hela cells, 41 MINFLUX revealed a pronounced age-associated shift toward lower TFAM localization density ( Figure 2C ), with redistribution from TFAM-dense to TFAM-depleted mt-nucleoids ( Figure 2D ). Three-dimensional MINFLUX imaging further confirmed these structural transitions ( Videos S1 – S3 ). Dual-color MINFLUX imaging further revealed age-associated changes in TFAM-mtDNA organization. Although mtDNA and TFAM remained colocalized in both age groups, aged neurons exhibited increased mtDNA area per nucleoid, consistent with mtDNA decompaction ( Figures 2E and 2F ). Across individual mt-nucleoids, mtDNA area was inversely correlated with TFAM localization density, such that larger, more decompacted nucleoids exhibited lower TFAM density ( Figure 2G ). Thus, neuronal aging is accompanied by a progressive transition from compact, TFAM-enriched nucleoids to decompacted, TFAM-depleted nucleoids ( Figure 2H ). Together with previous studies linking distinct mt-nucleoid packaging states to genome maintenance and transcription, 18 , 19 , 42 , 43 our MINFLUX analyses identify an aging-associated remodeling characterized by reduced TFAM localization density and impaired mtDNA packaging, potentially compromising mitochondrial gene expression. Reduced mtDNA transcript abundance in aged neurons To determine the functional consequence of aging-associated mt-nucleoid remodeling, we quantified mtDNA transcript abundance using single-molecule Hybridization Chain Reaction (smHCR). 44 We examined four mtDNA-encoded transcripts representing distinct ETC complexes: NADH dehydrogenase 1 (ND1, Complex I), cytochrome b (Cytb, Complex III), cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COXI, Complex IV), and ATPase 6 (ATP6, Complex V). Compared with young adult neurons, aged neurons exhibited a marked reduction in transcript abundance for all four mtDNA-encoded genes ( Figures 2I , 2J , and S4A ). Probe specificity was validated using mouse COXI probe in mouse DRGNs and human HeLa cells lacking the complementary mouse COXI sequence, which showed only background fluorescence ( Figure S4B ). Single-cell analyses demonstrated that the decline in mtDNA transcript abundance paralleled aging-associated mt-nucleoid remodeling.
