title: Network disruption in post-stroke depressive symptoms: a Bayesian multicohort study
abstract: Post-stroke depressive symptoms are common, but studies on the contributions of lesion locations to depression symptoms remain inconsistent. Bayesian statistics offer the possibility to clarify these inconsistencies by providing evidence in favor and against observed associations. We reanalyzed four previously published observational cohorts with 1,864 patients with stroke characterized for depressive symptoms from France, Korea, Germany and the USA. We performed voxel-wise Bayes factor mapping using general linear models. Lesion maps were used to test for associations of post-stroke depressive symptoms with lesion location. Network level associations were tested based on structural disconnection and functional lesion network maps estimated by reference to normative connectome data. Due to a sample size with broad lesion coverage, Bayesian inference was informative in large parts of the brain. Lesion associations were found in clusters in the right hemisphere including cortical (frontal, insular, parietal) and subcortical regions (striatum, amygdala, hippocampus) and adjacent white matter. Evidence of no contribution to post-stroke depressive symptoms was observed in large parts of the left hemisphere. Structural disconnection was linked to depressive symptoms in the bilateral frontal white matter prominently involving the corpus callosum and anterior thalamic radiation. Lesion network mapping revealed evidence of an association of post-stroke depressive symptoms with network connectivity in the left posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, and less consistently, the bilateral anterior insula, along with widespread absence of associations in other regions. Depressive symptoms were most strongly associated with right frontal lesions and right-dominant structural disconnection in frontal cortico-subcortical circuits.

title: Gaze reinstatement during working memory for natural scenes
abstract: The information we hold in mind with working memory (WM) may propagate beyond the cortex and out to the peripheral motor system. For instance, directionally biased hand and eye movements can express simple visuo-spatial features during WM maintenance. If such sensorimotor inflections are a form of WM representation, they may also express more detailed and task-adaptive information about WM content. Here, we ask whether gaze patterns carry item-specific detail about complex stimuli held in mind, and whether gaze during WM maintenance adapts to upcoming behavioral demands. To do this, we tracked male and female human eye movements during WM for naturalistic images, and we manipulated which image properties were most task-relevant (visual or semantic). In two experiments, we found that the eyes moved in item-specific spatiotemporal sequences during WM maintenance. Delay period gaze patterns retraced the scanpaths from stimulus encoding, echoing the 'gaze reinstatement' that has been observed during long-term memory retrieval. Therefore, gaze patterns during WM may reinstate visual encoding processes for maintenance. We also used time-resolved representational similarity analyses, guided by convolutional neural network modeling, to test the specificity of WM gaze patterns across a trial. We found that gaze representations were more distinct when the task prioritized visual detail, and they also ramped up in anticipation of the WM probe. Therefore, oculomotor WM signals are malleable to when and how the content will be used. WM may recruit the most primary structures in sensorimotor processing, where eye movements reflect flexible and future-oriented WM content information. Significance Statement  The eyes are an outwardly accessible extension of the brain. They filter sensory input and enact motor output, but may also offer a rich window into underlying cognition. For instance, pupil dilation can reflect changing cognitive load, and biased eye movements can reflect basic spatial information about content held in mind with working memory (WM). WM is a critical neuro-cognitive function, but its physiological bases remain under debate. Here, we show that during WM the eyes can move in intricate patterns that read out the complex, real-world stimuli held in mind. This work shows how cognitive states influence oculomotor functions, and also advances theories of WM maintenance to include the most basic structures in sensorimotor processing.

title: Learning-dependent hippocampal-striatal reorganization during sequential decision-making in pigeons
abstract: Adaptive sequential decision-making requires animals to learn how actions shape future states and rewards while adjusting behavioral strategies as experience accumulates. Although the hippocampus is implicated in state-structure representation and the striatum in value learning, how learning strategies evolve from exploratory sampling to efficient exploitation and how hippocampal-striatal interactions reorganize alongside this transition remain unclear. We trained six pigeons of undetermined sex to perform a probabilistic two-step decision task while simultaneously recording behavioral choices and hippocampal-striatal local field potentials. Strategy evolution was tracked using a dynamic reinforcement-learning framework in which model-based, model-free, and weighted model-based/model-free models were fitted across sliding windows. Hippocampal-striatal functional coordination was assessed using phase-locking analysis, and directed predictive influence was quantified using kernel Granger causality. The weighted model best explained choice dynamics, indicating a shift from model-based-like control during early acquisition toward model-free-like control during later stable performance. This behavioral shift was accompanied by two complementary neural changes: hippocampal-striatal phase coordination increased across learning, whereas hippocampus-to-striatum directed predictive influence decreased and covaried positively with model-based-like strategy weight. Direction-ratio analysis showed that hippocampus-to-striatum remained the predominant direction throughout learning, indicating reduced influence rather than directional reversal. After acquisition, hippocampus-to-striatum directed influence was not uniformly reduced but remained relatively preserved during rare, low-value, unrewarded, or less expected events. Together, these findings reveal a learning-dependent reorganization of hippocampal-striatal dynamics, in which increasing functional coordination is accompanied by reduced but condition-dependent hippocampal-to-striatal influence as behavior becomes more stable and efficient. Significance Statement  Adaptive learning requires coordinated changes in behavioral strategy and neural interactions as animals progress from exploration to stable performance. Here, we show that pigeons gradually shifted from flexible, model-based-like control toward more stable, model-free-like behavior during sequential learning. In parallel, hippocampal-striatal interactions underwent a complementary reorganization: phase coordination progressively increased, whereas hippocampus-to-striatum directed predictive influence decreased with declining model-based-like control. Importantly, this directed influence remained relatively preserved during rare, low-value, or unrewarded events. These findings link behavioral strategy transition to the dynamic reorganization of hippocampal-striatal interactions, revealing how neural systems may simultaneously support efficient learned behavior while retaining sensitivity to behaviorally informative events.

title: Single-neuron encoding of rapidly learned visual information reshapes human perception
abstract:
Abstract Any study of learning must capture neural or behavioural changes over time. Stimuli are therefore presented more than once, before and after learning takes place—a sequence that cannot be randomised across time. This design creates vulnerability to temporal confounds that cause illusory neural effects. We investigate this issue in a classic ‘one-shot’ learning paradigm, in which ambiguous two-tone images become recognisable after viewing a photo cue. Across common fMRI designs, we found that spurious correlations driven by the temporal proximity of stimuli created strong artefacts in multivariate data. Among certain experimental designs, we found strong neural markers of perceptual learning depending on how stimuli were distributed across these artefacts. This paradigm-dependent effect was present not only in the primary visual cortex (V1), but also in a non-visual control region (S1), indicative of an artefactual origin rather than a genuine perceptual learning effect. We present a principled approach to correct for this temporal order confound. Once applied, the artefactual learning signature was eliminated from both V1 and S1, and while the corrected signal retained information about image identity in V1, this was absent in S1. Our work demonstrates how current multivariate neuroimaging approaches to understanding learning could be influenced by methodological artefacts that misdirect interpretations towards distributed neural processing, and offers a practical framework to distinguish true learning from measurement error.

1 Introduction Sensory representations are constantly updated as we learn. For example, long-term exposure to a particular species of animal can enhance their subtle features, while hearing a familiar voice can make you instantly recognise someone you had assumed was a stranger. In cognitive neuroscience, these perceptual dynamics are often studied with cueing tasks ( Carrasco, 2018 ; Schacter & Buckner, 1998 ), in which cues that manipulate knowledge or attention can alter neural responses to subsequent stimuli. With the emergence of multivariate fMRI techniques, this is typically measured via representational similarity analysis (RSA), where variations in neural representations to different stimuli are assessed by correlating their multi-voxel responses ( Kriegeskorte et al., 2008 ). While these measures are informative and robust to various univariate signal fluctuations ( Kriegeskorte et al., 2008 ; Roth & Merriam, 2023 ), structured noise in the temporal domain can affect their results ( Alink et al., 2015 ; Cai et al., 2019 ; Mumford et al., 2014 ). This could prove particularly problematic for learning paradigms, as they often require stimuli to be presented in a specific order (e.g., pre-cueing target, cue, post-cueing target), making full randomisation or counterbalancing impossible in the temporal domain. A popular cueing task uses two-tone images to study perceptual reorganisation, or ‘one-shot’ learning ( Armendariz et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2016 ; Davies et al., 2018 ; Dolan et al., 1997 ; Flounders et al., 2019 ; González-García et al., 2018 ; González-García & He, 2021 ; Hsieh et al., 2010 ; Lazarova et al., 2025 ; Ludmer et al., 2011 ; Teufel et al., 2015 , 2018 ; van Loon et al., 2016 ; Yoon et al., 2007 ). In this phenomenon, an unrecognisable two-tone image, created by smoothing and contrast-binarising a greyscale photo (see Fig. 1A ; Mooney, 1957 ), becomes recognisable only after exposure to the original photo. Perceptual reorganisation can therefore be robustly triggered by the sequential presentation of a two-tone image, its corresponding photo cue, and the same two-tone again ( Ramachandran, 1994 ). Because the newly acquired knowledge can provoke distinct perceptual experiences in response to two presentations of the same stimulus, two-tone paradigms offer a well-controlled approach for measuring top-down modulation of sensory inputs across the brain. RSA can reveal whether two-tone images are represented more similarly to their photo versions after cueing, in line with the phenomenological experience of perceptual reorganisation ( Fig. 1A ). Hsieh and colleagues were the first to identify this neural marker of perceptual reorganisation ( Hsieh et al., 2010 ). They observed increased correlations between photo and two-tone stimuli following cueing in both the Lateral Occipital Cortex (LOC)—a higher-order area known to play a critical role in object recognition ( Grill-Spector et al., 2000 ; Malach et al., 1995 )—and in the early visual cortex, suggesting widespread knowledge-based modulation of neural representations ( Hsieh et al., 2010 ). Van Loon and colleagues later extended these findings, observing perceptual reorganisation effects from the primary visual cortex (V1) to the posterior fusiform (pFs), including intermediate processing stages. These were diminished in lower-order areas when NMDA-mediated feedback processing was pharmacologically inhibited ( Van Loon et al., 2016 ). More recently, González-García and colleagues replicated findings of distributed knowledge-driven processing, and further identified classically ‘non-visual’ areas, such as the frontoparietal (FPN) and default-mode (DMN) networks, as encoders of perceptual reorganisation ( González-García et al., 2018 ; González-García & He, 2021 ). Strikingly, these studies find that early visual areas represent cued two-tones more similarly to their photo versions than to the same two-tones viewed before cueing ( González-García et al., 2018 ; Hsieh et al., 2010 ; van Loon et al., 2016 ). While top-down processing has previously been found to modulate representations throughout the visual hierarchy in other perceptual tasks ( Kok et al., 2012 , 2016 ; Lamme & Roelfsema, 2000 ; Poltoratski & Tong, 2020 ; Self et al., 2013 ; Yon et al., 2023 ), the findings from perceptual reorganisation studies extend this considerably by reporting effects of prior knowledge that are widespread across the cortex, and that can dominate incoming visual input. The above findings offer compelling insights into long-standing neuroscientific debates about the distribution of conscious perceptual processing, leveraging a range of paradigm designs to reach corroborating conclusions about the strength and distribution of top-down neural signals. However, the designs used share a feature that is common to all perceptual reorganisation paradigms: uncued two-tones (‘Pre’ condition) must always precede their corresponding photo versions (‘Cue’ condition), which, in turn, must always precede the corresponding cued two-tones (‘Post’ condition, Fig. 1A ). As this presentation order is necessary for triggering and measuring perceptual reorganisation, it results in a temporal consistency across subjects that cannot be avoided by trial randomisation or counterbalancing. This raises questions about the potential influence of temporal artefacts on RSA measures of perceptual reorganisation, which may be overlooked when using conventional methods of reporting these data ( Fig. 1C ). In fMRI, structured noise can arise from both physiological and methodological sources, and can act across multiple temporal levels. For example, the subject’s motion, breathing, heart-rate and attentional drift, alongside thermal fluctuations, scanner instability, equipment radio frequency signals, and preprocessing and analysis artefacts can alter neural signals between scanning sessions, within a single session, between fMRI runs, and within single runs ( Aguirre et al., 1997 ; Alink et al., 2015 ; Cai et al., 2019 ; Mumford et al., 2014 ). The combined impact of structured noise on multi-voxel patterns may therefore be complex, and variable across subjects, set-ups, and paradigm designs. To investigate this issue, we varied how stimuli were temporally distributed in four fMRI two-tone paradigms, including established designs used in the literature, and characterised the impacts of temporal effects at the single-subject level in each design. The paradigms differed in how stimulus conditions (Pre, Cue and Post) were arranged within and across fMRI runs, and should therefore vary in their sensitivity to structured noise across different temporal levels. In an across-run design ( Gorlin et al., 2012 ; Hsieh et al., 2010 ; Lazarova et al., 2025 ; van Loon et al., 2016 ), separate fMRI runs are dedicated to each stimulus condition. This allows trials to be fully randomised within each run without disrupting the required order of conditions, but results in long delays between presentations of corresponding stimuli (‘Across’ design; Fig. 1B , bottom row). In a ‘Mixed-Within’ design ( Flounders et al., 2019 ; González-García et al., 2018 ; González-García & He, 2021 ), Pre condition two-tones are presented in a separate run to the corresponding Cue and Post conditions, which are shown in the following run alongside new Pre images. This design counterbalances stimulus conditions more evenly across the experiment, but unsymmetrically across fMRI runs ( Fig. 1B , second row). In a Within-run design ( Hegde & Kersten, 2010 ; Ludmer et al., 2011 ), all conditions of a set of images are presented within a single run, meaning trials can only be randomised within subsections of each run, but effect sizes may be enhanced by avoiding across-run signal variability and minimising delays between presentations of corresponding stimuli ( Fig. 1B , first row). We also included a ‘Mixed-Across’ design to offer a logical alternative for managing temporal order constraints while counterbalancing stimulus conditions. Here, a single run can contain all three stimulus conditions, but Pre, Cue, and Post conditions of the same images are always separated across three consecutive runs, allowing for full randomisation of all images presented within a run ( Fig. 1B , third row). For each of the above four designs, we presented the same 20 images of natural and man-made scenes, and measured perceptual reorganisation behaviourally and cortically at the single-subject level. Our cortical regions of interest included primary visual cortex (V1) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) as a control region. While previous studies have reported strong patterns of perceptual reorganisation in V1 ( González-García et al., 2018 ; González-García & He, 2021 ; van Loon et al., 2016 ), S1, as a typically non-visual region, should not be sensitive to perceptual reorganisation of visual stimuli, but may show design-driven artefacts. Using conventional RSA measures, we find that some paradigms result in strong neural patterns of perceptual reorganisation across both V1 and S1, while others do not. This leads us to identify a substantial temporal artefact present in all paradigms tested, that confounds conventional measures of perceptual reorganisation depending on the distribution of stimulus conditions across fMRI runs. We further show how even in confounded paradigms, appropriate control analyses can mitigate these artefactually enhanced effects. Critically, without these corrections, the true extent of temporal confounds can be masked by conventional RSA practices ( Fig. 1C ), yet can emulate strong neural patterns of perceptual reorganisation across the cortex. Based on this example from perceptual reorganisation, we recommend three strategies for distinguishing genuine learning effects from temporal artefacts in multivariate fMRI studies. 2 Methods 2.1 Participants Nineteen healthy adults participated in the study. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and provided written informed consent before participating. Three participants were excluded: two due to poor task compliance and one due to a technical issue. Of the remaining 16 participants, 7 were female, 1 was left-handed, and the mean age was 26.3 years (age range: 19.8–30.9 years). The research was carried out in accordance with the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (project number 22397/001). 2.2 Stimuli Stimuli were generated from 20 images of animals and objects from The Berkeley Segmentation Dataset and Benchmark ( Martin et al., 2001 ) and the Open Images Dataset V7 ( Kuznetsova et al., 2020 ) using MATLAB R2022a ( The MathWorks Inc., 2022 ). Images were converted to greyscale and dynamically cropped to a square to create photo cues. Two-tone stimuli were created using methods previously described elsewhere (see Milne et al., 2024 ). Specifically, photo cues were smoothed with a 2D Gaussian filter and then thresholded to binarise pixel luminance to black or white, creating images with obscured edges. Smoothing levels and binarisation thresholds varied per image; standard deviation of Gaussian distribution ranged from 0.5–6.0 SD, binarisation thresholds ranged from 0.4–2.0 times the mean luminance of the greyscale image. An additional four two-tones generated with no smoothing were used in a practice task to test task comprehension. Five ‘Abstract’ two-tone images were also created by scrambling two-tone images, producing contentless two-tones for which photo cues do not exist, but are not used in analyses presented in this study. All stimuli were presented as a 13 degrees of visual angle square centred on a 50% grey background, and projected onto a screen at the back of the MRI scanner, which was viewed via a mirror. 2.3 Procedure During an experimental trial, participants viewed a two-tone or a greyscale image and judged whether the presented image was of an animal or a man-made object. Verbal recognition of the specific item in the image was recorded after each scan in a verbal recognition task. Each of the 16 participants completed one of four different task paradigms (see Fig. 1B ): Within (n = 4), Mixed-Within (n = 4), Mixed-Across (n = 4), and Across (n = 4). This between-subjects design is necessary for comparing one-shot learning paradigms, as behavioural effects would diminish if the task were to be repeated within subjects. All paradigms included 20 images shown in three conditions: ‘Pre’ two-tone condition, ‘Cue’ greyscale photo condition, and ‘Post’ two-tone condition. In each paradigm, images and conditions were distributed across fMRI runs in different ways (see below). The order of presented images was shuffled per participant, to allow for maximal randomisation while maintaining the sequential constraints of the task (see Fig. 1B ). Between fMRI runs, participants completed a verbal recognition task of the two-tone images to measure their pre- and post-cueing recognition. The single-trial structure of all fMRI paradigms was identical. Each trial started with a black fixation cross presented for 1 s, followed by a 0.2 s stimulus presentation of either a photo cue or a two-tone image. This was followed by a grey fixation cross presented for 1.8 s, prompting the participant to respond via button press to whether the image contained an animal or

title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy
abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

title: Filamin-A links transcriptional disruption to dopaminergic decline in progressive supranuclear palsy
abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy is a late-onset neurodegenerative disorder characterized by tau aggregation and prominent dopaminergic dysfunction, yet the upstream molecular processes linking transcriptional abnormalities to dopaminergic failure remain poorly understood. To explore these mechanisms, we performed an integrated multi-omics analysis using a mouse model with overexpression of human filamin-A, a cytoskeletal protein genetically implicated in progressive supranuclear palsy. Analyses were conducted in young adult mice (5-7 months) and aged mice (14-16 months) of both sexes, with transcriptomic, epigenomic, biochemical, metabolomic and behavioural profiling performed across multiple brain regions. In parallel, post-mortem human brain tissue from 11 individuals with progressive supranuclear palsy and five neurologically normal controls was analysed for biochemical validation using samples from the frontal cortex and striatum. Transcriptomic profiling identified immediate early gene-centred transcriptional dysregulation as a prominent and early molecular alteration. This change, accompanied by chromatin accessibility alterations, was associated with the activation of activator protein 1-dependent gene programmes and region-specific changes in dopaminergic protein markers across the cortex, striatum and midbrain. Multi-layered analyses revealed cortical monoamine depletion together with early striatal dopaminergic sensitization, indicating a close association between immediate early gene dysregulation and dopaminergic circuit imbalance. With ageing, the coupling was lost, coinciding with dopaminergic exhaustion and deficits in locomotor, cognitive and social behaviours. In human analyses, post-mortem brain samples from individuals with progressive supranuclear palsy showed reduced dopamine D2 receptor expression compared with neurologically normal controls, together with region-dependent alterations in c-Fos expression and enrichment of activator protein 1-related motifs in regions with reduced chromatin accessibility. Together, these findings suggest that filamin-A-dependent cytoskeletal stress acts as an upstream molecular context in which immediate early gene-centred transcriptional dysregulation emerges and becomes linked to dopaminergic vulnerability in progressive supranuclear palsy.

title: Opioid-glutamate interactions modulate intrinsically rewarded communication in European starlings
abstract: Affiliative, non-sexual vocal communication is essential for social learning and bonding, yet relatively little is known about its neural bases. Past research on songbirds demonstrates that song produced in affiliative, non-sexual flocks correlates positively with a bird's intrinsic reward state, and the link between song and reward is regulated by mu opioid receptors (MORs) in the medial preoptic area (MPOA). RNAseq studies also reveal a strong positive association between affiliative song and glutamatergic gene expression in MPOA, with NMDA receptor 1 (GRIN1) and glutamate receptor scaffolding protein (Shank2) correlating strongly with affiliative singing. In male European starlings we tested the hypothesis that MOR-glutamate interactions in the MPOA regulate affiliative communication. Peripheral administration of the MOR agonist fentanyl increased affiliative singing and calling behavior while reducing stress-related behavior, beak wiping. The effects on vocal but not stress-related behavior were prevented by administration of the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801. c-Fos mapping revealed that fentanyl increased neural activity in caudal MPOA (cMPOA) and interconnected regions implicated in social behavior, song production, and reward, and that these effects were reversed by MK-801. To identify a local site of MOR-glutamate interaction, we used AAV shRNA to downregulate Shank2 in MPOA. This manipulation prevented fentanyl from stimulating affiliative singing behavior, also without affecting stress reduction, suggesting that MOR-glutamate interactions in the MPOA facilitate social communication but not associated stress reduction. Together these findings provide the first experimental evidence that MOR-glutamate interactions within the MPOA, particularly the cMPOA, contribute to affiliative, rewarding vocal communication. Significance Statement  Affiliative, non-sexual vocal communication is fundamental to social cohesion and well-being, yet its neural mechanisms are poorly understood. This study identifies a critical role for interactions between mu opioid receptors and glutamatergic signaling in promoting non-sexual, rewarding vocal communication. In a songbird experimental system, we demonstrate that NMDA receptor activity and the postsynaptic glutamate receptor scaffolding protein Shank2 are required for opioid facilitation of affiliative song. Our findings further reveal the medial preoptic area, particularly its caudal subdivision, to be an important site of this opioid-glutamate interaction. Together, these results extend opioid-glutamate interaction frameworks beyond classic reward circuits and suggest the existence of a conserved neural mechanism supporting affiliative social behavior across vertebrates.

title: Childhood maltreatment and defenses: A meta-analytic review
abstract: Defenses are theorized to develop within early caregiving relationships, yet no meta-analysis has quantified their association with childhood maltreatment. This PRISMA 2020-guided meta-analysis, which was not preregistered, addressed this gap for Overall Defensive Functioning (ODF) and immature, neurotic, and mature defenses. We searched PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global through August 20, 2026. Eligible studies quantified maltreatment before age 18 and ODF or defense categories, excluding studies using only dichotomous maltreatment indicators or broad trauma inventories underrepresenting maltreatment. We rated study quality with an adapted NIH Quality Assessment Tool. Random-effects models pooled Fisher's z, back-transformed to r; meta-regression and subgroup analyses tested moderators. We included 35 cross-sectional studies (34 independent samples; N = 13,604). Greater maltreatment was associated with lower ODF (k = 7; r = -.17, 95% CI [-.20, -.13]) and greater reliance on immature (k = 30; r = .24, 95% CI [.18, .29]) and neurotic defenses (k = 21; r = .12, 95% CI [.06, .19]), whereas the mature-defense association was negligible (k = 24; r = -.04, 95% CI [-.09, .01]). Heterogeneity was substantial for defense categories but not ODF; publication bias was not evident. Exploratory moderator analyses suggested variation by maltreatment instrument and sex composition (immature), sample type (neurotic), and defense instrument (mature). Cross-sectional, retrospective evidence precludes causal inference. Findings are consistent with psychodynamic and developmental models in which childhood maltreatment shifts defensive organization toward less adaptive modes without precluding mature defenses; prospective longitudinal studies should test this proposition.

title: Do adolescent, parent, and dyadic behaviors during the family meal predict response to family-based treatment for anorexia nervosa?
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: In family-based treatment (FBT) for anorexia nervosa, patient and caregiver behaviors during the family meal (FM) predict treatment outcomes. Intensive parental coaching (IPC) includes a second FM, yet whether behaviors during IPC predict end-of-treatment (EOT) outcomes is unknown.

METHODS: Secondary data from a randomized controlled FBT trial (N = 83) were analyzed. Adolescents without early response (+2.4 kg by session four) were randomized to FBT-as-usual or IPC. Videotaped FM sessions were behavior coded. Logistic regressions tested, in the whole sample, whether FM1 behaviors predicted early response. Linear regressions tested whether FM behaviors predicted treatment outcomes at EOT among responders (n = 27) and nonresponders randomized to IPC (n = 17) separately. Lag sequential analyses explored, in the whole sample, whether dyadic transitions during FM1 predict early response.

RESULTS: During FM1, greater adolescent restriction (OR = 1.06) and negative affect (OR = 1.10) predicted nonresponse, whereas parental modeling eating predicted early response (OR = 0.97). Among responders, adolescent food approach (f 2  = 0.19) and meal arrangement (f 2  = 0.20) predicted psychological outcomes. Among IPC nonresponders, changes in parent meal preparation showed the largest associations with psychological outcomes (f 2  = 0.95), while changes in adolescent meal arrangement showed the largest associations with both psychological (f 2  = 0.33) and weight outcomes (f 2  = 0.20). Adolescent not eating followed by parent eating was the only dyadic transition predicting early response (OR = 0.20); most other behaviors and transitions either exhibited small effects or were not associated with outcomes.

DISCUSSION: FM behaviors may provide clinically relevant information about FBT and IPC response and potential intervention targets. However, given our modest sample size, conclusions remain tentative.

title: Enhancing Empathic Functioning in Married Individuals Experiencing Marital Conflict Through Mentalization-Based Therapy in Iran
abstract: Empathy impairment may contribute to the persistence of marital conflict. Although mentalization is theoretically relevant to understanding mental states and interpersonal functioning, limited research has examined whether Mentalization-Based Therapy (MBT) is associated with changes in empathy among married individuals experiencing marital conflict. This study examined the effect of MBT on self-reported empathy using a pretest-posttest control-group design. Thirty married individuals experiencing marital conflict were randomly allocated to an experimental group or a control group. The experimental group received 12 weekly 45-min MBT sessions. Empathy was assessed using the 28-item Davis Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI) and analyzed using analysis of covariance. After controlling for pretest empathy, the experimental group showed significantly higher posttest empathy than the control group, F(1, 27) = 12.643, p = 0.001, partial η 2  = 0.319. The findings provide preliminary evidence that participation in MBT may be associated with improved self-reported empathy in this population.

title: Virtual reality-supported mindfulness practice in relieving stress in postgraduate students: a pilot randomised controlled trial
abstract:
Background Virtual reality (VR)-based mindfulness intervention may be a potentially effective approach for stress relief in postgraduate students. This pilot study examined the preliminary effects of a VR-based mindfulness intervention on stress reduction among postgraduate students, in comparison with a conventional mindfulness intervention and a control condition. In addition, the study evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and user experience associated with delivering mindfulness through VR technology. Methods A three-arm, assessor-blinded pilot randomised controlled trial was conducted. Forty-five full-time postgraduate students were randomly assigned ( n = 15 per group) to a mindfulness group (15-minute audio-guided mindful practice twice a week for two weeks), a VR mindfulness group (VR-based mindfulness intervention twice weekly for two weeks), or a control group. The feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary effects of VR-based mindfulness intervention on relieving stress were examined. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with participants in the VR mindfulness group to explore their experiences following the intervention. Results This pilot study supported the feasibility of VR-based mindfulness intervention with satisfactory recruitment (54.88%), attrition (4.44%), and intervention completion (95.56%) rates. Participants in both the VR-based mindfulness group ( β = -0.422, 95%CI: -0.804 to -0.039, p = 0.031, g = -0.42) and the mindfulness group ( β = -0.563, 95%CI: -1.052 to -0.074, p = 0.024, g = -0.44) exhibited significant reductions in perceived stress scores compared to the control group at post-intervention. Additionally, significant reductions on total mood disturbance and negative mood were observed in both VR-based mindfulness group ( β = -16.553, 95%CI: -28.800 to -4.306, p = 0.008, g = -0.52; β = -22.159, 95%CI: -40.827 to -3.491, p = 0.020, g = -0.52) and mindfulness groups ( β = -16.004, 95%CI: -30.500 to -1.509, p = 0.030, g = -0.59; β = -23.029, 95%CI: -45.307 to -0.752, p = 0.043, g = -0.53). However, no statistically significant differences between groups were found in the total scores of mindfulness ( p > 0.05). Conclusion This pilot study demonstrated the feasibility and potentially preliminary effectiveness of VR-based mindfulness intervention for postgraduate students. Further multi-centre randomised controlled trials with a larger sample size and longer follow-up are recommended to ascertain the effects of VR-based mindfulness intervention for stress relief among postgraduate students. Trial registration This study has been registered in ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT05948280 ) on 17th July 2023.

Introduction In the pursuit of academic and personal goals, university students are continuously evaluated by their institutions, which exposes them to various stressors [ 1 ]. Postgraduate students, in comparison, experience even higher levels of stress, with prevalence significantly higher than undergraduates [ 2 ]. Common sources of stress for postgraduate students include schoolwork, financial pressures, research assistant or teaching assistant responsibilities, career planning, and family issues [ 3 , 4 ]. Furthermore, as postgraduates tend to pay more attention to academic performance rather than integrating into campus life, they may have limited access to psychological support through campus activities and organisations, which negatively affects their mental health and stress levels [ 2 ]. Excessive stress levels not only compromise students’ overall well-being, such as increasing their risk of illness, poor sleep quality, eating disorders, increased healthcare utilisation, and depression, but also adversely affect academic performance, including higher dropout rates, reducing academic achievement and social functioning, and even suicidal ideation [ 5 ]. Mindfulness can benefit one’s emotions in a ‘non-judgement’ way, which is achieved by adjusting one’s breathing, training oneself to be ‘present at the moment’, and adopting attention-focused mindfulness practices to reduce ruminations (i.e., thinking about negative things repeatedly) and negative emotion [ 6 ]. Previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have shown that mindfulness-based programmes, including mindfulness-based stress reduction, are associated with reductions in psychological distress, perceived stress, and other mental health-related outcomes in non-clinical adult populations [ 7 ]. Evidence from undergraduate and graduate student populations also suggests that stress-reduction interventions, including mindfulness-based approaches, may be beneficial for reducing stress [ 8 ]. Given the substantial academic demands and limited time availability among postgraduate students, brief mindfulness formats may offer a particularly feasible and practical approach for stress management in this population [ 9 ]. As an emotion-regulation skill, mindfulness can be further enhanced through virtual reality (VR) technology. VR uses a headset with a display that projects an interactive, audiovisual 360-degree virtual environment [ 10 ]. VR enables users to generate vivid environments that can also be manipulated on demand, providing a sense of ‘being there’ during the process [ 11 ]. Immersive VR provides aesthetic environments, allowing users to be virtually present in a personalised setting [ 12 ], while audio guidance replaces the role of the trainer traditionally performed in mindfulness training, ensuring consistency in the quality of training. The interaction between environment and training enhanced participants’ feelings of involvement and the efficacy of meditation [ 13 ]. Consequently, VR-based mindfulness intervention may offer advantages over traditional approaches by enhancing present-moment awareness and minimising external distractions. In recent years, a combination of mindfulness and/or meditation training with VR has been promoted. Studies have examined the feasibility of incorporating VR mindfulness training, whereas participants found that VR-based mindfulness intervention improved calmness and relaxation and reduced stress [ 14 ]. Furthermore, several studies have concluded that VR demonstrated high acceptability for the practice of mindfulness and significantly promoted treatment adherence [ 14 – 18 ]. Notably, in the case of university students, the implementation of additional VR scenarios into the practice of mindfulness meditation is particularly well accepted because of their high affinity for new technologies [ 19 ]. Nevertheless, previous systematic reviews have pointed to limitations of VR-based mindfulness interventions, including poor video quality and the discomfort caused by the weight of VR headsets [ 12 ]. At present, little is known about how VR may facilitate or hinder mindfulness practice, or how specific design features of headsets (e.g. comfort, weight, and degree of immersion) may impact the perceived benefits of VR-supported mindfulness. Therefore, addressing these gaps is essential for informing intervention design and ensuring the acceptability of future mental health interventions in postgraduate populations. The current pilot study aims to test the feasibility and acceptability of a VR-based mindfulness intervention in postgraduate students. We also aim to test the preliminary effects of VR-based mindfulness practice in improving stress in postgraduate students as compared to conventional mindfulness and control. Additionally, the experience of using VR for mindfulness was also explored in this population. Methods The study was conducted and reported in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) 2010 extension for randomised pilot and feasibility trials [ 20 ]. Study design This study is a three-arm, assessor-blinded pilot randomised controlled trial (RCT) conducted from August 2024 to January 2025. Participants Students studying postgraduate programmes at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, were recruited. Eligible participants are (1) aged 18 or over; (2) enrolled in a postgraduate programme; (3) experienced stress (with a score of the perceived stress scale > 13); (4) able to speak and write in English. Students who are (1) diagnosed with psychiatric disorders, or (2) currently taking psychotropic medication, (3) have history of photosensitive epilepsy or previous experience of severe simulator sickness, (4) receiving or have just completed other psychological interventions (e.g. stress management, mental health support, peer support, etc.) within the last six months was be excluded. The sample size was selected to provide preliminary estimates of key feasibility parameters, including recruitment, retention, questionnaire completion, intervention completion, and acceptability, to inform the design of a future full-scale trial. Methodological guidance suggests that sample size determination for pilot and feasibility trials should be linked to feasibility objectives and the precision with which key parameters can be estimated, rather than hypothesis testing [ 21 , 22 ]. With a total sample of 45 participants, an overall feasibility proportion of approximately 80%-90% could be estimated with an approximate 95% confidence interval half-width (margin of error) of ± 9% to ± 12%, which was considered acceptable for descriptive feasibility assessment in this pilot study. For the two active intervention groups, 30 participants provided initial information on intervention completion and adherence. In addition, the target of 15 participants per group exceeded the commonly cited minimum of 12 participants per group for pilot studies [ 23 ]. Therefore, 45 participants were recruited and randomly assigned to the mindfulness group, VR-based mindfulness group, or control group, with 15 participants in each group. According to the rule of thumb, a minimum of 12 participants in each arm should be considered [ 23 ]. A total of 45 participants were recruited in this study and randomly assigned to either the mindfulness group, the VR-based mindfulness group or the control group, with 15 participants in each group. Recruitment, randomisation and blinding Convenience sampling was used to recruit participants at the postgraduate hall. The principal investigator approached potential participants with a brief explanation of the study. Those who agreed to join the study were asked to write informed consent and complete the baseline evaluation. The randomisation procedure was performed after the baseline evaluation by a research assistant who was not involved in recruitment, enrollment, or the study process and had no knowledge of the study aims. Participants were randomly assigned at a 1:1:1 ratio to the mindfulness intervention, the VR-based mindfulness intervention, or the control group using a permuted block design in a computer-generated random sampling procedure ( https://www.sealedenvelope.com/ ) with randomly variable block sizes of 4 and 6. Allocation was informed to interventionists through email, whereas participants were informed through opaque, sealed envelopes prepared by the research assistant. Participants were required not to share the group-related information they were involved with others to avoid the contamination issue. The allocation list was concealed in an encrypted file on a password-protected computer. Since this study involves a psychological intervention, blinding the interventionist and participants is difficult. Nevertheless, assessors who collected data and performed data analysis were blinded. Intervention Mindfulness group Participants in the mindfulness group received a 15-minute mindfulness practice guided by the interventionist twice a week for two weeks. The interventionist sent participants an audio recording on how to do mindfulness meditation and stretching via WhatsApp. Participants received a mindfulness stretching intervention combining gentle movements with breath and body awareness. The audio guidance was self‑recorded by the interventionist using a validated script that was reviewed by two experts and the supervisor to ensure content validity. VR-based mindfulness group Participants in the mindfulness plus VR group received a VR-based mindfulness intervention twice weekly (on different days) for two weeks. In the first week, the interventionist provided face-to-face guidance, while in the second week, participants practised independently, with compliance recorded in self-practice logs. Each session lasted approximately 15 min and included mindfulness practice delivered in a virtual environment with voice-guided meditations. All virtual scenarios were designed by the research team and had been used previously in different institutions [ 24 ]. The VR kit comprised a set of VR goggles and optional headphones. A first‑generation smartphone‑based VR headset was used, into which participants inserted a smartphone displaying 360° mindfulness animation videos. The research team designed natural environment scenarios with a cartoon character and a female voiceover to guide mindfulness meditation and stretching. The pre‑validated software was an Android application, installed in the same version by all participants via a standardised download link. Interaction was passive and observational: seated participants could shift their viewing angle by turning their heads without any handheld controllers. This design adopted a distraction‑based approach, whereby immersive engagement restricts processing of stress‑related cues. The mindfulness narrative and audio were identical to those in the standard condition; only the presentation format differed (360° immersive video versus audio‑only guidance). Before using VR, the interventionist checked the general health of the participant (e.g. any history of epilepsy, vertigo, or serious mental illness), explained VR use, and adjusted the headset. Participants sat in a chair that allowed them to rotate their bodies to view the omnidirectional environment and familiarise themselves with the VR device before starting. After ensuring that no further questions arose, the researcher began the VR-based mindfulness intervention. Control group Participants in the control group did not receive the mindfulness or VR-based mindfulness intervention. Treatment fidelity The interventionist was a PhD in nursing with extensive experience in mindfulness‑based interventions. To ensure treatment fidelity, the interventionist attended bi-monthly meetings with supervisors to review challenges, improve skills, and discuss strategies for enhancing participant engagement. All sessions were audio-recorded, with randomly selected samples reviewed by supervisors to provide feedback. Interventionists also maintained the day-to-day self-reflection diary to identify and correct potential errors. The extent of VR-based mindfulness implementation was evaluated using attendance records from the interven

title: Effects of digital stress-management interventions in breast cancer patients 18 months after intervention access
abstract:
Purpose Digital stress-management tools show promise, but their long-term impact remains unclear. In the Coping After Breast Cancer (CABC) trial, the app-based stress-management program StressProffen , with either cognitive behavioral therapy intervention (CBI) or a mindfulness-based intervention (MBI), showed no advantage over usual care after six months of access. However, benefits may emerge gradually, as users need time not only to become familiar with the content and techniques, but also to internalize, apply and automatize their use in response to real-life stressors. The a priori defined aims of the current study were to examine; 1) whether extended (18 months) access to the digital stress-management interventions CBI and MBI were associated with changes in perceived stress (stress) (primary outcome), measures of health-related quality of life, mindfulness, fatigue, coping, anxiety, depression, and sleep (secondary outcomes), 2) association between app use and changes in stress level and investigate baseline characteristics as moderators of change in stress in the intervention groups, and 3) identify predictors of change in stress among patients with breast cancer. Methods Of 430 patients randomized to MBI, CBI, or usual care, 76% ( n = 327) completed the 18-month survey. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess between-group differences in primary and secondary outcomes. Moderator analyses were performed to examine whether specific baseline characteristics modified the intervention effects on stress levels. Predictor analysis of change in stress was performed for the total sample. Results At 18 months, all three groups showed stable trends over time, with no significant difference between either intervention group and controls. A larger stress reduction was observed among younger participants (≤50 years) in both CBI and MBI compared to controls. Higher baseline stress levels predicted significantly larger stress reductions in the total sample, but the moderator analysis showed that the effects were only significant in the CBI group. Conclusion Neither CBI nor MBI showed statistically significant improvements at 18 months compared to controls. The results however suggest that long-term access to stress management interventions may help young women with breast cancer and those with high initial stress to reduce their stress levels. Clinicaltrials ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT04480203 . Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10549-026-08117-x .

Background A breast cancer diagnosis can be stressful, bringing worry and uncertainty about the disease, treatment, prognosis and risk of recurrence. These factors can affect the ability to cope with stress [ 1 ] as well as physical pain, and may influence psychological well-being and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) [ 2 – 4 ]. Individual differences in perceived stress and stress responses among breast cancer patients may depend on the appraisal of challenges (stressors) and expectations regarding outcomes (response outcome expectancies). When patients believe they can cope with stressors, the stress response may be reduced. Conversely, feelings of helplessness or hopelessness may sustain the stress response [ 1 , 5 ]. Psychosocial stress-management interventions such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and mindfulness-based interventions [ 6 , 7 ] have been associated with reduced cancer-related challenges such as stress, anxiety, depression, fatigue, insomnia, and pain, as well as improved HRQoL [ 8 – 17 ]. However, these interventions are typically delivered in person either individually or in groups over multiple sessions, and are not always readily accessible. Consequently, research on digital psychosocial stress-management interventions, which may improve access, is increasing [ 18 – 23 ]. Compared with care-as-usual controls, the original digital stress-management intervention StressProffen TM , with mainly CBT content and aspects of mindfulness, found larger effects among cancer survivors at 6 months compared to 3 months, and these enhanced effects appeared to persist after 12 months of intervention access [ 24 ]. The original StressProffen intervention was later adapted into two distinct versions: a cognitive behavioral intervention (CBI) and a mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) [ 25 ]. Both versions incorporated varying amounts of newly developed content, while retaining the original StressProffen program layout [ 25 ]. These two interventions were tested in women with breast cancer in the Coping After Breast Cancer (CABC) trial [ 25 – 27 ]. After 6-months of access to these interventions, no statistically significant effect on perceived stress level, HRQoL or other cancer-related side effects were found among breast cancer patients receiving either intervention compared to usual care controls [ 26 ]. Although engagement with all interventions often declines over time, benefits from stress-management programs may persist or, in some cases, become apparent after the intervention period if participants continue to apply acquired coping strategies [ 28 – 31 ]. In the original StressProffen trial, findings of reduced stress, symptoms of depression, self-regulatory fatigue and improved HRQoL also persisted after 12 months access [ 24 ]. Persistent effects on perceived stress level or HRQoL have also been shown for a few digital stress-management interventions in cancer patients [ 32 – 34 ]. In general, long-term follow-up beyond 6 months of use is important to evaluate whether intervention effects are sustained or emerge over time [ 10 ]. The current study hence hypothesized a priori that effects could be present at 18 months, even if they were minimal after 6 months. Additionally, several factors, including age and family status, may moderate the impact of psychosocial interventions [ 35 – 37 ] and should be specifically studied. The a priori objectives of the study were: Objective 1: To determine between-group (MBI, CBI and controls) effects on change in perceived stress level (primary outcome), measures of HRQoL, mindfulness, fatigue, coping, anxiety, depression and sleep (secondary outcomes) from baseline to 18 months after intervention access. Objective 2: To determine whether application (app) use (from baseline to 18 months) affected changes in perceived stress level, and whether baseline characteristics (age and living with children under 18 years [ 37 ], baseline stress levels [ 38 ], expectations on effect of stress-management intervention, response outcome expectancies (hopelessness, helplessness and coping)[1], breast cancer stage and educational level at baseline moderate percieved stress reduction at 18 months in the two intervention groups. Objective 3: To determine whether baseline characteristics, relationship status, body mass index (BMI), alcohol use, smoking and exercise assessed at baseline predict changes in percieved stress from baseline to 6 and 18 months in the total study sample. Methods Study design and participants The CABC trial is a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 430 Norwegian breast cancer patients aged 21–69 years, enrolled on average 8 months following diagnosis [ 26 , 27 ]. Eligible participants were women aged 21–69 with ductal carcinoma in situ or stage I–III breast cancer that were HER2-positive and/or ER-negative, identified from the Cancer Registry of Norway. These subtypes were selected to avoid overlapping with ongoing trials [ 27 ]. Inclusion also required completion of the population-based digital Cancer Registry of Norway patient reported outcomes measures survey. This survey is sent to all breast cancer patients ≥ 21 days post-diagnosis [ 39 ]. The response rate for breast cancer patients is about 50% [ 27 , 40 ]. Participants were randomized to receive access to the modified StressProffen digital stress-management program containing 10 modules with various stress-management related educational material and exercises with either CBI or MBI content, previously described in detail [ 25 – 27 ]. The CBI intervention contains a combination of psychoeducational CBT-based content and related exercises (e.g., thought challenges, diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, visualization), while MBI centered around observation-, awareness- and acceptance-related content and exercises [ 25 ]. In accordance with the original StressProffen trial [ 24 ], participants were required to complete each module before gaining access to the subsequent module. Access to the next module was delayed by 3 days to encourage participants to reflect on and practice the content and exercises before progressing. After completion of module 4, the order of modules 5–9 could be chosen freely. Module 10 provided a review of the program and offered suggestions for the way forward [ 27 ]. Participants assigned to the intervention groups received a brief introductory telephone call shortly after randomization, during which they were encouraged to start using the intervention immediately. To support adherence and address potential barriers, participants also received brief follow-up calls at approximately 1, 3, and 6 weeks after randomization [ 26 ]. The control group only received requests for survey completion of the digital CABC survey [ 26 ]. The CABC trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier NCT04480203 ) first registered on 09.07.2020. Outcome measures Primary and secondary outcomes were assessed with the CABC survey at baseline (6–9 months after diagnosis), at 6 months [ 26 , 27 ], and at 18 months post inclusion. The primary outcome, perceived stress, was measured using Cohen’s 10 item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) with a score from 0 to 40, which was also categorized into low stress (0–13 points) and moderate-to high perceived stress level (14–40 points) as recommended [ 41 ]. There were several secondary outcomes. The RAND Corporation 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (RAND-36) was used to assess eight domains related to HRQoL (general health perceptions, physical functioning, role limitations caused by physical health problems, role limitations caused by emotional problems, vitality (emotional wellbeing), mental health, social functioning and bodily pain [ 42 ]. Baer’s 5 Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire was used to assess Mindfulness score based on 15 items [ 43 , 44 ]. The Theoretically Originated Measure of the Cognitive Activation Theory of Stress (TOMCATS) [ 45 ] was used to assess three response outcome expectancies (coping, helplessness and hopelessness). Fatigue was assessed with Chalder’s Fatigue Scale (CFQ) (11 items) [ 46 ]. Anxiety and depression were assessed with the Patient Health 4-item Questionnaire (PHQ-4) [ 47 ]. Sleep (duration and quality, in total 10 items) was measured by the Norwegian Shift Work, Sleep and Health survey [ 48 ]. Sociodemographic characteristics Information on sociodemographic characteristics such as educational level, relationship and family status, household income, lifestyle behaviors (i.e., physical activity, smoking status, alcohol consumption), and self-reported height, weight (of which BMI was calculated as kg/m 2 ) were collected at both baseline and at 18 months (i.e., reported in Table 1 ). Age and clinical information regarding breast cancer diagnosis was obtained from the Cancer Registry of Norway at the time of diagnosis, and previously reported [ 26 ]. Expected effects of interventions All participants were at study enrollment asked about their expectations regarding potential effects of stress-management interventions on perceived stress level with the following categories: no, low, some, high expectations and don’t know. Program use Data on program use (e.g., application (app) activity, time spent using the app, duration of use, and number of completed modules) were extracted from user logs stored on a secure research server at the Services for Sensitive Data, University of Oslo. App-use up to 18 months are presented. Statistical analysis A statistical analysis plan was evaluated by the CABC main project group in advance and implemented for all a priori defined outcomes and the planned statistical analyses. Sociodemographic characteristics are presented as means, standard deviations, medians and range for continuous variables, or counts and percentages for categorical variables. All analyses were done using StataNow version 18.0 [ 49 ]. Objective 1, between-group intervention effects: Linear mixed effects model with person as the random effect was used for analysis of between-group differences in outcomes at 18 months. The model included intervention group, time point and the interaction between group and time. The main effect of intervention group was omitted at baseline (32). All participants were included in the analyses according to the intention-to-treat principle. Two participants had missing outcomes at all time points and were therefore removed from these analyses. Objective 2, moderator effects: For the primary outcome of change in perceived stress level at 18 months, exploratory subgroup analyses were performed to test associations with app completion (0–6 vs. 7–10 modules) up till 18 months of use, and to test for moderation of the intervention effects by the following baseline characteristics: perceived stress level (low vs. moderate/high), self-reported expected effect of stress on stress-management (no/low vs. some/high and don’t know), hopelessness/helplessness/coping at baseline (TOMCATS score above vs. below median), stage (Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) vs. invasive) in addition to the predefined potential confounders [ 26 ] (also assessed at baseline): education level (primary/secondary vs. university/college), living with children < 18 years, and age categorized in tertiles (≤50 years, 51–57 years, >57 years). Objective 3, predictor analysis: Predictors of change in perceived stress level in the total sample from baseline to 6 months and from baseline to 18 months (i.e., change scores rather than perceived stress levels over time) were identified using backwards variable selection. Predictors at 6 months were included because they were not prestened with the 6-month intervention results [ 26 ]. The initial model included all baseline characteristics explored in the moderator analyses, as well as the social demographic variables relationship status, BMI-categories (normal- and overweight and obese), alcohol use (yes/no), smoking (never, former and current), and exercise (five categories from no exercise to 4+ hours/week) assessed at baseline. The least statistically significant variables were removed iteratively until all predictors had p -values < 0.10. title: Effects of a jail-adapted dialectical behavioral therapy skills group on in-custody outcomes and reentry preparedness: A randomized controlled trial
abstract: People who are involved in the criminal-legal system often experience difficulty regulating emotions, refraining from impulsive behaviors, and communicating effectively. Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), particularly the skills training group component, may be well-suited to address the risks and needs of correctional populations, but adaptations of DBT in these settings have outpaced rigorous evidence for their effectiveness. This gap is especially notable in short-term jail detention settings, underscoring the need for large-scale randomized evaluations of DBT skills groups on both psychological outcomes and prerelease readiness among jail inmates. The current preregistered randomized controlled trial evaluated the effects of a jail-adapted DBT skills group on in-custody changes in coping, psychiatric symptoms, and jail misconduct and on reentry-related preparedness. Participants were 640 individuals (83% male, 69.2% White, 13.8% Hispanic) incarcerated in a county jail randomized to receive a 12-session DBT skills group or control treatment. They completed baseline and prerelease assessments of relevant outcomes. Small effects of DBT were observed for improved adaptive coping, decreased antisocial behavior in custody, and positive perceptions of reentry capabilities and support. Findings from the present study highlight the insights gleaned from examining effects of DBT group treatment in regard to both behavioral outcomes and expectations for reentry.
