title: Narrative identity, mental illness, and recovery: A systematic review across diagnoses
abstract: Individuals across a range of mental illnesses struggle with identity problems. These problems are important to investigate because they may represent vulnerability to mental illness, emerge as consequences of psychopathology, and pose barriers to recovery. The narrative identity approach is especially suited to illuminate identity problems because it combines a first-person perspective with systematic quantitative studies and provides a strong theoretical foundation for recovery-oriented care. We present a pre-registered systematic review across diagnoses to examine 1) how mental illness is associated with narrative identity and 2) whether narrative identity is related to recovery. After screening 2,327 abstracts, we identified 75 relevant papers. The studies sampled individuals with a range of diagnoses and employed a multitude of narrative identity and recovery measures. Our synthesis suggests that across the examined mental illnesses, narrative identity is less coherent and with adversely affected meaning-making and self-event connections as well as more negatively emotionally toned with lower agency and lower communion themes. The evidence was most robust for schizophrenia, which was more often studied. Regarding relations between narrative identity and recovery, we could not detect consistent patterns, likely due to the complex pairing of multiple narrative identity and recovery measures combined with small sample sizes. Future research could examine a broader array of mental illnesses with respect to transdiagnostic and disorder-specific narrative identity problems and prioritize well-powered, prospective and carefully controlled studies to gain a deeper understanding of the sources of narrative identity problems and the predictive power of narrative identity in relation to recovery.

title: Pilot trial of a brief tailored online treatment for rumination and worry in premenstrual dysphoric disorder
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) affects up to 8% of menstruating individuals and involves severe cyclical mood disturbance. Accessible psychological interventions are needed. Repetitive Negative Thinking (RNT; rumination, worry) is implicated in PMDD severity and represents a novel treatment target.

METHODS: This open, single-group pilot trial examined the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary outcomes of a brief, clinician-supported online CBT intervention targeting RNT in PMDD. N = 37 Australian women with elevated premenstrual distress (91.9% [n = 34] of whom had provisional PMDD) and elevated RNT received the 4-module program over 4-8 weeks. Assessments were conducted at baseline, post-treatment, and 5-week follow-up (one menstrual cycle post-treatment). Primary outcomes were PMDD symptom severity and impact (PSST). Secondary outcomes included RNT, rumination, worry, depression, suicidality, anxiety, distress, wellbeing, and functioning. Satisfaction and qualitative feedback were collected post-treatment.

RESULTS: Satisfaction was good (93% mostly-very satisfied), and participants reported improved understanding of PMDD and gaining practical skills to manage RNT and premenstrual symptoms. Two thirds (64.9%) completed the program. Linear mixed models showed significant, large improvements from baseline to post-treatment and follow-up in PMDD symptom severity and impact (ps < 0.001; g = 1.18-1.81), as well as RNT, rumination, worry, depression, anxiety, wellbeing, and functioning (ps < 0.05; g = 0.52-1.82).

CONCLUSIONS: This pilot supports the preliminary feasibility, acceptability, and positive outcomes of a brief RNT-focused online CBT intervention for PMDD. Future research should examine how to improve completion rates, and evaluate the program in a randomised controlled trial with prospective symptom charting to confirm PMDD diagnoses.

title: [The design process and protocol for a cognitive-behavioral intervention to reduce electronic cigarette use among university students]
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Electronic cigarette use has become an emerging Public Health concern among university students due to its increasing prevalence and the risks associated with nicotine exposure. Cognitive-behavioral interventions have shown promise in addressing this behavior; however, evidence on structured interventions adapted to the Mexican context remains limited. The aim of this study was to design an intervention to reduce electronic cigarette use among university students and establish the protocol for its implementation.

METHODS: The intervention was developed through the stages of discovery, design, and refinement. Its components were based on the Theory of Planned Behavior, while its activities were informed by the taxonomy of behaviour change methods. Subsequently, a pilot experimental longitudinal study with pretest, posttest, and three-month follow-up assessments will be conducted. A total of sixty university students aged eighteen/twenty-four years from a Mexican public university will be recruited through convenience sampling and randomly assigned to the study groups. The intervention will consist of six fifty-minute face-to-face sessions incorporating educational components, cognitive restructuring, and social and personal skills training. Statistical analyses will be exploratory and will include between-group comparisons, repeated-measures analyses, and estimation of effect sizes.

CONCLUSIONS: The protocol will provide preliminary evidence on the feasibility and initial evaluation of an intervention aimed at reducing electronic cigarette use, generating information to inform the design of future studies and prevention strategies for the Mexican university student population.

OBJECTIVE: El consumo de cigarrillos electrónicos constituye un problema emergente de Salud Pública entre los jóvenes universitarios debido al incremento de su uso y los riesgos asociados a la exposición a la nicotina. Las intervenciones cognitivo-conductuales han mostrado utilidad para abordar esta conducta; sin embargo, existe limitada evidencia de intervenciones estructuradas adaptadas al contexto mexicano. El objetivo del presente estudio fue diseñar una intervención para disminuir el consumo del cigarrillo electrónico en jóvenes universitarios y establecer el protocolo para su implementación.

METHODS: La intervención fue diseñada mediante las etapas de descubrimiento, diseño y refinación; los componentes incluidos se fundamentaron en la Teoría de la Conducta Planeada y las actividades a partir de la taxonomía de métodos de cambio de comportamiento. Posteriormente, se realizará un estudio piloto experimental y longitudinal con mediciones pretest, postest y seguimiento a tres meses. Se incluirá a sesenta estudiantes universitarios de entre dieciocho y veinticuatro años de una universidad pública mexicana, seleccionados mediante muestreo por conveniencia y asignados aleatoriamente a los grupos de estudio. La intervención constará de seis sesiones presenciales de cincuenta minutos con componentes educativos, reestructuración cognitiva y entrenamiento en habilidades sociales y personales. Los análisis estadísticos serán exploratorios e incluirán comparaciones entre grupos, mediciones repetidas y estimación de tamaños del efecto.

CONCLUSIONS: El protocolo permitirá obtener evidencia preliminar sobre la factibilidad y evaluación inicial de una intervención para disminuir el consumo de cigarrillos electrónicos, aportando información para el diseño de estudios posteriores y estrategias de prevención en población universitaria mexicana.

title: Efficacy of cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety and depression symptoms in Parkinson's disease patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anxiety and depression are highly prevalent non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), severely compromising health-related quality of life. Conventional pharmacological management is frequently constrained by adverse effects, polypharmacy, and pharmacokinetic interactions. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) represents a promising structured non-pharmacological strategy, but an updated, comprehensive synthesis of clinical trial evidence is warranted.

OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate the efficacy and clinical safety profile of CBT for alleviating anxiety and depressive symptoms in patients with PD.

METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to October 2025. RCTs evaluating CBT (≥ 4 sessions over ≥ 4 weeks) versus control conditions (e.g., treatment as usual, waitlist, active controls) in adults with PD reporting anxiety and/or depression outcomes were included. Two reviewers independently screened literature, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled via random-effects models. Subgroup, sensitivity, and publication bias analyses were performed.

RESULTS: Twenty-one RCTs comprising 892 patients with PD (CBT: n = 465; control: n = 427) were included. Meta-analysis demonstrated that CBT was associated with statistically significant reductions in anxiety symptoms (16 studies; SMD = -0.66, 95% CI -0.83 to -0.50; P < 0.001; I 2  = 79.1%) and depressive symptoms (14 studies; SMD = -0.61, 95% CI -0.78 to -0.44; P < 0.001; I 2  = 86.6%). Subgroup analyses indicated enhanced therapeutic effects in interventions with durations exceeding 10 weeks and when evaluated using population-adapted instruments (e.g., GAI, GDS). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of pooled estimates, and Egger's tests revealed no significant publication bias.

CONCLUSION: CBT produces significant, clinically meaningful reductions in anxiety and depressive symptoms in patients with Parkinson's disease. Despite substantial between-study heterogeneity and variations in intervention delivery, structured CBT should be recommended as an integral component of multidisciplinary PD care. Larger multicenter RCTs with standardized disease-specific core outcome sets and longer follow-up are warranted.

title: Longitudinal trajectories of treatment response in patients with longstanding eating disorders
abstract: Debate within the eating disorders (ED) field has led to the proposal of novel, and sometimes controversial, approaches to addressing the needs of those with a long illness course. However, it remains unclear whether treatment response is indeed predictably determined by illness duration. This study utilized latent growth mixture modeling (LGMM) to examine symptom trajectories in response to Multi-Diagnostic Eating Disorder Dialectical Behavior Therapy (MED-DBT) and identified which classes patients with a longstanding ED (L-ED) were most likely to fall into. Participants were 278 adults (188 anorexia nervosa (AN), 90 bulimia nervosa (BN)) attending a partial hospitalization program delivering MED-DBT. Data were provided at admission, 1 month into treatment, discharge, and 6-month and 1-year follow-ups. Symptoms were assessed using the Eating Disorder Examination-Questionnaire (EDE-Q). Classes were compared on demographic and clinical characteristics including L-ED status. A 5-class model best fit the AN data and a 3-class model best fit the BN data. Class membership differed by treatment history, clinical impairment, and anxiety, and in BN also by depression and BMI. L-ED status was distributed across classes. Findings demonstrate that adults with L-ED show diverse trajectories of change and can experience meaningful improvement in response to MED-DBT. Results challenge assumptions that individuals with a L-ED are treatment-resistant and underscore the importance of continuing to deliver treatments that promote change for this population.

title: A proposed decision-making tool for addressing OCD and co-occurring PTSD within a MED-DBT framework
abstract: Co-occurring obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) are common and clinically consequential among adults with eating disorders (EDs), yet clear guidance for treatment prioritization and sequencing remains limited. This brief report introduces a structured decision-making tool designed to support Stage-2 prioritization of OCD versus PTSD treatment within a multi-diagnostic ED-dialectical behavior therapy (MED-DBT) program. The tool integrates readiness criteria, diagnostic confirmation, and decision points to guide clinicians in treatment planning. We describe the feasibility of integrating and delivering this structured decision-making tool within a MED-DBT program, along with preliminary clinical trends from a pilot sample. More than half of program admissions during the study period flagged for probable OCD/PTSD, though only a small subgroup met Stage-2 readiness criteria, consistent with patterns in higher levels of care. Among patients receiving protocol-based exposure and response prevention or trauma treatment, early symptom trajectories were favorable across ED, OCD, PTSD, and impairment domains. These preliminary findings support the feasibility of structured prioritization within MED-DBT and highlight pathways for future evaluation.

title: Why is lower family socio-economic status associated with conduct problems in children and adolescents? A systematic review of longitudinal studies
abstract: Socio-economic status (SES) has been extensively linked to child and adolescent conduct problems (CP). Understanding the origins of this link is important for informing policy to reduce social inequalities. Potential competing explanations have been investigated and a comprehensive review of the strength of this evidence is required to inform progress towards an integrated model of the underlying mechanisms. We systematically searched ten databases for studies published in English between 1960 and 2026. The eligibility criteria included a quantitative design, a community sample of children or adolescents, measures of SES and CP, longitudinal analyses of the association between SES and CP, and results informing on the potential mechanisms. We identified 45 papers that met the eligibility criteria, comprising 48 individual studies included in the review. Family stress pathways were the most frequently studied mechanisms; however, the results were mixed. There was some support for pathways involving warm and supportive parenting and somewhat weaker support for supervision and discipline pathways. Investment pathways involving cultural/educational resources, neighbourhood characteristics, and models incorporating family stress and investment pathways were found to have received considerable support. There was also evidence that factors such as child's diet and associations with antisocial peers may contribute. These findings support an integrated model of the mechanisms linking SES and CP. This model can provide targets for interventions aiming to reduce CP inequalities and sets the agenda for research to elucidate the mechanisms further.

title: The effectiveness of virtual reality-based rehabilitation in patients with neck pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract:
Background Neck pain is a widespread condition impacting daily functioning and quality of life. Virtual Reality (VR) technology has gained attention as a non-pharmacological intervention in rehabilitative medicine, offering potential benefits for pain management. This study systematically reviewed and conducted a meta-analysis on the effectiveness of VR rehabilitation for neck pain. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, a comprehensive literature search was performed across databases (e.g., PubMed) up to October 1, 2024, targeting randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing VR-based rehabilitation with alternative interventions for neck pain. Data extraction focused on outcomes like the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Neck Disability Index (NDI). Quality and bias were assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool, and the GRADE approach evaluated evidence certainty. Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) was also employed to ensure robustness in conclusions. This protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD42022334319). Results The meta-analysis, which included 11 randomized controlled trials with 476 participants, demonstrated that virtual reality-based rehabilitation significantly reduced VAS scores [471 patients, mean difference (MD) −0.70, p = 0.01] and NDI scores (411 patients, MD −3.06, p < 0.0001) within the first week. Furthermore, significant reductions in VAS (315 patients, MD −1.00, p < 0.05) and NDI scores (315 patients, MD −3.81, p = 0.005) were observed from the first week to 6 months in the VR-based rehabilitation group. Trial sequential analysis further confirmed the statistical strength and reliability of these findings. Improvements in cervical mobility were observed, as evidenced by increased neck flexion and extension. Conclusion VR-based rehabilitation shows promise as an effective strategy for managing neck pain, improving both pain levels and functional capacity. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42022334319 , identifier PROSPERO (CRD42022334319).

Introduction Neck pain represents a prevalent musculoskeletal condition, with epidemiological characteristics indicating substantial incidence and prevalence rates, imposing significant burdens on both individuals and society at large ( 1 ). More than 70 percent of the global population experiences neck pain at least once in their lifetime, with 50–85% likely to experience recurrence within 1–5 years of the initial episode ( 2 , 3 ). Neck pain is a prevalent condition across all age demographics and genders, exhibiting a particularly high prevalence among individuals aged 45 to 54 years and among females ( 3–5 ). Non-specific neck pain, characterized by the absence of detectable systemic disease as the underlying cause, constitutes the predominant form among neck pain cases ( 6 , 7 ). This condition not only hinders individuals’ daily functioning and vocational abilities but can also lead to chronic functional impairment and a reduced quality of life. Neck pain has become a significant public health issue, calling for effective interventional strategies to alleviate its substantial impact on both individual well-being and societal prosperity. Virtual Reality (VR) technology presents a groundbreaking approach to addressing this issue. VR generates immersive digital environments using head-mounted displays and other devices ( 8 ). With advanced head-mounted displays and related peripherals, users are immersed in a multisensory experience that integrates visual, auditory, and haptic feedback ( 9–11 ). In recent years, VR applications have experienced significant growth in rehabilitative medicine, showing remarkable effectiveness in pain management protocols. Scientific studies have highlighted VR’s ability to alleviate pain through mechanisms such as attention diversion, emotional modulation, and enhanced motor engagement ( 12–14 ). VR technology has emerged as a pioneering non-pharmacological intervention, increasingly integrated into neck pain rehabilitation protocols, showing particularly promising potential for pain alleviation and enhancing cervical mobility ( 15 , 16 ). Although several systematic reviews have examined the benefits of VR for neck pain, they may have inadvertently overlooked the nuanced short-term and long-term efficacy of VR in modulating neck pain ( 17 , 18 ). Furthermore, these studies may face the risk of false-positive outcomes due to multiple testing and the limitations of available data. With the rapid advancement of technological capabilities and rising service demands, there has been a corresponding increase in publications in this field. Consequently, there is an urgent need to update systematic reviews and meta-analyses, which will provide substantial value to both clinical practitioners and research investigators. The objective of this study was to conduct a thorough assessment of the effectiveness of virtual reality rehabilitation for patients suffering from neck pain. Additionally, the study implemented trial sequential analysis (TSA) to verify the statistical reliability and methodological robustness of the meta-analytic findings, thereby enhancing the validity and scientific rigor of the derived conclusions. Methods Protocol and registration This systematic review adhered rigorously to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to ensure thorough methodological rigor and comprehensive reporting ( 19 ). The study protocol was registered with the international open-access Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, number: CRD42022334319). Literature search An extensive literature search was performed using databases including PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library, covering publications from their inception until October 1, 2024. The aim was to identify all relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the use of virtual reality-based rehabilitation for neck pain. Search terms combined both indexed terms and medical subject headings (MeSH), such as “virtual reality,” “augmented reality,” “mixed reality,” “neck pain,” and “RCT.” Details of the search strategy applied to each database can be found in Additional file 1 . Study selection and inclusion criteria Inclusion criteria were: (1) population: patients experiencing neck pain; (2) intervention: implementation of virtual reality-based rehabilitation; (3) comparison: other interventions (e.g., non-VR approaches, standard care, or no intervention); (4) outcomes: evaluation using the visual analogue scale (VAS) and neck disability index (NDI); (5) study design: exclusively RCTs. Exclusion criteria encompassed: (1) studies lacking sufficient data; (3) studies without accessible full-text articles. Data extraction Data extraction was meticulously performed by two independent reviewers utilizing a piloted, standardized extraction form. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through consensus. Extracted data from each study included: (1) study characteristics such as authorship details, sample size, participant age, and specifics of the intervention versus comparator; (2) outcomes including VAS scores, NDI scores, and range of motion. Quality assessment The assessment of quality and potential bias was conducted using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool ( 20 ). This evaluation framework considers seven essential domains to determine methodological quality and bias risk: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other biases. Each bias domain was classified as high, unclear, or low risk. Risk of bias graphs were generated using RevMan software (version 5.3). The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach was applied to systematically appraise the methodological quality and reliability of the evidence ( 21 ). The evidence quality was categorized into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low, based on a thorough evaluation of several critical domains. Disparities between the reviewers were deliberated, and if unresolved, a third reviewer was consulted until consensus was achieved. Data synthesis Meta-analyses were conducted using RevMan 5.3 software. Continuous data were evaluated using mean differences with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For studies with consistent units, the weighted mean difference (WMD) with its 95% CI was preferred; however, when unit inconsistency or significant variability was present, the standardized mean difference (SMD) was applied. Statistical significance was determined at p < 0.05, recorded for each outcome measure. If the study results encompassed more than ten articles, a funnel plot should be constructed to evaluate the potential for publication bias. A sensitivity analysis was performed by excluding individual studies to evaluate their impact on overall conclusions, thus affirming result stability. To minimize the risk of false-positive outcomes due to multiple testing and the constraints of available data, TSA was implemented using TSA Viewer version 0.9.5.10 Beta. This analysis aimed to evaluate the robustness of cumulative evidence related to primary outcomes. We adjusted the required information size (RIS) for our meta-analysis and established trial sequential monitoring boundaries (TSMB) to gauge the reliability and definitiveness of the evidence presented ( 22 ). The interaction between the TSA boundary and the cumulative Z-curve was thoroughly examined after calculating sequential monitoring and necessary information size thresholds. If the cumulative Z-curve crossed a trial sequential monitoring boundary, the evidence was considered sufficiently robust to reject the null hypothesis under the prespecified TSA assumptions while accounting for the risk of random error. Exceeding a futility boundary suggested that the prespecified intervention effect was improbable. If neither a monitoring boundary nor a futility boundary was crossed and the required information size had not been reached, the available evidence was deemed inconclusive. Importantly, crossing a monitoring boundary was not interpreted as establishing the clinical importance of the observed effect, exclude systematic bias or unexplained heterogeneity, or suggest that additional research was unnecessary. TSA calculations were performed with a type-1 error α set at 5% and a predefined power (1−β) of 90%. Additional data were sourced from the average incidence across all included studies or those identified as having a low risk of bias ( 23 , 24 ). Results Study selection An extensive systematic literature search was performed across several key databases, including PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library, initially yielding 352 articles deemed potentially relevant ( Figure 1 ). After eliminating 54 duplicate records, the screening of 298 remaining titles and abstracts resulted in identifying 44 articles as potentially eligible for further analysis. A comprehensive full-text review of these articles led to the exclusion of 33 studies based on predetermined criteria, including inadequate data availability ( n = 13), classification as review articles ( n = 14), and being case reports ( n = 6). Consequently, this systematic review and meta-analysis incorporated a total of 11 RCTs encompassing 476 participants ( 15 , 16 , 25–33 ). Characteristics of the studies Table 1 presents the detailed characteristics of the 11 RCTs included in our meta-analysis. One study focused exclusively on young women aged 18 to 25 years ( 32 ). Another study specifically recruited participants who were young fighter and helicopter pilots ( 33 ). 7 of the 11 studies included patients who had been experiencing neck pain for a duration exceeding 3 months ( 15 , 16 , 25 , 26 , 29–31 ). Risk of bias assessment The comprehensive bias risk assessment of the included studies revealed an overall low risk ( Figures 2 , 3 ). It is worth noting that one study may have a high risk of bias because only the person in charge of the statistical analysis was blinded ( 28 ). Outcomes Primary outcomes VAS score within the first 1 week, VAS score from the first 1 week to 6 month postoperatively, NDI score within the first 1 week, NDI score from the first 1 week to 6 month postoperatively. The meta-analysis identified a significant association between virtual reality-based rehabilitation and a reduction in the VAS scores during the initial week (MD −0.70; 95% CI −1.25 to −0.14, P = 0.01, 471 participants, I 2 = 74%; Figure 4a ). Furthermore, patients undergoing this form of rehabilitation experienced a notable decrease in VAS scores extending from the first week to 6 months postoperatively (MD −1.00; 95% CI −1.55 to −0.45; p = 0.0004, I 2 = 51%, 315 participants; Figure 5a ). Additionally, virtual reality-based rehabilitation led to a significant reduction in the NDI scores within the first week (MD −3.06; 95% CI −3.84 to −2.29, p < 0.0001, I 2 = 0%, 411 participants; Figure 6a ). Regarding the incidence of NDI score changes from the first week to 6 months postoperatively, substantial benefits were observed (MD −3.81; 95% CI −6.45 to −1.18, p = 0.005, I 2 = 84%, 315 participants; Figure 7a ). Following harmonization of the outcome scales and reanalysis using mean differences (MDs), the cumulative Z-curves for all primary outcomes crossed both the conventional significance boundaries and the trial sequential monitoring boundaries. Under the prespecified TSA assumptions, these results suggest that the corresponding meta-analytic findings are unlikely to be attributable to random error arising from sparse data or repeated significance testing. The accrued information size, required information size, and TSA-adjusted confidence intervals for each outcome are presented in Figures 4 – 7 . These findings supported the effectiveness of virtual reality-based rehabilitation in successfully reducing both VAS and NDI scores. Concerning publication bias, the funnel plot assessing publication bias for the VAS score within the first week ( p = 0.338) and the NDI score the first week ( p = 0.760) demonstrated near symmetry, which suggested a low incidence of publication bias. Given that the number of studies incorporating VAS or NDI score from the first 1 week to 6 month postoperatively was fewer than ten, we failed to conduct a publication bias assessment ( Figure 8 ). title: Effects of mindfulness-based childbirth preparation education on psychosocial outcomes in pregnancy: a randomized controlled trial
abstract:
Background Mindfulness-based interventions have been increasingly integrated into antenatal education programs to improve maternal psychosocial well-being. However, evidence regarding their effects on perceived stress, depressive symptoms, childbirth self-efficacy, and postpartum post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) remains limited and inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education (MBCPE) on psychosocial outcomes in primiparous pregnant women. Methods This study was designed as a prospective, randomized controlled trial. The study was completed with 74 pregnant women, including 36 participants in the intervention group and 38 participants in the control group. The intervention group received Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education over eight weeks, while the control group received Information-Based Childbirth Preparation Education over four weeks. Outcome measures included the Perceived Stress Scale, Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, childbirth self-efficacy, and postpartum PTSD symptoms. Statistical analyses were conducted to compare group differences, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results A statistically significant difference was found between the intervention and control groups in terms of Perceived Stress Scale and Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale mean scores ( p < 0.05), indicating lower stress and depressive symptoms in the intervention group. However, no significant differences were observed between groups in childbirth self-efficacy or postpartum PTSD symptoms assessed at the fourth postpartum week ( p > 0.05). Conclusions Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education appears to be effective in reducing perceived stress and depressive symptoms during pregnancy and the postpartum period. However, it does not appear to provide an additional benefit for childbirth self-efficacy compared with the control group. No significant between-group difference was observed in postpartum PTSD symptoms assessed at the fourth postpartum week. These findings provide preliminary support for the inclusion of mindfulness-based components in antenatal education to enhance maternal psychosocial well-being. Trial registration The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov on November 1, 2023 ( NCT06111716 ).

Introduction Pregnancy, childbirth, and the transition to parenthood represent critical life events in a woman’s life. As childbirth is an inherently unpredictable and uncontrollable process, it is often accompanied by stress, fear, and anxiety [ 1 ]. In this context, high-quality prenatal care services play a crucial role in improving maternal and neonatal health outcomes. Childbirth preparation education is a key component of antenatal care, aiming to enhance women’s physical and psychosocial readiness for childbirth and the postpartum period and to facilitate a positive birth experience [ 2 ]. Childbirth preparation education can be delivered using various approaches, among which mindfulness-based interventions have gained increasing attention. Mindfulness is defined as the intentional and non-judgmental awareness of present-moment experience [ 3 ]. In a broader conceptualization, it refers to an open, accepting, and compassionate awareness of ongoing experiences [ 4 ]. Several structured mindfulness-based interventions have been developed, including Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR),3 Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) [ 5 ], Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) [ 6 ], and the Mindfulness-Based Childbirth and Parenting program (MBCP), which has gained increasing attention in perinatal research [ 7 – 11 ]. Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education integrates mindfulness practices such as meditation and yoga with standard childbirth education content [ 12 ]. The MBCP program, developed by Nancy Bardacke based on the MBSR model, provides structured education on labor, breastfeeding, and postpartum adaptation [ 7 , 13 , 14 ]. Although program duration varies across studies, adapted mindfulness-based childbirth education programs have commonly been delivered over eight weekly sessions [ 10 , 11 ]. The program aims to reduce stress and anxiety associated with pregnancy and childbirth while supporting maternal well-being through mindfulness practice during the perinatal period [ 7 , 10 , 11 , 15 ]. Evidence suggests that mindfulness-based childbirth interventions may reduce anxiety, depressive symptoms, and perceived stress while improving childbirth self-efficacy [ 8 , 10 , 16 – 18 ]. Moreover, higher levels of mindfulness have been associated with improved psychological well-being and maternal adaptation [ 19 , 20 ]. A systematic review has also indicated that mindfulness-based interventions may improve maternal perinatal mental health outcomes, including anxiety symptoms [ 21 ]. Recent evidence has further shown that mindfulness-based interventions may reduce fear of childbirth among pregnant women planning vaginal birth, thereby extending the evidence beyond general perinatal anxiety [ 22 ]. Despite growing evidence on the effects of mindfulness-based interventions on stress, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and childbirth self-efficacy, research examining their impact on postpartum post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms remains limited. Therefore, the present study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education (MBCPE) on psychosocial outcomes, including perceived stress, childbirth self-efficacy, depressive symptoms, and postpartum PTSD symptoms. Hypothesis-1: Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education has an effect on perceived stress during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Hypothesis-2: Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education has an effect on the perception of childbirth self-efficacy in pregnant women. Hypothesis-3: Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education has an effect on depressive symptoms during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Hypothesis-4: Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education has an effect on post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms in the postpartum period. Methods Study design and participants The current research was conducted as a prospective, randomized controlled trial to determine the effect of MBCPE on psychosocial outcomes in pregnant women. The “Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) 2018” guidelines were followed in this randomized, controlled intervention trial (Fig. 1 ) [ 23 ]. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov on November 1, 2023 ( NCT06111716 ). The registration was completed after participant recruitment had begun; therefore, the trial was registered retrospectively. The study population consisted of pregnant women who presented to the Pregnancy Outpatient Clinic and Faculty Member’s Outpatient Clinic of the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics of a university hospital. The sample size in the research was computed using the program G*Power (3.0.10). When determining the number of pregnant women to be included in each group, an effect size of 0.81 was used in accordance with the results of the research by Duncan et al. (2017). Based on a power of 95% and a significance level of 0.05, the required sample size was determined as 82 participants in total, with 41 participants in each group. Primiparous pregnant women aged 18 years or older, with a minimum of primary education, who volunteered to participate, were classified as having a low-risk pregnancy, were between 20 and 26 weeks of gestation, and had access to the internet and necessary devices (e.g., computer, smartphone) were considered eligible for inclusion in the study. Participants were excluded if they were multiparous, had previously received yoga or mindfulness training during or prior to their current pregnancy, or had communication impairments affecting hearing, speech, or comprehension. In addition, women with high-risk pregnancies—defined as pregnancies with medical, obstetric, or psychosocial conditions that could complicate maternal or fetal outcomes and require specialized care (e.g., preeclampsia, gestational diabetes requiring insulin therapy, multiple gestation, placenta previa, severe anemia, chronic medical conditions, or significant psychiatric disorders)—or those receiving psychiatric treatment during pregnancy or the postpartum period were excluded from the study. After randomization, participants were considered to have discontinued the study if they did not complete the assigned education program, were unable to continue because of pregnancy-related complications or preterm birth, or could not be reached for follow-up assessmen. All interventions were delivered according to standardized protocols to ensure intervention fidelity. Preliminary preparation and creation of education content The primary researcher (SO), who delivered the intervention, had previously obtained a certified Mindfulness and Childbirth Preparation Educator Training Certificate. To ensure content validity and appropriateness of the Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education (MBCPE) program, expert feedback was obtained from four professionals with substantial experience in mindfulness-based interventions and childbirth education. The educational content was reviewed by a five-member expert panel comprising three midwifery academics with research experience in childbirth preparation education and mindfulness, and two psychology academics whose research focused on mindfulness. The experts evaluated the content in terms of relevance, clarity, suitability for pregnant women, and consistency with the principles of mindfulness-based childbirth preparation. The program was revised in line with their feedback. Following expert consultation, the MBCPE curriculum was revised in line with both expert recommendations and current evidence-based literature [ 24 , 25 ]. Prior to the main trial, a pilot study consisting of eight sessions was conducted with four pregnant participants by the principal researcher (SO) using the same online Zoom format planned for the main intervention. After each session, participants provided verbal feedback on the clarity, structure, duration, comprehensibility, and applicability of the educational content. This pilot phase enabled the identification of ambiguous or unclear components, refinement of session duration and instructional strategies, and confirmation of program feasibility. Data obtained from the pilot study were used exclusively for program refinement and were not included in the final analysis. The pregnant women who participated in the pilot study were not included in the main study sample. Randomization and group allocation Eligible participants were randomly assigned to either the Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education (MBCPE) intervention group or the Information-Based Childbirth Preparation Education (IBCPE) active control group using a web-based randomization system ( https://www.randomizer.org ). As this study was conducted as part of a doctoral dissertation, the allocation sequence was generated by the supervising researcher (TY), rather than by the principal researcher (SO), who recruited the participants and delivered the interventions. The supervising researcher was not involved in participant recruitment, screening, intervention delivery, or outcome assessment, thereby maintaining allocation concealment. No research assistants were involved in the study. Due to the nature of the educational interventions, participants and the principal researcher (SO) could not be blinded to group allocation. Participants who met the inclusion criteria were assigned sequential identification numbers based on the generated randomization list, ensuring an equal probability of allocation to each study arm. Participants were therefore allocated to either the MBCPE intervention group or the IBCPE control group . A CONSORT flow diagram illustrating participant recruitment, randomization, and group allocation is presented in Fig. 1 , while the timeline of interventions and outcome assessments is shown in Fig. 2 . Interventions To ensure comparability between groups, both the intervention and control groups received a total of 16 h of educational intervention. Although the overall educational exposure was equivalent across groups, the distribution of sessions differed in accordance with the nature of the interventions. The Information-Based Childbirth Preparation Education (IBCPE) was delivered over a 4-week period with longer weekly sessions, primarily emphasizing structured knowledge transfer. In contrast, the Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education (MBCPE) was implemented over an 8-week period with shorter weekly sessions to support repeated mindfulness practice, gradual skill acquisition, and the integration of mindfulness into daily life. The sessions were delivered online through Zoom by the researcher, who is a midwifery academic with experience in antenatal education and mindfulness-based practices. Accordingly, the difference in session scheduling reflects the theoretical foundations of the educational approaches rather than an imbalance in intervention dose. The content, structure, and implementation methods of the educational programs provided to both groups are described in detail below. Information Based Childbirth Preparation (IBCPE) The IBCPE program covered topics including physical and psychological preparation for childbirth, the childbirth process, non-pharmacological methods to reduce labor pain and facilitate delivery, postpartum characteristics, maternal physiological and psychological changes, adaptation to the maternal role, and newborn care. As participants were recruited from the 20th week of gestation, topics specifically related to early pregnancy were excluded from the curriculum. The content was adapted to the participants’ gestational stage and was delivered in a practical, non-technical, and participant-centered format rather than as a formal academic teaching curriculum. The education was delivered in four weekly sessions, each lasting four hours (total: 16 h). Participants unable to attend a scheduled session were offered an alternative make-up session.. At the end of each session, participants received homework assignments, which they were instructed to complete prior to the following session. Compliance with homework was monitored by the educator through participants’ self-reports shared via WhatsApp. Participants who reported not completing the assigned homework received brief reminders and encouragement from the educator. To reinforce learning, the content delivered during the sessions was reviewed with participants weekly via WhatsApp messages until the end of the fourth postpartum week. Participation in these reminders was tracked to ensure engagement and adherence to the intervention protocol. Mindfulness-Based Chi

title: Comparative effectiveness of cognitive behavioral therapy versus group-based optimism training on psychological outcomes in hemodialysis patients: a randomized controlled trial
abstract:
Background Patients undergoing hemodialysis (HD) face significant psychological challenges that affect their well-being. Nevertheless, no comparative investigation has yet examined the efficacy of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) versus group-based optimism training on psychological outcomes in this population. Hence, this study aimed to compare the effectiveness of CBT versus group-based optimism training on psychological outcomes in HD patients. Methods This three-arm, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial was conducted from September 2024 to May 2025 with a sample of 135 HD patients. Participants were selected through simple random sampling and were randomly allocated to two experimental groups and one active control group. Prior to the intervention, all three groups completed the relevant questionnaires. The CBT and group-based optimism training programs were then implemented for the first and second experimental groups, respectively, each consisting of eight 90-minute sessions delivered once per week for eight consecutive weeks. The control group received standard educational interventions. Following the completion of the training sessions, the questionnaires were completed again immediately and again two and four-months later. The data were analyzed using SPSS software version 21. Ethical considerations All procedures performed on human participants complied with the ethical guidelines of the relevant institutional and national research committees, as well as the Helsinki Declaration and its subsequent revisions, or equivalent ethical frameworks. Results Repeated-measures ANOVA revealed significant time × group interactions for anxiety (η² p = 0.068), depression (η² p = 0.085), optimism (η² p = 0.101), and hope (η² p = 0.073), all p < 0.001. Both CBT and optimism training significantly improved all outcomes versus control ( p < 0.001). However, optimism training showed superior long-term effects over CBT for depression (d = 0.45, p = 0.032) and optimism (d = 0.36, p = 0.041), while both interventions were equally effective for anxiety and hope ( p > 0.05). Conclusion The findings indicated that both CBT and group-based optimism training were effective in reducing anxiety and enhancing hope. Nevertheless, a distinction emerged at long-term follow-up, as optimism training yielded more sustained reductions in depression and greater improvements in optimism. This suggests that, although CBT is effective for acute symptom reduction, optimism training may offer additional advantages for sustained psychological well-being. Clinical trial number IRCT20240609062065N4, 2025-12-01, ‘retrospectively registered’. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05334-3 .

Introduction Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a leading cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide, characterized by a progressive and irreversible decline in renal function. When kidney function drops to approximately 10% of normal capacity, patients reach the end-stage renal disease (ESRD) phase, a life-threatening condition that requires renal replacement therapy [ 1 , 2 ]. According to the updated Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study, CKD currently affects approximately 850 million individuals worldwide. Of these, nearly 4.6 million patients receive kidney replacement therapy (KRT), including HD, peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplantation [ 3 ]. As the primary treatment for ESRD, HD imposes a significant psychological burden on patients. The procedure is inherently stressful and has been consistently associated with a high prevalence of psychosocial disorders [ 4 , 5 ]. Among these, depression and anxiety are the most commonly reported psychiatric comorbidities. Notably, depression is approximately three times more prevalent among HD patients than in the general population, a vulnerability that stems from the interplay of biological, psychological, and socioeconomic factors [ 6 , 7 ]. Beyond the direct stressors of treatment, patients with ESRD face profound disruptions in self-concept, familial roles, and social status. These challenges, compounded by financial dependency, often impede familial adaptation and social engagement, thereby perpetuating a maladaptive psychological cycle [ 8 ]. Given these multifaceted psychological challenges, the development of effective interventions to alleviate depression and anxiety in HD patients is of considerable clinical importance. Two therapeutic approaches have demonstrated particular promise: CBT and optimism training. Based on Beck’s cognitive theory, CBT could targets maladaptive thought patterns through cognitive restructuring and behavioral techniques [ 9 ]. Optimism training, rooted in positive psychology, employs structured exercises designed to cultivate positive future expectancies and has been shown to effectively reduce negative affective states [ 10 , 11 ]. A review of the literature indicates that several studies have been conducted in line with the present investigation. For example, Bahmani et al. demonstrated that cognitive‑existential group therapy significantly enhanced hopefulness and reduced depression in women undergoing HD [ 12 ]. Also, Shokrpour et al. examined the effectiveness of positive thinking training on stress, anxiety, depression, and quality of life in HD patients. At baseline, no significant differences were found between the groups. Following the intervention, stress and anxiety levels decreased considerably, and quality of life improved. However, depression scores did not change significantly [ 2 ]. Despite this promising evidence from previous studies, the clinical reality of HD in Iran is further compounded by unique socio‑cultural and systemic factors. These include considerable out‑of‑pocket treatment costs, cultural stigmas surrounding chronic illness, and alterations in family dynamics, all of which may intensify patients’ perceived burden and psychological distress [ 13 ]. Therefore, the present study aims to compare CBT versus group-based optimism training in terms of their effectiveness on psychological outcomes in HD patients, while also considering their cultural appropriateness and practical feasibility within the specific constraints of Iranian healthcare settings. Materials and methods Study design and setting This three-arm, parallel design, randomized controlled trial was conducted from September 2024 to May 2025 in HD units of Imam Hossein and Ayatollah Taleghani hospitals affiliated with Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran. Study participants In this study, HD patients were selected using sequential convenience sampling and were then randomly allocated into two experimental groups and one active control group using a random number table. The inclusion criteria were included: (1) a documented diagnosis of HD, and (2) willingness to participate in the research. Also, the exclusion criteria were included: (1) having a confirmed diagnosis of a psychological disorder by a psychiatrist, and (2) having disability that would prevent participation in the classes. Sample size The sample size was calculated using G*Power software (version 3.1) for a repeated measures ANOVA with a between‑within interaction design. The study comprised three groups and four measurement time points (baseline, post‑intervention, two‑months follow‑up, and four‑months follow‑up). With an effect size of f = 0.15, α = 0.05, power = 0.80, a correlation of 0.5 among repeated measures, and a non-sphericity correction of ε = 0.5, the minimum sample size was estimated as 42 participants per group (total N = 126). To account for an anticipated dropout rate of approximately 10%, the final sample size was set at 45 participants per group, yielding a total of 135 participants. Measurement instruments Hospital anxiety and depression scale (HADS) This scale is a self‑administered instrument consisting of 14 items, with seven items assigned to each subscale. Responses are recorded on a 4‑point Likert scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 3 (very often indeed), based on the individual’s condition over the previous week. The total score for each subscale ranges between 0 and 21, with higher scores denoting more severe levels of depression and anxiety. A score of 11 or above on either subscale was used as the cut‑off to identify cases of clinically significant anxiety or depression [ 14 ]. The Persian version of this scale has been previously translated and validated, and its psychometric properties, including reliability and validity, have been confirmed in Iranian samples [ 15 ]. Life orientation test (LOT) The Life Orientation Test (LOT) was employed to measure optimism and pessimism. This instrument consists of ten items: three items measure optimism (e.g., “I’m always optimistic about my future”), three items assess pessimism and are reversely scored (e.g., “I hardly ever expect things to go my way”), and four items are neutral and excluded from the total score (e.g., “It’s easy for me to relax”). Responses are rated on a 5‑point Likert scale from 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree), yielding a total score between 0 and 24, with higher scores reflecting greater optimism. Regarding its psychometric properties, the internal consistency of the optimism and pessimism subscales, as measured by Cronbach’s alpha, was 0.78, and the test‑retest reliability coefficients were 0.68, 0.60, 0.56, and 0.79. Furthermore, the face and content validity of the scale were confirmed as adequate (CVI = 0.81) [ 16 , 17 ]. In the Iranian context, Dadfar et al. (2016) reported a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.74 for both subscales. Construct validity was also supported through confirmatory factor analysis, with factor loadings of 0.81, 0.73, and 0.76 for optimism, pessimism, and the total scale, respectively. Additionally, the concurrent validity of the LOT ranged from 0.64 to 0.72 [ 18 ]. Snyder’s hope scale The scale was originally developed by Snyder et al. and includes 12 items, of which four measure agency thinking (items 1, 4, 6, and 8), four measure pathways thinking (items 2, 9, 10, and 12), and the remaining four are filler items (items 3, 5, 7, and 11). Responses are scored on a 4‑point Likert scale ranging from 1 (definitely false) to 4 (definitely true). The possible total score for each of the agency and pathways subscales ranges from 4 to 16, with higher scores reflecting stronger agency and pathways thinking. The test‑retest reliability of the scale was reported by Snyder et al. as 0.85, 0.73, and 0.76 over 3‑, 8‑, and 10‑week intervals, respectively [ 19 ]. In Iran, the psychometric properties of the scale were evaluated by Kermani et al., who reported a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.86 [ 20 ]. Data collection procedure This study was conducted after obtaining approval from the Ethics Committee of Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences and relevant institutional authorities. Prior to the intervention, all three groups completed the relevant questionnaires (HADS, LOT, and Snyder’s Hope Scale). Subsequently, the CBT and group-based optimism training programs were implemented for the first and second experimental groups, respectively, over eight 90-minute sessions (one session per week for eight consecutive weeks), while the control group received standard medical rehabilitation training. The sessions were conducted using a workshop format, incorporating group discussions, question-and-answer sessions, and practical exercises. Upon completion of the interventions, the questionnaires were completed again by all groups immediately after the intervention, as well as at the two-months and four-months follow-ups, in order to compare the effectiveness of the interventions. Finally, the summary of educational contents of the group-based optimism training programs and CBT are presented in Tables 1 and 2 . Ethical considerations In this study, all research procedures were carried out in strict compliance with the standards outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, thereby ensuring full adherence to established ethical principles [ 21 ]. To this end, the research protocol was formally reviewed and approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences (IR.SBMU.PHNS.REC.1403.028). A comprehensive explanation of the study’s objectives and methodology was then provided to the participants. The confidentiality of participants’ names and information was guaranteed. Furthermore, the participants were informed that their participation in the study was voluntary and that they had the option to withdraw at any time. All participants were required to provide written informed consent before participating in the study. Statistical analysis Data analysis was conducted using SPSS version 21.0. To assess the normality of the primary study variables, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was employed. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were compared across groups using one-way ANOVA for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables to ensure group homogeneity. For each outcome variable, a 3 (Group: CBT, group-based optimism training, Control) × 4 (Time: T1, T2, T3, T4) repeated measures ANOVA was performed. Prior to the main analyses, the sphericity assumption was evaluated using Mauchly’s test; when violated, the Greenhouse-Geisser correction was applied. For significant interactions, post-hoc pairwise comparisons were conducted using the Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. Effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared (η²p) for the repeated measures ANOVA and Cohen’s d for pairwise comparisons, with all effect sizes presented alongside their 95% confidence intervals. A p-value < 0.05 was considered the significance level. The CONSORT flow diagram of the study is presented in Fig. 1 . Results The study findings showed that the average age of participants in the CBT, group-based optimism training, and control groups was 44.5 ± 13.4, 44.1 ± 13.0, and 44.2 ± 13.2, respectively. In addition, the results indicated that in all three groups, most participants were female, had an educational level of diploma or higher, and had more than 5 years of dialysis history. The three groups were homogeneous with respect to demographic and clinical characteristics at baseline (all p > 0.05) (Table 3 ). Prior to the main analyses, the sphericity assumption was evaluated using Mauchly’s test. Since the assumption was violated for all variables ( p < 0.05), the Greenhouse-Geisser correction was applied to adjust the degrees of freedom.
