title: Autism, anorexia nervosa, and the prevention of death: evidence supports adapted treatment, not assisted death
abstract: The practice of assisted death (AD) for people with eating disorders (EDs) is expanding, and a concerning revelation is the over-representation of autistic individuals among those with EDs who are offered (and complete) AD. Informed by our lived experience with EDs and being diagnosed with autism in adulthood, we examine the intersection of autism, EDs, and AD. We believe that the lack of autism assessment, autism-affirming treatment, and the over-specialization of ED care, exacerbated by futility narratives, are systemic failures that have contributed to autistic people with EDs being offered, and sometimes complete, AD. We challenge the notion of futility in ED care that justifies AD for autistic people with EDs and advocate for neurodiversity-affirming, trauma-informed adaptations to treatment that address the challenges autistic individuals may face in recovery, such as Multidiagnostic Eating Disorder Dialectical Behavior Therapy. We propose changes to safeguard autistic individuals and ensure they are offered meaningful pathways to treatment rather than being abandoned to premature death.

title: The Gambler's Fallacy Fallacy Fallacy (Commentary on Xiang et al., 2025)
abstract: Xiang et al. concluded that the gambler's fallacy does not originate in biased beliefs. Reanalyzing their data, we arrived at the opposite conclusion. We show, more generally, that their main analysis-examining whether the median belief is biased-is not diagnostic of the presence of the gambler's fallacy, whereas our test of the share of probability estimates for the streak ending above or below 50% is diagnostic. We also report results from a new study in which at least 80% of gambler's-fallacy predictions originated in biased beliefs.

title: Speech categorization consistency is robustly associated with receptive oral language performance
abstract:
Speech perception research on individual differences and clinical populations has traditionally emphasized the gradient/categorical dimension of categorization. Recent work, however, highlights categorization consistency—trial-by-trial response variability—as a more informative index of individual differences. Whether this index is relevant for language functions remains unknown. Across three experiments, we tested whether speech categorization consistency, rather than gradiency, was associated with receptive oral language ability. In Experiment 1 , English-speaking adults ( n =57) completed a speech Visual Analog Scaling (VAS) task, rating a speech continuum on a continuous scale, alongside two language assessments. Greater consistency in speech categorization was strongly associated with better receptive oral language performance, whereas gradiency showed no such relationship. Experiment 2 ( n =76) added a visual VAS task in which participants performed the same task with a visual continuum, to determine whether the observed effects reflected domain-general categorization mechanisms. Speech consistency again showed a strong association with language ability, and commonality analyses indicated that this effect was largely unique to speech, not to visual consistency. Experiment 3 ( n =95) equated the number of speech and visual continua and added a non-verbal IQ measure. Despite shared variance across domains, speech categorization consistency retained a unique association with language performance beyond visual categorization consistency and non-verbal IQ. These findings suggest that categorization consistency reflects both domain-general and speech-specific components, with speech consistency showing the most robust relationship to receptive oral language performance. This reframes individual differences in speech categorization by highlighting categorization consistency as an important dimension linking perceptual processing and broader language function.

Introduction A crucial component of speech perception is the ability to map a continuous and variable acoustic signal onto phonetic categories (e.g., /b/ and /p/). These categories, in turn, form the foundation for higher-order language processes like word recognition and sentence comprehension. This process is far from trivial because speech is highly variable, with variability arising from numerous factors, such as differences among talkers, speech rates, and phonetic contexts ( Holt & Lotto, 2010 ; McMurray & Jongman, 2011 ). As such, the mechanisms listeners employ to solve these perceptual challenges are foundational for broader communicative competence. Given its importance, it is perhaps unsurprising that individual differences in speech perception have been linked to a range of language-related clinical outcomes. A substantial body of work has documented associations between speech perception and various real-world consequences, including dyslexia ( Robertson et al., 2009 ; Serniclaes et al., 2004 ; Werker & Tees, 1987 ), brain damage ( Blumstein et al., 1977 ; Dial et al., 2019 ; Wolmetz et al., 2011 ), understanding speech-in-noise ( Myers et al., 2024 ; Rizzi & Bidelman, 2024 ), and success in second/foreign language acquisition ( Honda et al., 2024a , 2024b ; Kapnoula & Samuel, 2024 ). This has also been extensively investigated in the context of Developmental Language Disorders (DLD) ( Coady et al., 2005 ; McMurray et al., 2014 ; Robertson et al., 2009 ; Ziegler et al., 2005 ), a disorder affecting 10–12% of children ( Bishop & Snowling, 2004 ; Catts et al., 2005 ) characterized by poor oral language in the absence of other obvious causes. Here, a longstanding hypothesis argues that poor language ability (or DLD) stems from a deficit in lower-level speech perception: impaired speech perception is an early obstacle for language development that can delay other aspects of language ability. Importantly, DLD is widely seen as the lower end of a continuous distribution of language ability ( Leonard, 1991 ; Tomblin, 2014 ; Tomblin & Zhang, 1999 ). Thus, this hypothesized relationship between speech perception, language development, and DLD is relevant to broader variation in functional language ability, even within the typical population. Despite decades of work, the relationship between speech perception and language abilities remains unsettled. Evidence has been inconsistent, and findings are often difficult to reconcile (e.g., Bishop & McArthur, 2004 ; McMurray et al., 2014 ; Robertson et al., 2009 ). One contributing factor may lie in how speech perception is typically assessed. Most studies used traditional forced-choice tasks, in which listeners identify sounds along a continuum between two phonemes (e.g., /b/-/p/) by selecting one of two discrete options. These responses are used to construct a psychometric function that estimates the boundary location and the steepness—or slope—of the categorization function. In the context of individual differences, particularly for populations with language-related disorders, it is often assumed that categorization should be discrete ( Joanisse et al., 2000 ; Ziegler et al., 2005 ). Thus, shallower slopes are typically interpreted as reflecting noisier or less precise category representations. However, this interpretation rests on the assumption that speech categories are inherently discrete. Recent theoretical work in speech perception challenges this view, suggesting that speech categories are inherently gradient, which allows for more flexible speech perception ( Schouten et al., 2003 ; Toscano et al., 2010 ) ( McMurray, 2022 , for a review). From this perspective, it is unclear whether a shallower slope indicated by the forced-choice task represents a disrupted or a more gradient system. Moreover, forced-choice tasks constrain responses to binary categories, potentially obscuring the underlying dimensionality of any differences. To address these limitations, researchers have increasingly turned to the Visual Analog Scaling (VAS) task ( Kapnoula et al., 2017 ; Kong & Edwards, 2016 ) (based on Massaro & Cohen, 1983 ), which offers a continuous alternative to the forced-choice task. In the VAS task, listeners also hear tokens from a speech continuum (e.g., beach-peach ), but they rate them on a continuous scale. This continuous response format allows for a more direct mapping between continuous levels of category activation and the response space by avoiding the imposition of binary responses. Over the past decade, the VAS task has proven effective in delineating individual differences in speech categorization. While listeners generally perceive speech sounds in a gradient manner, they vary in how gradient or categorical their responses are (e.g., Kapnoula et al., 2017 ). These differences are stable over time ( Kong & Edwards, 2016 ) and have been linked to various downstream speech processes ( Kapnoula et al., 2021 ), functional and structural neural correlates ( Fuhrmeister & Myers, 2021 ; Kapnoula & McMurray, 2021 ), and second language learning ( Fuhrmeister et al., 2023 ; Honda et al., 2024a , 2024b ; Kapnoula et al., 2021 ). Despite this growing body of research, two critical limitations remain. First, these studies have largely focused on the relationship between variation in speech categorization and cognitively adjacent processes (e.g., cue integration, second language speech sound learning, auditory neuroscience). They have not asked about more distal relationships, such as the relationship between speech sound categorization in the VAS task and language as a whole. Second, to date, most studies using the VAS task have focused on the slope of the categorization function as the primary metric of interest. The slope (gradiency) indexes how abruptly listeners transition between categories, with steeper slopes reflecting more categorical perception and shallower slopes indicating more gradient use of intermediate ratings. This emphasis reflects the centrality of categorical or gradient modes of perception to theoretical models of speech perception, which posit that shallower slopes reflect greater perceptual flexibility, which may confer advantages in downstream processing (see McMurray, 2022 , for a review). In line with this view, several studies have reported that individuals with more gradient speech categorization—indicated by shallower slopes—tend to exhibit more efficient or successful outcomes across a variety of tasks ( Kapnoula et al., 2021 ; Kapnoula & McMurray, 2021 ; Kapnoula et al., 2017 ; Rizzi & Bidelman, 2024 ). However, this singular focus on slope overlooks another critical dimension of individual variability that can be revealed by the VAS task: categorization consistency . While slope captures the overall shape of the function (sharp vs gradual change), consistency reflects the trial-by-trial variability in how listeners map acoustic inputs onto a scale. That is, how reliably a listener produces the same response when hearing the same stimulus across multiple encounters. It can be indexed as the root mean squared error (RMSE) between individual trial ratings and the fitted function for each continuum step. This dimension cannot be indexed by forced-choice tasks in which the trial-by-trial variability is conflated with the slope of the mean function. 1 For instance, if a shallower slope represents noise imposed on a categorical system, listeners should predominantly use the endpoints of the scale, with lower categorization consistency at intermediate steps. In contrast, if listeners are more gradient, their responses should align linearly with continuum steps, with trial-by-trial responses clustered around this function. Emerging evidence suggests categorization consistency is a stronger predictor of language-related outcomes than slope. A recent study of 3rd-grade children ( n = 237) ( Kim, Klein-Packard, et al., 2025 ), including those with DLD and/or dyslexia, used VAS tasks alongside standardized language and reading assessments. Contrary to expectations, neither condition was related to the slope of the response function. Instead, both lower language (or DLD) and reading (or dyslexia) were strongly associated with lower categorization consistency. Notably, consistency predicted continuous measures of both language and reading ability over and above phonological processing skills (explicit awareness of speech sounds) that are known to be critically linked to both abilities ( Bishop & Snowling, 2004 ; Snowling & Hulme, 2012 ). These findings suggest that categorization consistency may reflect a foundational perceptual process with broad relevance for language and reading functions ( Kim et al., 2026 ). Further support for the robustness and generalizability of this dimension comes from a recent study that examined the stability of VAS indices across multiple speech continua in adults ( Kim, McMurray, et al., 2025 ). Categorization consistency exhibited stronger cross-continuum correlations than slope, suggesting it is a more trait-like and generalizable feature of individual perceptual systems. Together, these findings reinforce the view that categorization consistency provides a more precise and reliable index of individual differences in speech perception—one that is more stable and strongly linked to real-world language-relevant outcomes than slope (gradiency). This work suggests that the enhanced precision of the VAS task may offer a clearer and more precise picture of the relationship between overall language ability and speech perception. Building on this work, the current study asks three central questions. First, while our prior work has established a link between categorization consistency and language ability (or DLD) in childhood, we ask if these associations are confined to this specific developmental window, or if they persist into adulthood and across a broader, more typical range of language abilities. Core language skills are highly conserved and robust from infancy to adolescence ( Bornstein et al., 2018 ), and deficits in even low-level skills like phonological processing linked to DLD persist through adolescence and adulthood ( Clegg et al., 2005 ). Yet little is known about whether these persistent individual differences in language function are accompanied by differences in lower-level speech categorization, as this has not been assessed even with traditional forced-choice methods. From a developmental standpoint, two possibilities follow. One is that robust speech categorization skills are most critical during early development; however, by adulthood, individuals with initially poor speech categorization may have compensated or caught up. Under this view, speech categorization differences in adults may no longer be associated with language outcomes. Alternatively, speech categorization skills may exert a lasting influence, such that individuals with less gradient or less consistent perception continue to experience subtle language processing difficulties throughout life. Second, if speech categorization predicts language function in adulthood, an equally important issue is which dimension of categorization—gradiency or consistency—is more functionally relevant for language. As we described, prior work on individual differences in adult speech perception has largely emphasized gradiency ( Kapnoula et al., 2021 ; Kapnoula et al., 2017 ). However, this assumption has not been directly tested against the alternative possibility that consistency may better explain language outcomes. Experiment 1 addressed these two questions. Participants completed a VAS task with speech continua, alongside language assessments that measure language comprehension ability and receptive vocabulary. We focused on these two domains because stable speech categorization supports robust phonological representations, which are critical for lexical access and higher-level sentence processing. Inconsistent encoding of speech sounds may introduce noise into lexical representations, making it more difficult to access word meanings efficiently and to maintain and integrate information across a sentence. Receptive vocabulary and sentence comprehension also represent clinically central domains of oral language ability: both are commonly assessed in standardized measures used to characterize DLD ( Tomblin et al., 1996 ), and DLD is widely viewed as the lower end of a continuous distribution of language ability rather than as a sharply bounded category ( Leonard, 1991 ; Tomblin, 2014 ; Tomblin & Zhang, 1999 ). Thus, these measures provide a theoretically motivated and clinically relevant index of broader oral language ability. As a result, receptive vocabulary and sentence comprehension provide particularly sensitive downstream measures of how individual differences in speech categorization relate to broader language function. If speech categorization plays a lasting role in supporting langua

title: Sequential Sampling from Memory Underlies Perceptual Decisions Unyoked from Actions
abstract: Perceptual decision-making refers to the class of decisions in which sensory evidence is used to categorize percepts and guide actions. Conventionally, categorical decisions are thought to precede motor actions. However, recent studies in nonhuman primates challenge this assumption-when perceptual decisions were uncoupled from the actions they bear upon, animals postponed the decisions until relevant response options were revealed. To determine whether this postponement stems from cognitive limitations unique to nonhuman primates, we conducted a similar experiment with human participants. Naive participants viewed a random dot motion (RDM) stimulus that was difficult to categorize. After a delay period following the RDM, two choice targets were presented and participants decided which target lay closer to the perceived motion direction. Decision accuracy varied across participants, reflecting individual differences in ability to integrate motion evidence. Notably, participants with higher decision accuracy showed prolonged deliberation after choice-target presentation. Furthermore, the time they took to report their decisions depended on the strength of the motion evidence. This pattern of accuracy and decision reporting time could be accounted for by a bounded diffusion model in which participants sequentially sample stored sensory information from memory during the target selection phase. When the RDM was challenging to categorize, the subsequent appearance of the targets provided a framework to interrogate stored evidence and render a decision. Our results reveal a strategic feature of working memory of retaining information based on its future utility. This observation opens new avenues for investigating how memory and decision-making interact.

title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers
abstract: Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

title: Conflict between representational formats and procedures constrains visual tracking
abstract: Computer-assisted design software, such as PowerPoint, groups separate elements to create structured objects whose parts can be manipulated relative to the whole. Might visual perception perform a similar operation, grouping scene elements and representing them with internal reference to the emergent structure? The proposal is central yet perennially controversial in cognitive neuroscience and philosophy of mind. In a series of seven preregistered tracking experiments, we identify internally referenced representations in human vision by relying on the logic that, as in computer-assisted design, a representation will make certain procedures easy to access while limiting others. Participants tracked a target among identical nontargets organized into geometric shapes. When the shapes rotated, performance was high, suggesting the use of internally referenced, shape-centered representations that naturally support rotational transformations. In contrast, performance declined in translation conditions, where constituent items moved independently, revealing a mismatch between the internally structured representation and the requisite, externally oriented tracking procedure. This effect replicated across diverse stimuli, including occluded, rounded, and irregular shapes, and was reduced when structure-inducing cues were disrupted. These findings identify representational format and its compatibility with task procedures as an important determinant of visual performance.

title: Visual and interoceptive factors shape affective and aesthetic evaluations of body postures
abstract: The influence of internal body rhythms, such as heartbeats, on affective and cognitive processes remains an area of research, informing how bodily states shape perception of the world. Studies of facial expression evaluation show that emotional (negative vs. neutral) faces are detected more easily and perceived as more intense when presented during systole rather than diastole, two phases of the cardiac cycle. Whether similar cardiac phase effects extend to affective and aesthetic evaluations of human bodies remains unclear. In this preregistered study, participants without dance training rated upright and inverted body postures from motion capture recordings of contemporary dancers for emotional intensity and likability. Each image was presented during either the participant's ventricular systole or diastole. We assessed interoceptive accuracy (via the Heartbeat Counting Task; HBCT) and collected emotional valence and bodily arousal ratings for each stimulus. Contrary to predictions, emotional intensity and likability did not increase during systole. Instead, we found that cardiac-related effects were conditional. Emotional intensity was positively associated with bodily arousal, except for inverted postures during systole. How this relationship depended on orientation was modulated by HBCT performance. Likability was positively associated with valence, with this relationship becoming stronger as HBCT performance increased. These findings suggest cardiac-related factors may contribute to affective and aesthetic evaluations of dance-like body postures, as a function of body orientation, stimulus affective characteristics, and individual differences in heartbeat perception. They indicate that ongoing physiological states may shape how others are evaluated beyond facial information, extending to both affective and aesthetic domains.

title: Computational complexity improves recognition memory for reward-relevant attributes
abstract: Computational complexity in optimisation tasks is often seen as impairing optimal choice. We test whether it could have beneficial effects on memory. In a preregistered lab experiment (N = 131) using the NP-hard 0-1 knapsack problem, we manipulated knapsack capacity to create instances differing in two objective complexity metrics: phase transition proximity and Sahni-k. As predicted, solving a more complex instance resulted in a 44% (d = 0.45) increase in above-chance recognition memory relative to a lower-complexity instance. Participants spent longer on the complex instance and clicked on items more often. A plausible interpretation of these findings is that the increased processing requirements of search algorithms under complexity may have resulted in enhanced encoding through frequent revisiting of reward-relevant information. These findings provide a formal framework to generate hypotheses about the memory consequences of complexity and the effects of cognitive offloading in real-world decisions.

title: The role of bilingualism and executive functions in the comprehension of which-questions by typically developing and autistic children
abstract: Bilingualism has been associated with enhanced Executive Functions (EFs) in typically developing (TD) children and autistic children, although findings remain mixed. Furthermore, while studies investigating the effect of bilingualism on complex syntax in autistic children are still scarce, they tend to show that bilingualism does not exacerbate performance. The main aim of this study is to examine whether bilingualism enhances particular EFs which, in turn, has a cascade effect contributing to the improved comprehension of which-questions. We tested 134 verbal autistic and 234 TD children aged 3 to 13. Bilingualism was examined both categorically (monolingual vs. bilingual) and continuously (proficiency, length of exposure, length of use, balance of exposure, and balance of use) using the parental Quantifying Bilingual Experience questionnaire (De Cat et al., 2025). Executive functions were assessed using performance-based tasks measuring working memory, inhibition and shifting, alongside a parent-report measure of attention. Furthermore, all children completed a character selection task to assess comprehension of subject and object which-questions. Results showed specific bilingual experiences (e.g., balance and length of language exposure and use) indirectly supported comprehension of which-questions through their influence on EFs. The mediating EF domains differed for TD and autistic children, highlighting the need to consider cognitive diversity in bilingualism research. These findings suggest that bilingual experience may serve as a cognitive-linguistic resource, especially for autistic children, by enhancing domain-specific EFs that underpin complex language processing.

title: Confounds in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging-Part III: Auxiliary Data
abstract: In the first part of this series, we reviewed the pathways that bring about confounding nuisance signals in fMRI. Then, in the second part, we considered how human factors can modify these pathways. In this, the third and final part, we review auxiliary data that may allow researchers to identify and perhaps correct for nuisance signals and their modifiers. We consider three broad categories of data: (1) measures that can be collected synchronously with the fMRI, (2) other MRI scans that either capture trait information or attempt to define the state that exists during an fMRI scan in the same session, and (3) non-MRI measures that can be collected before or after the scan and that also capture trait or relevant state factors influencing the fMRI. We conclude with some recommendations on ways to improve fMRI experiments going forward.

title: Distributed Neural Dynamics Underlie the Shift from Movement Preparation to Execution
abstract: Understanding how neural population activity supports the transition from movement preparation to execution remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience. Invasive recordings in nonhuman primates indicate that motor preparation and execution occupy orthogonal subspaces within the primary motor cortex (M1), yet how these neural dynamics evolve across broader networks and support skilled, memory-guided action remains poorly understood. We used source-resolved magnetoencephalography during a memory-guided finger-sequence task to track population dynamics across a cortico-hippocampal network. Manifold trajectories and decoding revealed that preparation and execution of movement sequences occupy distinct, yet not fully orthogonal, neural subspaces-a separation that generalized across all regions but was most pronounced in motor regions. Crucially, we identified a hierarchical spatio-temporal transition across the brain: The state shift originated in the hippocampus via theta-band modulations and rippled through the pre-SMA, SMA, and lateral premotor areas before culminating in M1 via broadband activity. This progression follows the functional hierarchy of descending motor pathways, with M1 shifting last, 160 msec before the first button press. Although sequence identity could be decoded from all areas during execution, only the hippocampus and M1 maintained predictive representations of upcoming sequences during preparation. These findings demonstrate that the initiation of complex motor sequences relies on a well-timed integration of hippocampal memory systems with primary motor output, rather than being a process localized to the motor cortices alone.

title: When looking away means looking inward: contextual interpretation of gaze aversions determines their attentional value
abstract: Eye movements are typically understood as supporting outward orienting, directing attention toward locations of interest in the external environment. However, not all eye movements reflect outward orienting. Gaze aversions, the common tendency to look away during effortful cognitive processing, serve as social signals of inward-oriented attention and ongoing processing. Because observers continuously monitor others' eye movements and use gaze-related cues to guide their own behavior, distinguishing between outward-oriented gaze-shifts and inward-oriented gaze aversions is a basic challenge in human interaction. Here, we examine the hypothesis that this distinction depends on the context in which gaze shifts appear. While participants reorient their attention following an outward-oriented gaze shift, they withhold doing so when the context suggests that the gaze shift reflects inward-oriented processing. To test this hypothesis, we relied on the Gaze Cueing Effect (GCE), an attentional orienting to observed gaze shifts that is known to be modulated by top-down context and interpretation. In two pre-registered experiments (total N = 90), participants performed a gaze-cueing letter-discrimination task while viewing identical gaze shifts within different contexts. One group was led to interpret the gaze shifts as occurring during effortful thinking, whereas the other group received no thinking-related context. Across both experiments, attentional orienting was significantly reduced when gaze shifts were perceived as reflecting internal cognitive processing rather than attention shifts. These findings demonstrate that gaze aversions function as communicative signals that dynamically regulate interpersonal attention, and that gaze following depends fundamentally on the inferred social meaning of the observed eye movement.

title: The folk concept of moral agency
abstract: Whether a particular entity is a 'moral agent' determines the sense in which its behaviour is morally evaluable. Theories of moral agency aim to capture and explain commonsense distinctions between the possession or absence of moral agency across different kinds of being. But little is known about the ordinary concept of moral agency, its application across different entities, and its relation to the more specific notion of moral responsibility. In this paper, we investigate the folk concept of moral agency through philosophical analysis and two empirical studies. We draw conceptual distinctions between three components of moral agency: intentional action (acting rather than behaving), moral action (acting morally rightly or wrongly), and responsible action (being blameworthy for one's actions). We then investigate whether people differentiate between the three components of moral agency, and the extent to which their judgments depend on the perceived psychological and behavioural capacities of the entity in question. We find that people attribute varying degrees of moral agency to different entities while differentiating between the proposed components. These moral agency attributions are partly, but not fully, explained by people's attributions of underlying capacities. While intentional action ascriptions were linked to the attribution of mental states like desires, beliefs, and sensations, moral action and moral responsibility were linked to ascriptions of capacities for a 'deep self'. Philosophical theories of moral agency should account for these patterns in folk attributions.

title: From linguistic anchors to acoustic skeletons: the dual-pathway model of voice identity representation
abstract: Achieving perceptual constancy for voice identity across the speech-song continuum represents a fundamental cognitive challenge. Does the auditory system rely on precise linguistic cues to "anchor" identity, or does it utilize multi-dimensional acoustic variability to build a generalized prototype? In this study, we trained listeners to recognize voices via three modalities, i.e., reading (linguistic focus), non-lexical singing on /la/ (structural focus), and singing (dual focus). We then tested their recognition of the voices under immediate, cross-modal, and one-week delayed conditions. Experiment 1 revealed that training with lyrics (reading and singing) yielded high initial accuracy, demonstrating a rapid encoding advantage of linguistic cues. However, Experiments 2 and 3 uncovered significant asymmetries. While identities learned through singing transferred seamlessly to non-lexical singing, those learned through reading incurred substantial cross-modal processing costs and marked retrieval latencies despite remaining above chance level. After a one-week delay, testing the reading group on non-lexical vocable singing revealed a behavioral dissociation. While identification accuracy remained well above chance (M = 0.62), response times spiked dramatically to 4722 ms. This latency reflects an active, exhaustive memory search triggered by persistent coarse acoustic invariants when fine-grained lexical and phonetic anchors are missing. These findings refine a Dual-Pathway Model of voice processing in which a linguistic-phonetic pathway provides language-bound precision, while an acoustic-melodic pathway exploits acoustic variability to extract a domain-general acoustic skeleton that is robust against cross-modal transfer and temporal decay.

title: Accuracy of parent and teacher reports of early math skills
abstract:
BACKGROUND: It is important for parents and teachers to understand preschooler's early mathematics skills to best provide appropriate mathematics support. Comparing parents' and teachers' accuracy in reporting children's mathematics skills may help to ensure developmentally appropriate early math support in home and classroom environments.

AIM: The present study examined the accuracy of parents' and teachers' reports of preschoolers' early mathematics skills (i.e., counting, numeral identification, and quantitative and spatial word knowledge).

SAMPLE: Participants included 117 children 3 to 5 years old (M = 4.27, SD = .63, 49.6 % female) and their parent and Head Start teacher.

METHOD: Parents and teachers completed surveys reporting on each child's understanding of mathematics concepts via items from different mathematics measures. Children were directly assessed on their mathematics skills via the same or similar items.

RESULTS: Generally, parents' and teachers' reports were positively associated with direct assessments of children's mathematics skills. Parents' and teachers' reports of children's mathematical skills ranged from 47 % to 75 % accurate, and parents were more accurate than teachers in reporting children's quantitative word knowledge. The direction of inaccuracies (over-or underestimation) varied by mathematics skill type, such that caregivers tended to overestimate children's numeracy skills and underestimate their mathematical language knowledge.

CONCLUSION: Future research is needed to examine how the accuracy of parents and teachers reports influences early mathematics development, and how potentially improving caregiver accuracy might support children's mathematics learning.

title: Knowledge and Misinformation Regarding Autism Risk Factors in a Survey of US Adults
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: With the rise of misinformation about autism risk, including recent statements from US government officials, the extent to which the public understands environmental autism risk factors is not known.

OBJECTIVE: To characterize beliefs about autism risk factors among US adults and identify characteristics influencing these beliefs.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cross-sectional survey study used data from an internet-based survey of adults aged 18 years or older residing in all 50 US states and the District of Columbia and was administered between December 18, 2025, and January 27, 2026. Multiple regression models assessed sociodemographic and other individual characteristics, including political affiliation and trust in institutions, for association with endorsement of misinformed beliefs.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was endorsement of individual risk factors, scored on a 5-point Likert scale from definitely false to definitely true.

RESULTS: Of the 30 388 adults who completed the survey, 100 did not provide an answer to the childhood vaccination item, leaving 30 288 in the analysis. Among the 30 288 participants (mean [SD] age, 46.6 [15.9] years), 13 702 (45.2%) identified as men, 16 393 (54.1%) as women, and 193 (0.6%) as nonbinary. The most commonly endorsed cause was genetic factors (20 380 of 30 254; unweighted, 67.4%; weighted, 66.7%), an evidence-based risk factor. However, 8370 of 30 288 (unweighted, 27.6%; weighted, 26.6%) endorsed childhood vaccinations and 7140 of 30 211 (unweighted, 23.6%; weighted, 23.1%) endorsed acetaminophen in pregnancy as autism risk factors. In regression models, endorsement of vaccine-autism risk beliefs was greatest among adults aged 35 to 44 years (vs 18 to 24 years, adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.64; 95% CI, 1.44-1.86) and lowest among those aged 65 years and older (aOR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.55-0.74). Endorsement was also associated with men (aOR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.19-1.34), African American or Black race (compared with White race, aOR, 1.25; 95% CI, 1.15-1.35), Hispanic ethnicity (aOR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.03-1.24), and strength of Republican political affiliation (strong Republican vs strong Democrat, aOR, 3.83; 95% CI, 3.47-4.24). More frequent social media use was associated with lower odds of endorsing misinformation (multiple times daily vs less than weekly, aOR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.66-0.78).

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Results of this survey study suggest that non-evidence-based beliefs about autism risk were prevalent among US adults and were strongly associated with sociodemographic differences and political affiliation. Limiting public health impact of such non-evidence-based information will likely require targeted interventions that recognize the heterogeneity of such beliefs.

title: A Systematic Review of Qualitative Research Upon the Perceptions of Parents and Caregivers of Children with Autism About Health, School, and Community Support Networks
journal: Evid Based Pract Child Adolesc Ment Health
abstract: Background : Family members and caregivers of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) report challenges and barriers in accessing support networks, which are associated with detrimental impacts on clinical, social, and quality-of-life outcomes. Objective : To explore how parents and caregivers of children with ASD, experience the support network provided by health and education services and the community. Method : This is a systematic review of the qualitative research about health, school and community support networks for parents and caregivers of children with ASD using a thematic synthesis of the studies. We searched the terms in the PubMed, EMBASE, ERIC and APA PsychNet databases for qualitative studies (interviews, focus groups and questionnaires with open questions) and produced a thematic synthesis by codes and themes based on the selected qualitative studies. Results : The synthesis resulted in 24 selected articles. Three themes emerged: health support networks (search for diagnosis, emotional support, post-diagnosis, financial and family impacts, access to specialized services); school support networks (inclusive school, training, emotional support); and community support networks (stigma and social exclusion, judgments, and emotional support). Parents and caregivers of children with ASD perceive difficulties in their trajectories with the various support networks. Conclusions : The limited emotional support received by parents was a common perception in health, school and community networks. Socioeconomic, demographic, ethnic and cultural characteristics seem to influence differently the perceptions on support networks.

title: Region-Adapted Multi-Nutrient Supplementation in Chinese Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A 12-Week Pilot Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Nutritional supplementation has produced inconsistent effects on autistic symptoms, and the evidence base is largely derived from Western populations. This study evaluated the preliminary efficacy and tolerability of a region-adapted multinutrient intervention in Chinese children with autism spectrum disorder. In this 12-wk pilot, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 50 children were assigned to receive either the intervention or a placebo. The primary endpoint was the change in the Autism Behavior Checklist total score. Secondary outcomes included developmental functioning assessed using the Psychoeducational Profile, Third Edition; gastrointestinal symptoms assessed using the Gastrointestinal Severity Index; and sleep assessed with the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire. Between-group differences were analysed using baseline-adjusted models. All participants completed follow-up, and no serious adverse events were reported. The change in the Autism Behavior Checklist total score did not differ between groups (p=0.44). Receptive language on the Psychoeducational Profile, Third Edition improved more in the intervention group (difference in change=2.38; 95% confidence interval, 0.19-4.57; p=0.03). Other subscales showed mixed findings, including problem behaviour favouring control. Regarding tolerability, while abdominal pain improved in the intervention group (p=0.01), reports of night waking (p=0.01) and looser stools (p=0.05) increased. The prespecified primary endpoint was not met. Exploratory findings suggested a signal in receptive language, alongside tolerability trade-offs. These results require confirmation in adequately powered trials with refined endpoint selection and structured safety monitoring.

title: Outcomes of sensory integration therapy in children with autism spectrum disorder: a non-randomized pre-post intervention study
abstract:
Background Sensory processing abnormalities have been linked to autism symptoms. Sensory integration therapy (SIT) affects autism symptom severity, sensory profile and related socio-demographic/clinical variables. Methods Thirty patients, aged 3 to 10 years, meeting autism spectrum disorder (ASD) case definition were recruited from SIT clinic, Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Department, Okasha Institute of Psychiatry, Ain Shams University, Cairo, between May 2023 and January 2025, assessed by socio-demographic/clinical questionnaire, Arabic versions of Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children Present and Lifetime Version, Stanford–Binet Intelligence Scale Fifth Edition, Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), and Sensory Profile Caregiver Questionnaire. Participants received a 12-week SIT program (one 30-minute session weekly), then post-intervention reassessment using CARS and Sensory Profile. Results The most common age was 3–5 years (46.66%), with males comprising 80%. Most participants (73.33%) IQ scores were 60–64. Mean CARS scores decreased from 33.9 ± 3.42 to 31.95 ± 3.4, mild autism increasing to 76.67%, moderate decreasing to 10% and unchanged severe cases. Mostly affected domains were vestibular processing, emotional/social responses, behavioural outcomes of sensory processing and fine motor/perceptual. Post-intervention, the most improved were vestibular processing, emotional/social response, emotionally reactive, inattention/distractibility ( p -value < 0.001), auditory processing, modulation of body position and movement affecting activity level ( p -value 0.001). The least were sensory processing related to endurance/tone and low endurance/tone. Conclusion SIT effectively reduced autism severity and improved key sensory and behavioural domains of sensory processing, particularly in mild to moderate cases. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06882642 , registered March 2025 (retrospectively registered).

Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, together with restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities [ 1 ]. Sensory processing differences, including hyper-reactivity, hypo-reactivity, and sensory-seeking behaviors, are recognized as a core diagnostic feature of ASD in the DSM-5-TR and are highly prevalent across the spectrum [ 1 ]. These sensory differences are associated with impairments in daily functioning, emotional regulation, attention, and social participation [ 2 ]. Sensory integration therapy (SIT), originally developed by A. Jean Ayres, aims to improve the brain’s ability to process and integrate sensory input through structured, play-based activities. Despite its widespread clinical use, the evidence base for SIT remains mixed. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have reported variable outcomes, with some studies demonstrating functional improvements and others showing limited or inconsistent effects. In a systematic review, Schoen et al. identified six eligible studies of Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI) in children with ASD, including two high-quality randomized controlled trials. The review concluded that ASI may improve functional performance, participation, and individualized goal achievement in children with ASD [ 3 ]. In a systematic review by Case-Smith et al. a total of 19 studies were reviewed: 5 examined the effects of sensory integration therapy and 14 sensory-based intervention. The studies defined sensory integration therapies as clinic-based interventions that use sensory-rich, child-directed activities to improve a child’s adaptive responses to sensory experiences. Two randomized controlled trials found positive effects for sensory integration therapy on child performance using Goal Attainment Scaling [ 4 ]. In one of the largest randomized controlled trials to date, named Sensory Integration Therapy for sensory processing difficulties in children with Autism spectrum disorder (SenITA trial), there were no significant benefits of SIT over standard care on primary behavioral outcomes, although subgroup and secondary findings suggested potential benefits in specific domains [ 5 ]. Most sensory integration therapy (SIT) research has been conducted in North America, Europe, and other high-income countries, with relatively limited evidence from low- and middle-income countries and under-represented populations. Furthermore, much of the literature originates from controlled research settings rather than routine clinical outpatient practice [ 3 ]. Although previous studies have evaluated sensory outcomes, functional performance, or behavioral measures separately, relatively few investigations have concurrently examined changes in autism severity and detailed sensory processing profiles following SIT [ 4 ]. Understanding which domains are most responsive to SIT, and whether clinical variables influence outcomes, remains of clinical relevance. The present study aimed to evaluate the effects of a 12-week SIT program on autism severity and sensory processing patterns in children with ASD. A secondary aim was to explore potential predictors of treatment response. We hypothesized that participation in the 12-week sensory integration therapy program would be associated with a reduction in autism severity and improvements in sensory processing domains among children with autism spectrum disorder. Methods Study design and setting This study employed a single-arm, non-randomized pre–post interventional design. Participants were recruited from a sensory integration therapy outpatient clinic within Ain shams university-affiliated child and adolescent psychiatry department, Cairo, Egypt, between May 2023 and January 2025. Sampling method Convenient sample. Participants Inclusion criteria included children aged 3–10 years, if they met DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for ASD and demonstrated sensory processing difficulties based on caregiver report. Exclusion criteria included comorbid neurological disorders (e.g., epilepsy, cerebral palsy), significant sensory or motor impairments, intellectual functioning below an IQ of 60, or typical performance on the Sensory Profile. Patients did not receive medications or other neuro modulatory intervention, or had past history of last receiving medications or neuro modulatory interventions, maximum 3 months before the start of study. Ethical considerations The study was approved by the institutional research ethics committee of the Faculty of Medicine, Ain Shams University ( Approval No. FMASU MD71/2023 ). All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. An informed written consent was obtained from all participant guardian in the study before conducting the interview with ensured confidentiality. Measures A designed questionnaire to collect demographic and clinical data: such as age, gender, educational level, residence of the patient. Perinatal history including maternal exposure to pollution, drug intake during pregnancy and maternal and paternal age at pregnancy, developmental history of the patient, past history of any medical condition, family history of any psychiatric disorders and history of parental consanguinity. Clinical picture of ASD in patients diagnosed according to criteria of DSM-V: Arabic version of Schedule for Affective disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children- Present and Lifetime Version, (K-SADS-PL): It is an interviewer-based, semi-structured for children use to assess current and lifetime history of psychiatric disorders, episodes of psychopathology and to make categorical diagnosis according to DSM-V criteria. Both the child and parents are interviewed by the psychiatrist. It was used as a diagnostic instrument to confirm psychiatric diagnoses and exclude relevant psychiatric comorbidities during participant selection [ 6 , 7 ]. Autism severity : Assessed using the Arabic version of Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS): a clinician-rated instrument designed to evaluate the severity of autism symptoms in children aged ≥ 2 years. The scale consists of 15 items assessing social interaction, emotional responses, communication, stereotyped behaviors, sensory responsiveness, play skills, and adaptation to change. Ratings are based on direct observation and caregiver information and typically require 5–10 min to complete. In the present study, CARS was administered by a trained psychologist. Each item is scored on a scale from 1 to 4, with half-point intervals permitted, yielding a total score ranging from 15 to 60. Total scores were interpreted as follows: non-autistic range (15–29.5), mild autism (30–33.5), moderate autism (34–36.5), and severe autism (37–60). The CARS is a widely used instrument with established reliability and validity, demonstrating high internal consistency, inter-rater reliability, and good diagnostic accuracy for identifying autism spectrum disorder [ 8 , 9 ]. Sensory processing : Evaluated using the translated Arabic version of Dunn Sensory Profile Caregiver Questionnaire, a standardized tool assessing sensory processing patterns in children: a 125-item caregiver-reported measure evaluating children’s responses to sensory experiences in daily life. The questionnaire assesses sensory processing, modulation, and behavioral/emotional responses and includes domains such as sensory seeking, sensory sensitivity, poor registration, emotional reactivity, inattention/distractibility, low endurance/tone, oral sensory sensitivity, sedentary behavior, and fine motor/perceptual functioning. The questionnaire was completed by the same caregiver before and after the intervention, with assistance from the psychiatrist when needed. Items are scored according to the frequency of the child’s behaviors and summed to obtain raw scores. Based on normative data, scores are classified as Typical Performance (within 1 standard deviation of the mean), Probable Difference (1–2 standard deviations from the mean), or Definite Difference (> 2 standard deviations from the mean). The Sensory Profile has demonstrated good reliability and validity for assessing sensory processing patterns in children [ 10 , 11 ]. Cognitive functioning : Intellectual ability was assessed using the Arabic version of Stanford–Binet Intelligence Scale, Fifth Edition: The SB5 test is divided into two domains: verbal and non-verbal and the test measures five CHC factors: fluid intelligence (Gf), crystallized knowledge (Gc), quantitative knowledge (Gq), visual processing (Gv), and short-term memory (Gsm) with verbal and non-verbal subtest each. So, it consists of 10 subtests in total that yield composite scores of a verbal IQ (VIQ), a non-verbal IQ (NVIQ), and full-scale IQ (FSIQ). It was applied by the psychologist [ 12 , 13 ]. Study procedure Phase I : the participants were assessed by the following: Designed questionnaire and K-SADS-PL, Stanford Binet Intelligence scale fifth edition. CARS and Sensory Profile Caregiver questionnaire. This was followed by a standardized sensory integration program where participants received 12 weekly sessions, each lasting 30 min. Participants attending fewer than 10 sessions were considered dropouts. Therapy was delivered by a trained clinician in a multisensory therapeutic environment designed to provide vestibular, proprioceptive, tactile, auditory, and visual stimulation. Sessions emphasized active child engagement, individualized challenge, and play-based activities which are consistent with Ayres sensory integration principles [ 3 ]. In this study, in Okasha institute of psychiatry, the sensory tools are present in the 3 sensory rooms. Every child was trained in all three rooms during each session, yet activities were individualized according to each child’s sensory needs and treatment goals. Sensory room 1 A cushioned swing, Ultraviolet lamp, fibre optic boards, lightening cube, rotating color changing disk displaying spotted light with effects, auditing stimulation speakers in room corners with sounds of nature. Touch pad with different sensations, vibrator, brushes and massage tools. Sensory room 2 Cushion swing, padded stairs and slide, wooden stairs with a pool of plastic colored balls underneath, balance pad, bouncing ball, tunnel. Pads for foot massage and balance. Sensory room 3 A projector presenting images from rotating disks purposely designed for sensory room (circles, squares, zigzag lines), a rotating mirror ball and 20 strands of fibre optic threads with lightening colours. Interactive bubble tubes (lava lamp), in the corner between two mirrors, interactive lightening games displaying family members, interactive lightening pads pressed on by feet displaying colours with their names, sounds of birds, animals, and an interactive lightening board displaying colours as an equalizer when the child speaks through the microphone. Board with fine motor skill tools as counting colouring discs, opening and closing door with different locks and tying shoe-laces. Phase II : after completing the sensory integration program participants were reassessed by: CARS and Sensory Profile Caregiver questionnaire (by the same caregiver). Sample size calculation Referencing a study done in 2019 by Novakovic et al., using PASS 15 program for sample size calculation and setting power at 80% and alpha error at 0.05, it was estimated that sample size of 27 children would be needed to detect medium effect size difference between assessment scores before and after intervention (d = 0.50). Sample size was increased by 10% (30 children) [ 14 ]. Statistical analysis Data were analyzed using Statistical package for Social Science, SPSS version 27. Paired t-tests were used to assess pre–post differences in continuous outcomes. Categorical changes were analyzed using marginal homogeneity tests. Correlation analyses were conducted using Spearman’s rho, and exploratory linear regression was performed to examine predictors of treatment response. To account for multiple comparisons across Sensory Profile domains and factor scores, p-values were adjusted using the Holm sequential correction procedure, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results In the period from May 2023 to January 2025, eighty-six children were screened, of whom 48 met eligibility criteria, 38 of them were excluded as 15 patients had IQ below 60, 4 patients had co-morbid epilepsy, 1 patient had co-morbid optic atrophy, 8 patients had co-morbid ADHD, 6 patients were diagnosed as cerebral palsy and did not meet criteria of diagnosis with ASD and 4 patients scored typical performance in sensory profile.
