title: Associations between neurodevelopmental traits and perinatal depression: a prospective study in Japanese women
abstract:
Purpose This study examined how attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) traits relate to depressive symptoms from late pregnancy through early postpartum in Japanese women, alongside perinatal factors. Methods In a multicenter prospective study, 1,104 women completed questionnaires at late pregnancy (T1), 2 weeks postpartum (T2), and 1 month postpartum (T3). Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), ADHD traits with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS), and ASD traits with the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ). Chi-square tests evaluated timepoint-specific associations, multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of EPDS positivity at T2, and a linear mixed-effects model assessed longitudinal changes. Results EPDS scores and EPDS positivity were highest at T1 and declined postpartum (16.7%, 8.6%, 4.0%). Scores were correlated across timepoints. In univariate analyses, antenatal EPDS positivity showed associations with ASD traits (AQ+: OR = 6.08, 95% CI 2.17–16.99) and ADHD traits (ASRS+: OR = 4.86, 95% CI 3.06–7.72). In multivariable analysis, independent predictors of EPDS positivity at T2 included ADHD traits (OR = 1.37, 95% CI 1.13–1.66), primiparity, psychiatric treatment history, and antenatal EPDS scores. ASD traits were not associated with T2 EPDS positivity after adjustment for antenatal EPDS scores. In the mixed-effects model, both ADHD and ASD traits were associated with higher EPDS scores during pregnancy, with attenuated effects postpartum. Conclusion Neurodevelopmental traits are associated with perinatal mental health, and trait- and timing-informed support may enhance maternal psychological stability and caregiving outcomes. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s00737-026-01781-4 .

Article Highlights ADHD traits were associated with depressive symptoms from pregnancy through postpartum. ASD traits were associated with depressive symptoms mainly during pregnancy. Risk factors for postpartum depression include first-time mothers, psychiatric history, elevated antenatal EPDS scores. Many neurodevelopmental traits remain unrecognized in clinical settings. Personalized support based on trait profile and timing can improve maternal mental health. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s00737-026-01781-4 .

Introduction Perinatal depression is a major mental health concern that affects approximately 10 − 20% of women worldwide (Bauman et al. 2020 ; Tokumitsu et al. 2020 ; Wang et al. 2021 ). It is associated with a range of adverse outcomes, including impaired bonding, increased maltreatment risk, and later child difficulties (Dubber et al. 2015 ; Ayers et al. 2019 ; Sasayama et al. 2025 ). Previous studies have identified obstetric and sociodemographic predictors, including psychiatric history, primigravidity, cesarean delivery, and male infant birth (Liu et al. 2022 ; Yang et al. 2022 ). While psychiatric history remains a well-established psychological predictor, emerging evidence suggests that neurodevelopmental traits, specifically those associated with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), may represent significant yet underrecognized vulnerability factors. Core features of ADHD (inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity) and ASD (communication and social difficulties, restricted interests, sensory atypicalities, and limited adaptability) may substantially hinder adaptation to pregnancy and parenting, thereby increasing the risk of depression. An umbrella review by Kang et al. ( 2024 ) reported an odds ratio (OR) of 3.0 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.53–5.92) for depression among individuals with ADHD traits. Similarly, a meta-analysis by Hudson et al. ( 2019 ) found that 48.6% of individuals with ASD experienced depression. In the perinatal context, women with ADHD face multiple risks during pregnancy and early parenting (Kittel-Schneider et al. 2021 ). Dorani et al. ( 2021 ) reported that 57.6% of women with ADHD experienced postpartum depression exceeding the rate in the general population. Likewise, qualitative studies have shown that women with ASD often struggle with communicative and sensory aspects of pregnancy and parenting (Gardner et al. 2016 ; Rogers et al. 2017 ). Hirokawa et al. ( 2019 ) conducted a large-scale study of Japanese women and used the Autism-Spectrum Quotient-10 (AQ-10) Japanese version to assess autistic traits, focusing on characteristics often described as part of the broader autism phenotype (BAP). They reported that women with such traits were at increased risk of postpartum depression and insecure maternal attachment at one month. Taken together, these findings suggest that women with neurodevelopmental traits may have heightened vulnerability to perinatal depression, underscoring the importance of early screening and timely intervention. However, few studies have prospectively examined how such traits relate to depressive symptoms across the perinatal period. In this manuscript, the term “perinatal depression” refers to depressive symptoms occurring during pregnancy and the early postpartum period. In the context of our study design, “perinatal” corresponds to the assessment window from late pregnancy to one month postpartum. Although DSM-5 defines postpartum depression as a major depressive episode with peripartum onset, in this study we distinguish between “antenatal depression” and “postpartum depression” based on the timing of assessment. Given that the study was not preregistered, the analyses were exploratory in nature. Accordingly, this study examined how ADHD and ASD traits relate to depressive symptoms from late pregnancy through the early postpartum period, aiming to provide practical insights for more inclusive screening strategies and tailored mental health interventions in maternal care. Materials and methods Procedure and participants A prospective longitudinal survey was conducted at four obstetric facilities in Nagano Prefecture, Japan between January 14 and December 31, 2020 (Clinical trial number: not applicable). Eligible participants were pregnant Japanese-speaking women aged 20 years or older who were able to complete the questionnaires. Gender identity was not assessed in this study. We therefore use the term “women” throughout this manuscript, consistent with the recruitment setting and the perinatal literature, while acknowledging that not all pregnant individuals identify as women. At the 36–37 weeks antenatal checkup (T1), participants received the first survey set and provided written informed consent. Those who agreed completed questionnaires on neurodevelopmental traits, depressive symptoms, and sociodemographic characteristics. The second and third surveys were administered at the 2-week (T2) and 1-month postpartum checkups (T3), assessing depressive symptoms, childbirth experiences, and childcare. Neurodevelopmental traits were not reassessed postpartum as these traits are considered relatively stable over the short study period. All data were anonymized and stored securely. Responses obtained at 14 ± 7 days postpartum were classified as T2, and those at 30 ± 7 days as T3. Questionnaires with missing data at a given timepoint were excluded from the corresponding analyses for that timepoint, while available data from other timepoints were retained. Measures Three standardized self-report questionnaires were used to assess depressive symptoms and neurodevelopmental traits associated with ADHD and ASD. Edinburgh postnatal depression scale The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is a widely used 10-item screening tool designed to assess depressive symptoms during the perinatal period (Cox et al. 1987 ). The validated Japanese version (Okano et al. 1996 ) was used, with a cutoff of ≥ 9 indicating depressive risk. Although originally developed for postpartum use, later work has shown that the EPDS is applicable throughout the perinatal period, including antenatal assessments (Cox et al. 2014 ). Antenatal use has also been widely reported internationally (Evans et al. 2001 ; Limlomwongse and Liabsuetrakul 2006 ; Tendais et al. 2014 ). Because a validated antenatal cutoff has not been established in Japan, we applied the postpartum cutoff of ≥ 9 during pregnancy to ensure consistency across timepoints. Antenatal scores were interpreted cautiously, and analyses using continuous EPDS scores were also conducted. Adult ADHD self-report scale The Japanese version of the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale v1.1 (ASRS) was used to assess ADHD traits (Takeda et al. 2017 ). The scale has 18 items with Part A containing six items most predictive of ADHD. Only Part A was analyzed. Participants with four or more positive responses were classified as ASRS-positive (ASRS+). Autism spectrum quotient The Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) is a self-report measure of autistic traits (Baron-Cohen et al. 2001 ). The validated Japanese version (Wakabayashi et al. 2004 ) was used. The scale includes 50 items across five domains: social skill, attention switching, attention to detail, communication, and imagination. A total score ≥ 33 was defined as AQ-positive (AQ+). For four domains with established cutoffs, scores above each threshold were coded as positive (Social Skills ≥ 6, Imagination ≥ 6, Attention Switching ≥ 7, Communication ≥ 6). The applicability of the AQ during pregnancy has been reported by Zain et al. ( 2023 ). Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS Statistics software (version 29.0; IBM, Armonk, NY) and R (version 4.2.2). Descriptive statistics were calculated for mean EPDS scores and EPDS positivity at T1–T3. Spearman’s rank correlation assessed relationships among EPDS scores across timepoints. Cross-tabulation and chi-square tests were used to examine univariate associations between perinatal background factors and EPDS positivity, as well as neurodevelopmental characteristics (ASRS positivity and AQ positivity), with odds ratios calculated accordingly. Exploratory post hoc analyses were additionally performed for AQ subscales. Multivariable logistic regression was conducted to identify independent predictors of EPDS positivity at T2. ASRS, AQ, and antenatal EPDS scores, all measured at T1, were entered as continuous variables, with primiparity, neonatal complications, and psychiatric treatment history as covariates. The term “predictor” refers to temporal precedence and does not imply causality. Longitudinal changes in EPDS scores across T1–T3 were examined using a linear mixed-effects model (LMM). ASRS, AQ, time, and their interaction terms were included as fixed effects, with participant ID as a random intercept. Primiparity, neonatal complications, and psychiatric treatment history were included as covariates, as in the logistic regression model. Fixed-effect significance was evaluated using Type III ANOVA (Supplementary Table 7 ). Because the analyses were exploratory, no correction for multiple testing was applied. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results Participants and characteristics A total of 1,146 individuals participated (Fig. 1 ). After excluding 36 who did not meet eligibility criteria, 1,110 were enrolled. Data from 1,104 women with singleton live births were analyzed. Table 1 summarizes participant characteristics. The mean age was 32.4 years (SD = 4.9) and mean gestational age at delivery was 39.6 weeks (SD = 1.1). Overall, 37.8% were primigravidas and 44.8% were primiparas. Most deliveries were vaginal (75.4%). A history of psychiatric treatment was reported by 138 women (12.5%). Table 2 shows psychiatric diagnoses, with depression being the most common ( n = 41). Six women had a prior ADHD diagnosis, and two had a previous ASD diagnosis. Screening identified 27 ASRS+ participants in the treatment-history group, although only three had a formal ADHD diagnosis. Seven were AQ+, although none had a formal ASD diagnosis. EPDS scores and correlations Figure 2 shows mean EPDS scores and EPDS + at each timepoint. Depressive symptoms were most prevalent at T1 (16.7%), followed by T2 (8.6%) and T3 (4.0%). Spearman’s correlation analysis showed significant positive associations among EPDS scores across timepoints, with the strongest correlation between T2 and T3 (ρ = 0.627, p < 0.001). Associations between perinatal factors and EPDS positivity Table 3 presents associations between perinatal factors and EPDS+. A history of psychiatric treatment was consistently associated with EPDS + at all three timepoints (T1: OR = 3.39, 95% CI 2.28–5.04, p < 0.001; T2: OR = 4.48, 95% CI 2.79–7.21, p < 0.001; T3: OR = 5.14, 95% CI 2.70–9.81, p < 0.001). At T1, aside from a history of psychiatric treatment, having a male fetus was the only significant factor (OR = 1.40, 95% CI 1.01–1.94, p < 0.05). At T2, primigravidity (OR = 4.01, 95% CI 2.49–6.46, p < 0.001) and primiparity (OR = 5.18, 95% CI 3.00–8.92, p < 0.001) were significant. At T3, primiparity remained significant, and neonatal complications also emerged as significant. No significant associations were found for infertility treatment, prior miscarriage or stillbirth, pregnancy complications, or mode of delivery. Associations between neurodevelopmental traits and EPDS positivity Table 4 shows associations between neurodevelopmental traits and EPDS+. Individuals who screened ASRS + had higher odds of EPDS + at all three timepoints (T1: OR = 4.86, 95% CI 3.06–7.72, p < 0.001; T2: OR = 3.65, 95% CI 2.07–6.42, p < 0.001; T3: OR = 4.23, 95% CI 2.00–8.96, p < 0.001). In contrast, those who screened AQ+ showed elevated risk only at T1 (OR = 6.08, 95% CI 2.17–16.99, p < 0.001), with no significant associations at T2 or T3. Post hoc domain-specific analyses showed that higher scores on the social skill, attention switching, and communication subscales were associated with EPDS + at all timepoints. The imagination subscale showed no significant associations. Four participants exceeded both ASRS + and AQ+ cutoffs. Their mean EPDS scores were 8.75 at T1, 5.75 at T2, and 3.50 at T3, with EPDS+ rates of 75%, 25%, and 0%, respectively. Because this subgroup was extremely small, only descriptive results were reported. Predictors of postpartum depression Multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to examine the independent contribution of neurodevelopmental traits to postpartum depressive symptoms (Table 5 ). The outcome variable was EPDS + at T2. This timepoint was selected because EPDS + was higher at T2 than at T3, and because T2 closely reflected early postpartum mental health, as shown in Fig. 2. ASRS and AQ total scores were entered as continuous predictors. In Model 1 (unadjusted), higher ASRS ( p < 0.001) and AQ ( p = 0.012) scores were ass

title: The Cognitive Functions of Youth With Obesity: A Meta-Analysis
abstract:
ABSTRACT Background This meta‐analysis examined the associations between obesity and performance across seven cognitive domains (inhibition, cognitive flexibility, working memory, verbal fluency, planning, attention, and intelligence quotient [IQ]) in youth under 18 years. Developmental stage (school‐aged children vs. adolescents) and sample sex composition examined as moderators. Evidence on executive function in youth with comorbid obesity and attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) was synthesized qualitatively. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, 22 studies comparing youth with obesity to normal‐weight peers were included. Effect sizes (Hedges’ g ) were pooled using a random‐effects model. Subgroup analyses compared school‐aged children and adolescents; meta‐regression examined age and proportion of female participants as study‐level moderators. Results Youth with obesity performed significantly worse than normal‐weight peers on inhibition ( g + = −0.193), cognitive flexibility ( g + = −0.499), working memory ( g + = −0.652), verbal fluency ( g + = −0.420), attention ( g + = −0.526), and IQ ( g + = −0.288); planning could not be estimated. School‐aged children showed deficits on inhibition, working memory, and attention; adolescents on working memory and attention only. Between‐subgroup tests were non‐significant for all domains ( p ≥ 0.26), so developmental differences should be interpreted with caution. Meta‐regression showed that a higher proportion of female participants in a study sample, a study‐level characteristic rather than an individual‐level effect, was associated with larger working memory deficits ( p = 0.002); age did not moderate any domain. Two ADHD‐comorbidity studies received qualitative synthesis only. Discussion Obesity is associated with poorer cognitive performance in youth across several domains, with sex composition of the study sample emerging as a moderator of the working memory finding; differences between school‐aged children and adolescents were not significant and should be interpreted cautiously. Substantial heterogeneity, predominantly observational designs, inconsistent BMI criteria, and limited ADHD‐stratified data constrain causal inference. Future studies should standardize weight definitions, report age‐ and ADHD‐stratified data, and consider bidirectional pathways.

1 Introduction Childhood and adolescent obesity has become an increasingly important global health concern. According to the World Health Organization, more than 390 million children and adolescents aged 5–19 years were overweight in 2022, and within this age group the prevalence of overweight increased from 8% in 1990 to 20% in 2022, while obesity rose from 2% to 8% over the same period (World Health Organization 2024 ). Overweight and obesity among young people have increased across both developed and developing countries (Ng et al. 2014 ), and are associated with elevated rates of hypertension, flatfoot, anxiety, and depression in children and adolescents (Zhang et al. 2024 ). Beyond these physical and psychological consequences, obesity may also be related to how children and adolescents think, regulate their behavior, and control their impulses. Executive functions such as inhibition, working memory, and cognitive flexibility support learning, classroom behavior, decision‐making, and everyday self‐control, and are considered foundational to healthy development (Diamond 2013 ); attention follows a partly distinct developmental course governed by alerting, orienting, and executive‐attention networks (Posner and Petersen 1990 ), and general intellectual ability (IQ) draws on this same prefrontal‐dependent architecture while also indexing broader academic and occupational outcomes (Nisbett et al. 2012 ). Several distinct mechanisms could plausibly link obesity to weaker performance across these domains: systemic low‐grade inflammation associated with excess adiposity (Samoilova et al. 2024 ), sleep‐disordered breathing and other sleep disturbances common in pediatric obesity (Pearce, Mackey, et al. 2018 ), structural and functional differences in prefrontal and reward‐related circuitry (Moreno‐López et al. 2012 ; Ronan et al. 2020 ), shared genetic liability affecting dopaminergic reward and self‐regulatory systems (Herzog et al. 2024 ), and shared environmental disadvantage, such as socioeconomic deprivation that affects both diet and cognitive stimulation (Li et al. 2023 ). Because prefrontal‐dependent cognitive systems are still maturing across childhood and adolescence, this developmental window is also when obesity‐prevention and cognitive‐support interventions may have the greatest long‐term benefit—the central stake motivating the present synthesis. Despite this rationale, the empirical literature linking obesity to cognitive performance in youth has already been synthesized several times, with converging but incomplete conclusions. Liang et al. ( 2014 ), Reinert et al. ( 2013 ), Yang et al. ( 2018 ), and Favieri et al. ( 2019 ) each report small‐to‐moderate obesity‐related deficits concentrated in inhibition and working memory, alongside considerable inconsistency across primary studies and domains; of these, only Yang et al. ( 2018 ) conducted a formal meta‐analysis, while the others synthesized the evidence narratively. Most recently, Ásgeirsdóttir et al. ( 2026 ) conducted a preregistered meta‐analysis restricted to adolescents with obesity and found a small, domain‐general executive‐function deficit ( g = −0.314) that did not differ significantly across specific domains, with age, BMI range, and the proportion of female participants in each sample moderating effect size. These reviews leave gaps that motivate the present synthesis: most combine overweight and obesity into a single category, obscuring any dose‐related pattern; none directly contrasts school‐aged children and adolescents within a single set of analyses; and, with the partial exception of Ásgeirsdóttir et al. ( 2026 ), none extends beyond core executive‐function domains to attention and IQ. Primary studies further illustrate why pooling, rather than additional narrative review, is needed: significant deficits associated with obesity have been reported for inhibition (Blanco‐Gómez et al. 2015 ; Kamijo et al. 2014 ; Kittel et al. 2017 ), cognitive flexibility (Alatorre‐Cruz et al. 2021 ; Blanco‐Gómez et al. 2015 ; Bozkurt et al. 2017 ; Maayan et al. 2011 ; Özer et al. 2024 ; Yau et al. 2014 ), working memory (Alatorre‐Cruz et al. 2021 ; Bozkurt et al. 2017 ; Kamijo, Khan, et al. 2012 ; Maayan et al. 2011 ; Özer et al. 2024 ), verbal fluency (Maayan et al. 2011 ), planning (Qavam et al. 2015 ), attention (Bozkurt et al. 2017 ; Chojnacki et al. 2018 ; Fields et al. 2013 ; Kittel et al. 2017 ; Logan et al. 2021 ; Maayan et al. 2011 ; Meo et al. 2019 ; Özer et al. 2024 ; Parisi et al. 2010 ), and IQ (Krombholz 2013 ; Maayan et al. 2011 ; Pearce, Mackey, et al. 2018 )—while other studies of the very same domains report no significant group differences: inhibition (Kamijo, Pontifex, et al. 2012 ), cognitive flexibility (Meo et al. 2019 ), working memory (Bauer and Manning 2016 ; Goldschmidt et al. 2018 ), planning (Qavam et al. 2015 ), attention (Li et al. 2008 ; Moss et al. 2023 ), and IQ (Akın et al. 2017 ; Bozkurt et al. 2017 ; Fields et al. 2013 ; Kamijo, Khan, et al. 2012 ; Logan et al. 2021 ; Parisi et al. 2010 ; Yau et al. 2014 ). This pattern—genuine disagreement across studies rather than a simple accumulation of confirmatory evidence—is the hallmark of a question that a systematic quantitative synthesis is needed to resolve: only by pooling effect sizes across studies can the field distinguish true variability in the obesity–cognition association from sampling variability in individual, often small, studies. We argue that this inconsistency is unlikely to be resolved by an overall pooled estimate alone, because there is good theoretical reason to expect the obesity–cognition association to vary systematically rather than to be uniform across youth. First, executive functions supported by the prefrontal cortex mature at markedly different rates across childhood and adolescence, and this maturation itself differs by sex, with prefrontal‐dependent networks—including those supporting working memory—tending to mature earlier in girls than in boys (Gur and Gur 2016 ; Lenroot and Giedd 2010 ). If obesity's association with cognition operates partly through, or interacts with, these maturational processes, the strength and pattern of obesity‐related cognitive differences should differ by developmental stage and plausibly by the sex composition of a given sample—predictions we test directly below using subgroup and moderator analyses. Second, ADHD offers a theoretically important test case for these mechanisms, because ADHD and obesity share overlapping neuropsychological correlates (inhibition, attention regulation, impulsivity, and working memory) that plausibly influence eating regulation and physical activity. Evidence directly linking obesity to executive functioning within ADHD populations is itself mixed: some studies report that higher body weight is associated with weaker inhibitory control and greater impulsivity among children and adolescents with ADHD (Graziano et al. 2012 ; Racicka‐Pawlukiewicz et al. 2021 ), while others find no such association (Hanć et al. 2018 ), and studies of specific executive domains in youth with both obesity and ADHD similarly disagree (Choudhry et al. 2013 ; Parhoon et al. 2023 ). This makes ADHD status a theoretically motivated candidate moderator of the obesity–cognition association. However, as described in the Methods, the literature search identified too few studies of children and adolescents with obesity that also report ADHD status to support a quantitative moderator analysis. We therefore treat ADHD‐related findings as a qualitative complement to the quantitative synthesis rather than as one of the moderators formally tested (see Section 3.2 ). The pediatric meta‐analysis most directly comparable to the present one (Pearce, Leonhardt, et al. 2018 ) synthesized executive and reward‐related functioning in youth with obesity, but it did not examine attention or IQ, did not separate overweight from obesity, and did not contrast developmental stages; the present review extends that work on all three counts and, unlike Ásgeirsdóttir et al. ( 2026 ), includes school‐aged children alongside adolescents. Based on the argument above, this meta‐analysis aimed to: (1) test whether obesity is associated with poorer performance across executive‐function domains (inhibition, cognitive flexibility, working memory, decision‐making, verbal fluency, planning) and broader neuropsychological outcomes (attention, IQ) in youth, predicting worse performance among youth with obesity consistent with prior meta‐analytic evidence (Yang et al. 2018 ; Ásgeirsdóttir et al. 2026 ); (2) test whether these associations differ by developmental stage and by the sex composition of study samples, predicting different patterns of association given the sex differences in the timing of prefrontal maturation noted above (Gur and Gur 2016 ; Lenroot and Giedd 2010 ); and (3) qualitatively synthesize the available evidence on obesity and cognition among youth with comorbid obesity and ADHD, given the theoretical but empirically underdetermined overlap between these conditions, without conducting a quantitative ADHD‐moderator analysis because too few directly comparable studies were available. 2 Methods This systematic review and meta‐analysis was not prospectively registered in a registry such as PROSPERO. This review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) reporting guideline to structure and document the review process (Table S1 ). Adherence to PRISMA is a reporting standard and does not, by itself, substitute for prospective registration; the absence of registration is acknowledged as a limitation of this review (see Section 4.7 ). 2.1 Study Selection and Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria 2.1.1 PECO The study's research question was structured according to the PECO framework as follows: (1) population: infant, preschool child, children, and adolescent; (2) index condition (hereafter “E,” retaining the PECO label, but denoting group membership rather than a temporal or causal exposure, consistent with the predominantly cross‐sectional design of the included literature): group with obesity; (3) comparator: normal weight group; (4) outcome: executive function, attention, or IQ test score were assessed, diagnosis with or without ADHD. We followed this PECO framework to generate our search terms for three databases: Medline, PubMed, and Embase (Table S2 ). 2.1.2 Literature Review A topic search was conducted in Medline, PubMed, and Embase to identify studies published up to December 17, 2024. For each database, search terms combining three concept blocks—(1) obesity/overweight, (2) executive function, attention, IQ, or ADHD, and (3) infant/child/adolescent/youth—were connected with Boolean AND/OR operators and adapted to each database's controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH, Emtree) and syntax; the complete, database‐specific search strings are provided in Table S2 . The search retrieved 7837 records from Medline, 1065 from PubMed, and 657 from Embase. All records were imported into EndNote 21 for reference management and screening. Titles and abstracts were screened first, followed by full‐text review for articles that appeared potentially eligible based on their title or abstract. The detailed study selection process is illustrated in Figure 1 . Two reviewers independently screened all titles, abstracts, and full‐text articles against the predefined eligibility criteria (Table 1 ). Disagreements were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached, and a third senior reviewer was consulted when discrepancies persisted. Data from each eligible study were extracted using a standardized, piloted data‐extraction form that recorded study characteristics, country, design, sample sizes, participant age and sex composition, weight‐classification criteria, the cognitive tasks administered, and the summary statistics (means, standard deviations, and sample sizes) required for effect‐size computation. Studies were eligible if they met all inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria below (Table 1 ). 2.1.3 Selected Studies The analysis included data from 22 studies comparing youth with obesity and normal‐weight participants. Across these studies, the most commonly assessed domains were attention (15 studies), inhibition (12 studies), IQ (12 studies), working memory (11 studies), and cognitive flexibility (10 studies). title: School-Based Interventions for Children with Behavioral Difficulties: Inconsistent Implementation of Evidence-Based Practices
journal: Evid Based Pract Child Adolesc Ment Health
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Children with behavioral difficulties, including those with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and their teachers frequently experience challenges at school, leading to school-based interventions.

OBJECTIVE: This exploratory study evaluated the utilization and evidence-base of school-based interventions for behavioral difficulties among school mental health professionals in Dutch schools.

METHOD: A survey was conducted among 102 school mental health professionals to assess their utilization of school-based interventions, attitudes toward evidence-based practice, knowledge about behavioral problems, and educational background. The evidence-base of reported interventions was evaluated, and associations of professionals' attitudes, knowledge, and educational background with the use of evidence-based interventions were analyzed. Interventions were identified based on a previous study of regularly used interventions in Dutch schools.

RESULTS: Large heterogeneity in evidence-based practice was found: 18.6% of school mental health professionals only used evidence-based interventions, while 38.2% used at least one evidence-based intervention alongside non-evidence-based ones. However, 26.5% used interventions without sufficient empirical support, and 16.7% indicated to not use any intervention for children with behavioral difficulties at all. About half of the currently used lack empirical support and evidence-based interventions specifically developed for behavioral difficulties were rarely used. No predictors were significantly associated with the use of evidence-based interventions.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings underscore the need for a better implementation of effective school-based interventions for children with behavioral difficulties. A multifaceted approach is required, including research into promising interventions, deimplementation of interventions that lack sufficient evidence, and enhanced support for implementing evidence-based interventions in schools.

title: Identification and multidimensional characterization of two distinct autism spectrum disorder subtypes
abstract:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) shows high variability in brain structure and behavior, complicating identification of biologically meaningful subtypes and their neuroanatomical and molecular bases. To address this, we analyzed structural MRI data from 1055 ASD and 1164 typically developing (TD) individuals. Gray matter volume (GMV) values from regions showing significant ASD–TD differences were extracted in ASD participants and used for supervised affinity propagation (AP) clustering. Subtypes were then characterized via individual differential structural covariance networks (IDSCN), followed by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) based on spatial transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) to identify molecular pathways associated with subtype-specific spatial GMV patterns. This integrative analysis identified two ASD subtypes with distinct neuroanatomical and molecular features. Subtype 1 showed widespread GMV reductions in social, limbic, and salience networks, reduced structural covariance, and enrichment in genes linked to neurodevelopment, neuronal differentiation, and synaptic organization. In contrast, Subtype 2 exhibited GMV increases in similar regions, stronger covariance, and enrichment in pathways involving cytoplasmic translation, mitochondrial organization, and synaptic signaling. These structural and molecular differences were also associated with variations in clinical symptom severity. Our findings reveal two ASD subtypes with distinct cortical morphometry, network patterns, and associated molecular signatures, emphasizing multiple neurodevelopmental paths and the value of biologically informed subtyping for precise diagnosis and personalized treatment.

Introduction Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by challenges in social communication and interaction, as well as the presence of restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviors, interests, or activities [ 1 , 2 ]. Moreover, the diverse genetic, environmental, and neurodevelopmental origins of ASD give rise to distinct subgroups and developmental patterns, leading to considerable variability in behavioral manifestations and communication abilities [ 3 ]. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) recognizes ASD’s phenotypic heterogeneity, and mounting evidence supports variability at neuroimaging and genetic levels as well [ 4 ]. ASD is increasingly understood as a highly heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition, characterized by substantial inter-individual variability in both behavioral profiles and underlying neurobiology [ 5 , 6 ]. Neuroimaging studies have identified widespread, though variable, differences in brain structure particularly in gray matter among individuals on the ASD spectrum. Lenroot and Yeung reviewed early neuroimaging research that sought to characterize subgroups within the ASD spectrum based on individual differences in behavior and brain organization. They emphasized the value of dimensional approaches for capturing the diversity of autistic neurobiology beyond traditional diagnostic categories [ 7 ]. Halliday et al. conducted a cross-modality review encompassing magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and other techniques. They concluded that although modality-specific inconsistencies exist, several brain regions including the anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, thalamus, and the default mode network (DMN) consistently exhibit differences across methods. These findings highlight both converging patterns and the neurobiological diversity observed across individuals on the ASD spectrum [ 8 ]. Mahajan and Mostofsky proposed that ASD spectrum traits may reflect multiple neurobiological profiles, each associated with different patterns of brain morphology and connectivity, potentially contributing to the observed diversity in individual experiences and responses to intervention [ 9 ]. These findings support the view that ASD encompasses a range of neurodevelopmental dimensions rather than representing a single underlying biological profile. To better understand the diversity within ASD, recent studies have adopted data-driven approaches to identify GM-based neurobiological subtypes. For instance, Chen et al. applied voxel-based morphometry and clustering techniques to group male participants on the ASD spectrum into three neuroanatomically distinct subtypes, each associated with differing behavioral characteristics and patterns of functional connectivity [ 10 ]. Similarly, Xu et al. utilized single-subject GM networks and graph-theoretical metrics to identify three subtypes with different topological organization and cognitive profiles [ 11 ]. Liu et al. employed a semi-supervised clustering framework to delineate two GM-based subtypes based on volumetric features derived from GM, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid [ 12 ]. In another study, Shan et al. used normative modeling and non-negative matrix factorization to identify three GM-based subtypes, each characterized by unique structural patterns and behavioral traits related to social communication [ 13 ]. Extending this work, Guo et al. introduced individual differential structural covariance networks (IDSCNs) to explore within-spectrum variability, identifying two subtypes with divergent frontal and subcortical covariance patterns associated with differences in repetitive behaviors [ 14 ]. Building on these findings, Zhang et al. further examined the reproducibility and robustness of IDSCN-based subtyping, supporting its potential utility in capturing meaningful neurobiological distinctions [ 15 ]. However, despite these advances, several limitations persist. First, most existing studies employ unsupervised clustering methods that require arbitrary pre-specification of the number of clusters, which may obscure latent heterogeneity in the data given the unknown true number of ASD subtypes. Second, while recent subtyping efforts have explored structural features such as voxel-level gray matter volume (GMV) and structural covariance, these modalities are often used in isolation, potentially limiting their ability to capture multidimensional neurobiological differences. For instance, although the individual differential structural covariance network has been used to identify ASD subtypes, its application as a primary clustering feature may overemphasize fine-grained covariance patterns while neglecting global volumetric variation. Nonetheless, IDSCN remains a valuable complementary tool for characterizing subtype-specific network features after subtype identification, offering validation of structural distinctiveness at the network level. Moreover, few studies have leveraged molecular or genetic data to contextualize neuroanatomical subtypes. To overcome these limitations, we propose an integrative subtyping framework that combines supervised machine learning and multimodal neuroimaging features. Specifically, we applied a supervised Affinity Propagation (AP) algorithm to GMV difference maps between ASD individuals and typical developing, enabling subtype discovery without the need to preset the number of clusters. This approach yielded two robust subtypes: Subtype 1, characterized by widespread GMV reductions in brain regions involved in social cognition, sensorimotor processing, limbic regulation, and salience detection, and Subtype 2, which exhibited GMV increases in the same networks. Beyond anatomical profiles, we further examined the IDSCN patterns within each subtype, revealing distinct structural covariance signatures aligned with symptom severity. Finally, to explore the molecular basis of these subtypes, we conducted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), which revealed different biological pathway enrichment patterns in Subtype 1 and Subtype 2. This multimodal characterization would provide novel insight into the neuroanatomical and molecular heterogeneity of ASD, and lays the groundwork for future biomarker-informed stratification and intervention strategies. The detailed flowchart of this study is summarized in Fig. 1 . Methods and materials Participants In this study, structural MRI data were obtained from the publicly available Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) database (https://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/). The study protocols and MRI acquisition procedures for participants in the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) repository were approved by the respective local ethics committees at each contributing site. To maximize statistical power and fully utilize the available ASD data, participants were drawn from both the ABIDE I and ABIDE II datasets. All available ASD and TD participants were initially considered. Subsequently, unified preprocessing and quality control procedures were applied, which included (1) visual inspection of the segmented images to identify artifacts or segmentation errors, (2) exclusion of scans with evident artifacts or failed segmentation, and (3) evaluation using the standard CAT12 Image Quality Rating (IQR). During these procedures, 18 participants were excluded following visual inspection because of obvious artifacts or segmentation abnormalities, 12 of them were excluded due to evident artifacts or failed segmentation, and 15 of them were excluded because their CAT12 image quality did not meet the predefined threshold. The scans included in the final analysis corresponded to a B− rating, indicating generally acceptable data quality. The demographic and clinical characteristics of the enrolled participants are summarized in Table 1 . Data preprocessing We used the CAT12 toolbox for voxel-based morphological preprocessing of T1-weighted structural data. The preprocessing steps included: (1) skull stripping, denoising, and bias correction; (2) segmentation of T1-weighted images into gray matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid; (3) registration of gray matter maps to the standard template using the diffeomorphic anatomical registration through exponentiated Lie algebra (DARTEL) algorithm, followed by resampling to an isotropic voxel size of 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 mm 3 , consistent with the default CAT12 preprocessing pipeline and prior studies on structural heterogeneity in psychiatric disorders [ 15 , 16 ]. This resampling strategy facilitates robust tissue segmentation and spatial normalization across subjects and sites, thereby helping to mitigate potential site-related variability in multi-site datasets; (4) estimation of total intracranial volume (TIV); and (5) spatial smoothing with an 8 mm full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) Gaussian kernel. Group GMV analysis between ASD and TD To identify GMV differences between individuals with ASD and TD, a voxel-wise two-sample t-test was performed while controlling for age, sex, and TIV as covariates. To account for multiple comparisons across all voxels within the predefined gray matter mask, a Bonferroni correction was applied at the voxel level. Specifically, the conventional significance threshold (<0.05) was divided by the total number of voxels included in the gray matter mask ( N = 332,316), yielding a Bonferroni-corrected voxel-wise threshold of p < 1.50 × 10⁻⁷. Although highly conservative, this approach was adopted to minimize false-positive findings and ensure robust identification of ASD-related GMV alterations. In practice, t-values were retained only for voxels surviving this corrected threshold, while all other voxels were set to zero, thereby minimizing the chance of false positives across the entire gray matter mask. A minimum cluster size of >50 voxels was additionally applied. Regions showing significant group differences in GMV were defined as regions of interest (ROIs). Pearson’s correlation analyses were then conducted between the GMV of each ROI and scores on the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) and Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R). The significance level for correlation analyses was set at p < 0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons using the false discovery rate (FDR) method. IQ-sensitive analysis Given the significant difference in IQ between ASD and TD participants and the incomplete availability of IQ data, an additional IQ-sensitive analysis was performed to evaluate the robustness of the observed group effects. Analyses were restricted to participants with available IQ measurements. For each ROI, a separate linear regression model was fitted with the ROI measure as the dependent variable and diagnostic group and IQ as independent variables. Diagnostic group was coded as a binary variable (ASD = 1, TD = 0), and IQ was included as a continuous covariate. title: Unveiling determinants and system optimization: a CFIR-ToC integrated approach to rehabilitation service utilization for children with autism spectrum disorder
abstract:
Background Addressing the research gaps, including incomplete analysis of influencing factors, limited scope of study populations, and insufficiently operational support systems, this study aims to extensively analyze the barriers and facilitators to service utilization among both service-engaged and non-engaged families of autistic children by adopting the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). Additionally, it intends to construct multi-stakeholder action pathways and networks in combination with the Theory of Change, thereby forming an operational rehabilitation support system. The ultimate goal is to enhance the health equity and overall health status of autistic children and their families. Methods A two-phase mixed approach was used: (1) CFIR-based semi-structured interviews and qualitative analysis with structured coding (alphabets for facilitators, numerals for barriers), following COREQ guidelines; (2) ToC-guided translation of CFIR-identified facilitators into stakeholder responsibilities (matched with barriers) to construct a support system with multi-stakeholder pathways/networks. Results 37 caregivers (30 service-engaged, 7 non-engaged) were interviewed, revealing 9/15 facilitators/barriers for engaged families and 2/9 for non-engaged ones. Universal barriers include high costs, geographical resource gaps, and insufficient caregiver skills. An evidence-based pathway clarifies stakeholder responsibilities to target barriers; a multi-level network defines collaboration among Core, Intermediate, and Collaborative tiers. Conclusions This study extensively analyzed the barriers and facilitators to rehabilitation service utilization among both service-engaged and non-engaged families of autistic children, addressing the research gaps of incomplete identification of influencing factors and limited representativeness of study populations. It constructed an evidence-based, multi-component action pathway involving multiple stakeholders and a multi-level, multi-stakeholders collaborative network, thereby forming an operational rehabilitation support system. This system provides a reference for global efforts to improve the accessibility, acceptability, geographic accessibility, and affordability of autism services, contributing to enhanced family well-being, improved social adaptability, and better health outcomes. Such a full-chain evidence-based pathway, spanning from problem analysis to solution formulation, offers an analytical framework for advancing health equity and overall health status among vulnerable populations. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-026-15318-z .

Background Ensuring early childhood development and equal resource access for persons with disabilities are enshrined in United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) Targets 4.2 and 4.5. Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), embodying the dual identities of “disabled” and “child,” make advancing their overall health and health equity a shared entry point and priority for achieving these strategic goals. ASD represents a pressing global health challenge. It was estimated that around 1 in 127 individuals worldwide lived with autism in 2021 [ 1 ] imposing substantial socioeconomic burdens on families and societies. Lifetime supportive care costs amount to $1.4 million in both the United States and the United Kingdom for autistic individuals without intellectual disability; for those with co-occurring intellectual disability, the lifetime cost rises to $2.4 million in the US and £1.5 million (equivalent to $2.2 million) in the UK [ 2 ].Globally, autistic disorder accounts for over 58 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) per 100,000 population, while other autism spectrum disorders contribute 53 DALYs per 100,000 population [ 3 ]. Rehabilitation services are important for improving the functional development and adaptive capacity of children with ASD and for providing sustained support throughout their developmental trajectories. Therefore, identifying the barriers and facilitators of rehabilitation service utilization and developing actionable pathways based on these determinants to promote effective service utilization is key to reducing familial and societal burdens. Although previous studies have identified multiple factors associated with rehabilitation service utilization among children with ASD, they have largely focused on sociodemographic factors, such as children’s gender [ 4 ], ethnicity [ 5 ], parental socioeconomic status [ 6 ], and educational pathways [ 7 ]. Meanwhile, inherent constraints of rehabilitation service delivery systems, including limited service capacity, workforce shortages, prolonged waiting times, and variable professional qualifications and communication quality, also affect families’ ability and willingness to access services [ 8 – 11 ]. However, procedural and contextual factors—including families’ recognition of rehabilitation needs, care-seeking decision-making, intra-family coordination, and communication with rehabilitation institutions—have received comparatively limited research attention. More importantly, research has predominantly focused on families whose children have already accessed rehabilitation or autism-related services. For example, previous studies have explored parents’ experiences with family-centered services in Ontario [ 12 ] and the service-access experiences of parents whose children had received autism care services during the preceding year [ 13 ]. Families whose children have never received rehabilitation services remain underrepresented in the literature, and their barriers to care-seeking, decision-making processes, unmet needs, and actual service expectations are insufficiently understood. This gap highlights the need for a stronger health-equity perspective, as families excluded from or unable to enter the service system may experience greater structural and social disadvantages. In addition, although prior research has recognized the roles of parents [ 14 – 16 ], community and non-governmental organizations [ 17 – 22 ], governments [ 23 – 25 ], healthcare institutions [ 26 , 27 ], educational systems [ 28 ], and cross-sectoral collaboration [ 29 , 30 ], substantial gaps remain regarding implementation pathways. Specifically, the core responsibilities of each stakeholder, the barriers they should prioritize, the relative priority of different actions, and mechanisms for inter-stakeholder collaboration have not been adequately clarified, limiting the operational feasibility of existing rehabilitation support systems. To address these gaps, this study aims to systematically identify the multilevel barriers and facilitators influencing rehabilitation service utilization among families of children with ASD. Benefiting from the full dimensional coverage and evidence-based analytical perspective of the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) in implementation science, this study adopts the framework to systematically explore influencing factors spanning features of evidence-based ASD rehabilitation interventions, external environments, organizational contexts, individual characteristics, and implementation processes [ 31 – 33 ]. By distinguishing between families who have previously used rehabilitation services and those who have never accessed such services, this study further examines how relevant barriers and facilitators manifest across different service utilization contexts. Based on the extracted determinants, the Theory of Change (ToC) framework is employed to develop actionable multi-stakeholder intervention pathways by mapping the logical chains among inputs, activities, intermediate outcomes and long-term goals [ 34 ]. Through an integrated analytical workflow including systematic determinant coding, contextual heterogeneity analysis and stakeholder-oriented action pathway construction, this study intends to provide empirical evidence for optimizing service utilization and improving relevant supporting system. More broadly, it deepens the understanding of the mechanisms underlying rehabilitation service utilization for children with ASD and delivers a transferable methodological framework for building service systems for other groups of people with disabilities. Methods Study design and instrument We developed a semi-structured interview guide based on the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR2.0) to systematically identify barriers and facilitators to rehabilitation service utilization among families of children with ASD. The guide was pilot-tested on June 5, 2024, with five parents of children with ASD to ensure clarity and relevance, leading to minor refinements (see eAppendix 1 . Pilot Study Description). The final guide comprised 19 open-ended questions across the five CFIR domains (see eTable 1 . Interview Outline Based on the CFIR Framework). This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of West China Fourth Hospital / West China School of Public Health, Sichuan University (Approval No.: Gw112025071). Participant recruitment Participants were recruited through purposive sampling with the assistance of rehabilitation specialists from primary healthcare centers. To ensure sample heterogeneity, we established the following inclusion criteria: (1) participants had to be immediate family members (e.g., parents) with primary caregiving responsibilities; (2) the sample needed to reflect a broad range of socioeconomic diversity, including varied educational backgrounds (from primary school to doctoral degrees), occupations, and income levels. The detailed process for accessing families of children with ASD is provided in the Supplementary Material (see eAppendix 2 . Participant Recruitment Process), which is accompanied by a recruitment flowchart (see eFigure 1 . Flowchart of the recruitment process for families of children with autism spectrum disorder). Data collection Interviews were conducted by researchers experienced in autism research and trained in qualitative interviewing techniques to maintain neutrality and rapport. Prior to each interview, researchers explained the study’s objectives and obtained informed consent for audio recording. Data collection was completed by August 2025, with one-on-one, face-to-face interviews conducted in private meeting rooms at participating primary healthcare centers. Each interview lasted approximately 40 min. All invited individuals agreed to participate, and no dropouts occurred. After completing 30 interviews with service-engaged families, no new major themes emerged, indicating that data saturation was largely achieved for this group. No new core themes were identified after conducting 7 interviews with non-engaged families; nevertheless, this can only be regarded as a preliminary judgment of thematic coverage due to the limited sample size. Data analysis Our data analysis followed a two-phase, mixed-methods approach. In the first phase, we conducted a qualitative content analysis guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to systematically identify and categorize the facilitators and barriers to service utilization. In the second phase, we adopted the Theory of Change (ToC) framework to construct a support system for rehabilitation service utilization among families of autistic children, and developed two components: “Component-based Multi-Stakeholder Pathway for Rehabilitation Utilization Among Families of Autistic Children” and “Multi-stakeholder Collaborative Network for Rehabilitation Utilization by Families of Autistic Children”. Phase 1: identification of barriers and facilitators for rehabilitation service utilization among families of autistic children based on CFIR The primary analysis of the interview transcripts was guided by a thematic approach rooted in the CFIR. Two independent researchers first analyzed an initial set of transcripts to develop a consistent coding scheme, resolving any discrepancies through discussion to ensure inter-rater reliability (see eAppendix 3. Hybrid Thematic Analysis Coding Steps and Disagreement Resolution Protocols). The researchers then systematically coded all transcripts. These codes were subsequently mapped onto five core CFIR domains: (1) Intervention Characteristics (the rehabilitation program), (2) Outer Setting (the external environment), (3) Inner Setting (the internal environment), (4) Characteristics of Individuals (family characteristics), and (5) Process (rehabilitation process). The entire coding process was managed using NVivo (Version 11) and cross-validated to ensure the trustworthiness of the results (see eFigure 2 . Six-stage procedural framework of hybrid thematic analysis). To delineate findings across participant groups, a structured coding system was developed within this framework. Facilitators were assigned alphabetic codes (e.g., a, b, c) and barriers were assigned numeric codes (e.g., ①, ②, ③). The coding was sequenced to first identify factors common to all families, followed by those specific to service-engaged families, and finally those unique to non-engaged families. The original verbatim interview quotations are provided in eAppendix 4 Details of interview findings on barriers and facilitators. For verification of the interview content, we drew on the Evidence Analysis Based on Internal Quality Improvement Reports from the participants’rehabilitation institutions (see eAppendix 5 . Evidence Analysis Based on Internal Quality Improvement Reports from Participants’ Rehabilitation Institutions and eTable 2 . Descriptive Statistics of Core Rehabilitation Indicators Among 70 Children with ASD Based on Internal Quality Improvement Reports). For a detailed comparison of subsidy policies across countries and regions, see eAppendix 6 – 8 and eTable 3 – 4 . For verification of the authenticity of the relevant policies, please consult the attached supplementary materials, namely eTable 5 . Local Subsidy Policy Issues Raised by Interviewees and Corresponding Supporting Policy Documents. We followed the COREQ guidelines for reporting qualitative content. title: Cardiovascular effects of methylphenidate, risperidone, and their combination in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a prospective 3-month observational study
abstract:
Background We aimed to evaluate changes in hemodynamic parameters and electrocardiographic (ECG) indices related to ventricular arrhythmia risk after three months of treatment with methylphenidate (MPH), risperidone (RIS), or their combination in children and adolescents with ADHD. Methods A total of 150 children and adolescents with DSM-5-diagnosed ADHD were prospectively enrolled at Qods Hospital. Participants received methylphenidate ( n = 50), risperidone ( n = 50), or combination therapy ( n = 50). Cardiovascular outcomes were assessed using age- and weight-adjusted two-way repeated-measures ANCOVA to evaluate changes over time and differences among treatment groups. Results Significant group × time interactions were observed for systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, and QTc interval after adjustment for baseline age and weight. After three months, systolic and diastolic blood pressure increased in the methylphenidate and combination therapy groups, while heart rate showed an overall increase, with the greatest rise observed in the methylphenidate group. QTc interval increased over time across all treatment groups, with the largest prolongation observed in the combination therapy group (377.9 ± 25.4 to 424.5 ± 24.9 ms). However, mean QTc values remained below commonly accepted thresholds for clinically significant QT prolongation, and no significant longitudinal changes were observed in QRS duration or PR intervals. Conclusion Treatment with methylphenidate, risperidone, and combination therapy was associated with modest changes in heart rate, blood pressure, and QTc interval over three months. These findings highlight the importance of baseline and follow-up cardiovascular monitoring in children and adolescents receiving ADHD medications.

Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders in childhood. A worldwide systematic review and meta-regression analysis estimated the pooled prevalence of ADHD among children and adolescents at approximately 5.3%, highlighting its substantial public health burden [ 1 ]. ADHD is characterized by developmentally inappropriate and impairing levels of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interfere with daily functioning and social, academic, and occupational performance [ 2 ]. Diagnostic classifications for ADHD have evolved over time, with differences between major international systems. In the 11th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), the World Health Organization adopted the term “attention deficit hyperactivity disorder” (ADHD), replacing the previous terminology of “hyperkinetic disorder” used in earlier ICD classifications [ 3 ]. Although ADHD diagnostic criteria in ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR are largely comparable, some differences exist regarding symptom thresholds, clinical presentations, and diagnostic requirements [ 4 ]. These diagnostic frameworks describe overlapping clinical constructs, while ADHD remains the preferred terminology in contemporary clinical practice [ 4 ]. The use of pharmacological treatments for ADHD has increased substantially worldwide over recent decades, with notable rises in medication prescribing among both children and adults [ 5 ]. Although randomized clinical trials and observational studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of ADHD medications in reducing core symptoms and improving functional outcomes, concerns regarding their long-term safety, particularly potential cardiovascular effects, remain an important clinical consideration [ 6 – 8 ]. Pharmacological treatment of ADHD includes both stimulant and non-stimulant medications. According to current clinical guidelines, stimulant medications, primarily methylphenidate- and amphetamine-based preparations, are considered first-line pharmacological options for many children and adolescents with ADHD. Non-stimulant medications, including atomoxetine, guanfacine, and clonidine, represent alternative treatment options, particularly for patients with inadequate response to stimulants or those experiencing adverse effects [ 8 , 9 ]. Methylphenidate (MPH), a central nervous system stimulant, is one of the most commonly used medications for ADHD, whereas risperidone (RIS), an atypical antipsychotic, is frequently prescribed for children and adolescents with ADHD-associated behavioral disorders. These medications may be administered as monotherapy or combination therapy when clinically indicated. Although effective, they may be associated with neurological, metabolic, and cardiovascular adverse effects [ 7 – 9 ]. Cardiovascular effects are of particular clinical importance in pediatric populations because stimulants and antipsychotics may influence heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac electrophysiological parameters. Previous studies have reported alterations in ECG parameters, including QT and corrected QT (QTc) interval prolongation, which may increase the risk of ventricular arrhythmias in susceptible individuals [ 10 – 14 ]. Therefore, careful assessment of ventricular repolarization parameters is essential, particularly in children receiving combined therapy. The present study was designed to investigate changes in ECG parameters and hemodynamic variables among patients with ADHD receiving MPH, RIS, or combination therapy. Methods This prospective observational cohort study was conducted in Qazvin, Iran, from October 2024 to January 2025 and included 150 children and adolescents aged 4–15 years diagnosed with ADHD. ADHD was diagnosed by a board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrist in accordance with the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) [ 15 ]. The diagnostic process was based on a comprehensive clinical evaluation, including interviews with the child and parents, review of the child’s developmental and medical history, and assessment of behavioral symptoms across different settings whenever possible. As this was an observational study conducted in routine clinical practice, standardized rating scales such as the Conners Rating Scale were not routinely used, and formal assessments of ADHD severity were not performed. In addition, ADHD presentations (predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, or combined) were not consistently documented and were therefore not included in the analysis. Only children and adolescents with a newly diagnosed with ADHD were included in the study. None of the participants had received previous pharmacological treatment for ADHD, and patients with comorbid psychiatric disorders were excluded to minimize potential confounding effects on the study outcomes. Participants were classified into three treatment groups (MPH ( n = 50), RIS ( n = 50) and MPH + RIS ( n = 50)). Patients in the methylphenidate group received immediate-release methylphenidate at an initial dose of 0.5 mg/kg/day. Patients in the risperidone group started treatment with 0.5 mg/day, which was the standard initial dose routinely used in our clinic during the study period. Participants in the combination group received both medications using the same initial dosing strategy. The initial doses were maintained throughout the three-month follow-up period. As the study was designed to evaluate the short-term cardiovascular effects of treatment, no dose adjustments were made during the study. Any clinically indicated dose modifications were considered only after completion of the three-month follow-up, in accordance with routine clinical practice. Although immediate-release methylphenidate is generally recommended for children aged 6 years and older, a small number of children younger than 6 years received this medication based on the clinical judgment of a board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrist. Treatment decisions were individualized following a comprehensive clinical assessment, taking into account symptom severity, functional impairment, and the expected benefits and potential risks of treatment. Sample size calculation: The sample size was calculated using G*Power software (version 3.1). Assuming a medium effect size (Cohen’s f = 0.25), a significance level of 0.05, and a statistical power of 80% for comparing three treatment groups, the required total sample size was estimated to be approximately 150 participants. Therefore, 150 patients were enrolled, with approximately 50 participants included in each treatment group. Participants Children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: (i) Iranian nationality, confirmed by official identification documents; (ii) age between 4 and 15 years; and (iii) clinical indication for treatment with MPH, RIS, or their combination, as determined by a board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrist according to standard clinical guidelines and recommended dosing regimens. Exclusion criteria included a history of congenital heart disease, patients with comorbid psychiatric disorders, baseline QTc prolongation or known cardiac arrhythmias, significant systemic illnesses, or concurrent use of medications with known cardiotoxic effects. These conditions were assessed through detailed medical history, clinical examination, review of medical records, and baseline ECG evaluation. Follow-up procedures Follow-up assessments for both monotherapy and combination therapy were conducted according to standard clinical practice guidelines for the management of ADHD in children and adolescents, including regular psychiatric evaluations and systematic monitoring of treatment response, adverse effects, and medication adherence [ 16 ]. Patients were routinely evaluated at baseline and at scheduled follow-up visits every 4 weeks during the study period. No participants were lost to follow-up during the study period, as all enrolled patients completed the scheduled clinical visits. In cases of missed appointments, patients were actively contacted by telephone, and follow-up visits were rescheduled within one week to ensure complete data collection. Data collection and measurements We performed a descriptive assessment of the demographic characteristics and cardiovascular parameters of the children and adolescents included in our study. Baseline information was collected for all participants, including age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). Cardiovascular monitoring consisted of ECG measurements, blood pressure recordings, and heart rate evaluation. A standard 12-lead ECG was performed for all participants at baseline and repeated three months after treatment initiation. All ECG recordings were obtained and interpreted by a board-certified pediatric cardiologist. QRS duration, PR interval, and corrected QT (QTc) interval were measured using standardized procedures, ensuring accuracy and consistency across all participants. The corrected QT interval (QTc) was calculated using Bazett’s formula (QTc = QT/√RR), with both QT and RR intervals measured in seconds. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure (BP) were measured at baseline and at the three-month follow-up using an automated pediatric sphygmomanometer. Measurements were performed according to standard pediatric protocols: participants were seated quietly for at least five minutes before measurement, and the appropriate cuff size was used. Three consecutive readings were obtained at each assessment point, and the average value was recorded. Heart rate was monitored simultaneously during each BP measurement. All measurements were conducted by trained clinical staff under the supervision of a pediatric cardiologist to ensure consistency and accuracy. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared (kg/m²) at baseline and at the three-month follow-up. Weight was measured using a calibrated digital pediatric scale, and height was measured with a stadiometer, both recorded to the nearest 0.1 kg and 0.1 cm, respectively. Measurements were performed in light clothing and without shoes, and each measurement was taken twice with the average value used for BMI calculation. Statistical analysis Data were entered, managed, and analyzed using SPSS version 26 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD), whereas categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages. Baseline demographic, anthropometric, and cardiovascular characteristics were compared among the three treatment groups using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for continuous variables and the chi-square (χ²) test for categorical variables. Between-group comparisons at the 3-month follow-up were performed using one-way ANOVA. Longitudinal changes in electrocardiographic and hemodynamic parameters were assessed using age- and weight-adjusted two-way repeated-measures analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with treatment group as the between-subject factor and time (baseline and 3-month follow-up) as the within-subject factor. The group × time interaction term was used to determine whether changes over time differed significantly among the treatment groups after adjustment for baseline age and weight. Effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared (ηp²). A two-sided P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results A total of 150 children and adolescents aged 4–15 years were included in the study, comprising 94 boys (62.7%) and 56 girls (37.3%). The mean BMI of the study population was 22.30 ± 1.90 kg/m².
